Slowly the wisdom, kept like a seed within the soul, begins to put forth tiny sprouts. And through many life experiences those sprouts are encouraged to grow. I love that image of the seed. Nothing in you is dead. The wisdom is only waiting for its season.

In many situations where there is ease within a life experience, he says, choices are not made, because in paradise the individual grows complacent and does not evaluate all things in the light of the original Thought. Inconsistency of motive causes an interruption in the vibratory pattern of growth. So the wilderness is not a failure of the plan. It is the plan working on the parts of you that comfort cannot reach.

He does not ask you to enjoy it. We do not ask you to truly rejoice in feelings of desolation, he says. And yet with enough determination, that wandering in the wilderness can one day herald what is described in your holy works as the voice of God crying in the wilderness to make straight the way of the Creator. When you are struggling to understand, the struggling may seem to go on interminably. But then, suddenly, the rocky places are made smooth. The mountains are made land. In your outer life it is possible nothing has happened to cause this breakthrough. It is your inner light that counts.

You cannot rechoose what is past. You can choose this moment at all times. To become totally conscious of the moment. To see love. To seek the Creator. These are inner things. They may never be brought into action on the dramatic plane. Some paths are dramatic, some are not. There is only one choice, my friends. The Creator is everywhere, within each choice.

The questions that night turn to frightening dreams, and Hatonn's counsel is the same wilderness logic. The voice you heard telling you to get out was the voice of your fear, he says. The answer to blackness is always light. If in your dream you had spoken and requested that your guides move you to the proper orientation, and if you had asked this in the name of the Creator, the obstacle would have been removed. There are no terrors of the deep that cannot be countered by constant repetition of that which is divine.

He closes with an image that belongs beside the seed. It is as though the creation were water, he says. What will you do? Will you simply be a sponge and soak up the creation and squeeze it out unchanged, untouched? Or will you accept the water as does the earth, filtering, giving minerals, giving taste to the water, the very essence of your creation, mixing so that life carves in you its channels and you give to life your essence? Do not fear to become intimate with life.

The wilderness is within you. Step forward fearlessly. Paradise is also within you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Three Companions
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the three companions.

It is a Monday in March, nineteen seventy-eight, and the first instrument struggles, so the contact moves to another. Hatonn wants to speak of what he calls understanding, and he begins with a distinction that sounds like a school lesson until you feel its weight. Consider your education in mathematics, he says. You are given a problem, and for that problem you must arrive at an answer. To know the answer is only a portion of solving the problem. You must understand the problem and the means by which to derive the answer. Knowledge and understanding are two separate factors which commune together.

So it is that man proceeds through his life, knowing many times the outcome of his actions, but not precisely understanding the intricate workings of his actions. With proper understanding, he says, man upon planet Earth could become the god on planet Earth. For indeed the difference between men and gods is understanding.

Then the definitions arrive, clean as stones in a row. Knowledge you have. It has been a portion of you always. Wisdom is the proper application of that knowledge. But understanding is the knowing when to apply that wisdom. Understanding is knowing how to arrive at the answer. Understanding is the most important ingredient in the overall spiritual growth of mankind. I love the plainness of it. Knowing is not enough. Knowing how to use what you know is wisdom. Knowing when is understanding.

He is honest about the distance. We of the Confederation have applied many of your years, more than you have ever imagined, to just gaining understanding of the universe. And we have yet to arrive at the point of total understanding. And we feel it to be true that we shall seek greater levels of understanding for eons to come. But as we have progressed in our understanding, we have seen our growth come more rapidly. The more you understand, the faster you grow, and the faster you grow, the more you understand.

Underneath the philosophy is physics, of a kind. All life within this universe is very simple, like that which you call mathematics. For all thought produces an energy wave, and an energy wave produces a certain action and a reaction. Each is able to be calculated if you have gained the understanding to monitor these thoughts. We of the Confederation know beforehand what our thoughts and actions will bring about. It is as with all things: practice is needed. Man upon planet Earth needs to begin to practice the monitoring of his thought-actions.

But man upon planet Earth presently proceeds to think improperly, he says, thus accumulating greater and greater degrees of misshapen conclusions to his thoughts and actions. And he continues to wonder why. But if man developed his understanding he would know why things are as they are. For he has created them and he, being the creator of his experiences, should accept upon himself the responsibility for those creations and begin to apply understanding.

And then the turn that makes this more than mental discipline. Understanding, my friends, is not only recognizing the functions and mechanisms of your thoughts and actions. Understanding is applying love. For in understanding your actions, you may determine whether they shed love to your fellow man, and if they do not, then we say that your actions are improper. That is the test. Not efficiency. Not correctness. Whether love was shed.

For whatever you do, it does indeed affect all mankind. Whether you see that effect or not, you have placed an energy into your atmosphere. An energy that will never die. An energy that will pass among many people and affect in some small way their own being. So you must care and love one another enough to gain the understanding so that you may create the environment that man upon planet Earth desires.

He is gentle about what they cannot do. We of the Confederation cannot do these things for any of you. We can only share our thoughts, hope that you accept them and apply them and work with them. And if they prove to be of no value to you we suggest that you refrain from using them. We are not a source of ultimate truth and shall never claim to be so. We are a source of limited truth and limited understanding, ever progressing, as is man upon planet Earth.

Later, through another instrument, Hatonn sums the whole evening into one sentence I want to leave you with. Understanding, my friends, is understanding of only one thing: the love of the Creator and creation. If, as you see through the eyes of your physical bodies, you do not see the Creator, you have not yet acquired understanding.

Seek it, therefore. To actively seek is to live. Those who do not seek are waiting. For what are they waiting? For the most part they are waiting for the physical death so that they may remember that they do not want to wait. You already know that you do not want to wait. You are eager for the adventure of understanding.

Knowledge you carry. Wisdom you practice. Understanding is knowing the hour. And the hour, according to Hatonn, is always the hour of love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Slums Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the slums within.

It is a Monday evening in March, nineteen seventy-eight, and the room is heavy with the news of the world. The questions circle the killings, the violence, the darkness of human against human. Hatonn does not flinch. And his first answer is a complete reframe of what a human being is. Imagine each human soul as a cell within a great organism, he says. What you do to one, you do to all. For each is part of the consciousness of the human race.

I want you to hold that image, because it changes what comes next. You would not cut your own arm off because it was diseased, he says. You would work very hard to help it to heal. You would find a medicine or a doctor or a counselor. In just this manner, you are all part of one being, and the diseases of that being are within your minds and the minds of all of the people of the planet. If you see others who are dark, do not condemn them, but realize they are in pain, and if you cut them out, it does no good. It only increases the pain of the whole organism.

Listen to how they put it. You have to reinstruct them, not cut them out. Even those of great darkness are needed by the whole. They cannot be cut out. They are needed to teach others what is not love, that others may make their choice. What, then, do you do with those who are not being loving? You love them. You give them love. Not as punishment. Not as correction. As medicine for the whole body.

Then Hatonn takes the teaching somewhere stranger and more beautiful. He asks them to consider consciousness as geography. Consciousness, he says, has an infinite geography. It is vast and wonderful, and there is great potential for travel. You can visit the mountains of consciousness or the valleys. You can travel to foreign places where the people are those you would call the entities of the higher planes. You can see the world from many different angles. The journey goes on, and on, and on. And the passport is love.

But most people, he says, live in only a small neighborhood of that vastness. They never leave the block they were born on. And what most needs your attention, he suggests, are the slums within your own consciousness. You have within your mind many places where the garbage has accumulated. You have within your mind many places where those who are poor in spirit live. And you must go to those places and bring them your love.

He is not speaking in metaphor only. He means the rooms of your own memory where you keep your shame. The streets of your inner life where the lights have gone out. You have these places too, my friends. We all do. And the instruction is not to demolish them, not to cut them out, but to go there, in meditation, in honesty, and bring them love. Reconstruct the slums of your consciousness with love, and the whole city of your mind begins to heal. The medicine for the whole body starts with one cell refusing to be dark.

Someone asks about a disturbing dream of death and killing, and Hatonn's answer ties the evening together. Yes, he says, you have experienced death in many incarnations. You have killed and been killed. But what matters is what you do with the knowledge of it. The memory of violence in the soul is itself one of those inner slums. Do not turn away from it. Bring it the light.

The evening's lesson is one sentence. You are cells in one body, and the body is hurting, and the only medicine any cell has to offer is love. Reconstruct your own slums first. Then, when you walk the streets of the outer world and see someone else's darkness, you will know what you are looking at. Not an enemy. Not a stranger. A neighbor in the same body, in pain, needing the same medicine you once needed.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Flame Through the Window
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the flame through the window.

It is a Monday in June, nineteen seventy-eight, and the evening belongs mostly to Hatonn, who speaks about preparation and service. He tells them that the time of preparation is not a waiting room but the work itself. Every day spent learning to love is a day of service already performed. You are not getting ready for the mission, he says. The getting ready is the mission. But near the end another voice comes through the channel, and it burns so brightly that the group will remember it for years. His name is Orkan. And he comes to talk about love as a flame.

I want you to hear how he begins, because it is the thesis of the whole passage. You are love. Not you should be love. Not you can learn love. You are love. I am love. The love we speak of is the living, breathing, throbbing, eternal, infinite, universal love that is the Creator. Do you understand? You are the Creator's love, breathing and walking and talking.

And then the image that gives this episode its name. You are a window, he says, through which the flame is seen. Think of it. The flame is not yours. It is the Creator's fire, burning behind you, within you, through you. Your job is not to generate it. Your job is to be transparent enough that it can be seen through you. The cleaner the glass, the clearer the flame.

But the world, Orkan says, will try to put its hands on the glass. There will be those who see the flame in you and want to own it, direct it, use it for their causes. He warns them plainly. Do not let them use your love. Do not let them make your transparency into their showcase. The flame is given to you for one purpose, and that purpose is service to others, freely given, with no expectation of return. The moment you begin to perform love, the window fogs. The moment you calculate what the flame will get you, the glass goes dark. And the saddest part, he says, is that the fogging happens so quietly you may not notice until the room has gone dim.

He speaks too of the temptation to hide the flame, to shutter the window when the world feels hostile. Do not, he says. A flame does not ask permission of the darkness. It simply burns, and the darkness, which has no substance of its own, retreats. Your only task when you are afraid is to keep the glass clean and let the fire do what fire does.

There is a hard part of the teaching too, and I do not want to skip it. He speaks of those who work against the light, and his counsel is not battle but refusal to be dimmed. You do not fight the darkness. You burn. That is all. That is everything. The darkness cannot argue with a flame. It can only flee from it or be consumed by it.

And the closing of his passage is pure poetry. We are the flame, he says. Not we carry the flame, not we serve the flame. We are the flame. I want you to sit with the difference. To carry something implies you could set it down. To be it means there is no distance between you and the burning. You do not go home from the flame at night. You go home as the flame.

Earlier in the evening Hatonn had spoken of preparation, of the long quiet work of becoming ready to serve. And now Orkan shows them what the readiness is for. All the meditation, all the discipline, all the seeking. It is window-cleaning. It is the slow work of making the glass of the self transparent enough that the Creator's fire can shine through without distortion. Every act of forgiveness is a wiped pane. Every act of kindness is the glass made clearer.

So the question for tonight is not whether you are loving enough. The question is whether you are transparent enough. Where is the glass fogged? Where have you let the world's hands smudge the window? And what would it take, today, to wipe one pane clean?

You are the window. The flame is already burning behind you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Voice in the Rubble
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the voice in the rubble.

It is a Monday in July, nineteen seventy-eight, and the evening is heavy with mortality. People are dying, the planet is groaning, and the questions keep circling back to the same fear. Hatonn's answer is not comfort in the ordinary sense. It is a complete picture of what is happening, and it begins with the planet itself. Your planet is dying, he says, and it is also being born. You are living in the time of the ending of one age and the beginning of another, and the birth pangs are real.

And he asks them to look at the human body the way he looks at it. You are, each of you, living in what he calls an underground prison. The body is a small dark room, and the soul is locked inside it, cut off from the light of the larger reality. Meditation is the key that opens the door. Not once, but daily. Each time you meditate, you step out of the cell and into the sunlight of who you actually are.

Someone asks the question that every seeker eventually asks. What is the purpose of the soul? And Hatonn answers with the simplicity that runs through everything. To love, and to share that love. That is the whole of it. Not to achieve. Not to acquire. To love, and to share that love. Everything else is the prison talking.

He speaks, too, of the ones being born into this hinge of history. The children coming in now, he says, are not like the generations before them. They carry a different vibration, a readiness for the new age that the old structures cannot hold. Do not try to force them into the molds of the dying world. Let them be what they are. They are the first citizens of the world that is being born beneath the rubble.

And when the questions turn to fear, his counsel is steady. You will feel the planet shake, he says, and you will be tempted to shake with it. Do not. The one who meditates daily, who keeps the key turning in the lock, will move through the birth pangs the way a mother moves through labor. With pain, yes. But with purpose. And with the certain knowledge that something is being born.

Then a harder question. What do you do when someone close to you seems to be on the wrong path? How do you help without judging? Hatonn's answer is one of the most practical pieces of advice in the whole archive. Do not be judgmental of others, he says. You do not know the path that another soul has chosen. You do not know what lessons they have come to learn. What looks like failure from the outside may be exactly the experience their soul requires. Your job is not to correct them. Your job is to love them, and to share that love, and to let the sharing do the teaching.

I love how this ties back to the prison. The moment you judge another person, you have locked yourself back in your cell. Judgment is the soul closing its own door from the inside. Discernment is different. Discernment sees clearly and chooses love anyway. You can see that someone is suffering, you can see that they are lost, and you can still refuse to make their lostness into your prison.

Laitos comes through later in the evening with a meditation that is itself a key turning in a lock. He asks them to feel the love moving through the circle, from person to person, until the whole room is one breathing organism of light. The prison has walls, he seems to say, but the walls are only as real as your attention makes them. Move your attention to the love, and the walls go thin.

And then the image that names this episode. Hatonn speaks of those who have died, and of the voices that remain. The rubble of the old world is everywhere, he says, but listen. Beneath the rubble there is a voice, and the voice is saying: love. The planet is dying and being born at the same time, and the voice in the rubble is the newborn world, already speaking.

You are not the prison. You are not the rubble. You are the voice. And the voice says only one word.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Unworn Side
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the unworn side.

It is a Wednesday in July, nineteen seventy-eight, two days after the previous session, and Hatonn opens with an image so ordinary it takes a moment to feel its weight. Think of a carpet, he says. The top side is worn thin by years of feet, faded by sunlight, stained by everything life has spilled on it. But turn it over. The underside is pristine. The colors are as vivid as the day it was woven. The pattern is perfect. Nobody ever walked on it.

That, he says, is you. The worn side is the personality, the daily self, scuffed by experience. The unworn side is the soul, untouched by everything you have been through. No matter how threadbare the top looks, the underside has never been touched. You have never been damaged. Not really. Not where it counts.

The questions that night are about death and what continues, and Hatonn's answers keep returning to the carpet. The people you have loved and lost have not gone anywhere, he says. They have simply turned over. You are looking at the worn side of the universe and grieving, but the other side is pristine, and they are there, whole, vivid, walking on the colors you cannot see from here.

He speaks of the inner planes, the levels of reality that interpenetrate your own, where those who have died continue their growth. Contact with them is not only possible but natural, he says. It is not a violation of anything. It is family members in different rooms of the same house, calling through the walls. The walls are thin for those who listen in meditation. And the listening itself is a kind of turning over, a practice of seeing the pristine side while you still walk the worn one.

Someone asks whether the dead can see us, whether they know our grief, and Hatonn's answer is tender. They see the unworn side of you, he says. They do not see the stains. They see the pattern as it was woven. So when you grieve, know that the one you grieve for is not grieving. They are standing in the vivid colors, waiting for you to remember that you are woven of the same thread.

And then the sea anemone. I want you to picture it, because Hatonn wants you to picture it. A sea anemone on the ocean floor, rooted to its rock, its tentacles waving in the current. It does not chase its food. It does not strive or plan or worry. It is rooted in love, and what it needs comes to it on the current. That is the posture of the soul that understands, he says. Rooted, open, receiving. Not grasping. Not running. Rooted in love, with its arms open to the current of the Creator.

I love that line. Rooted in love. Not climbing toward love, not earning love, not performing for love. Rooted in it, the way the anemone is rooted in the rock. The rock does not move. The love does not move. You move, your tentacles wave, your life happens, but the rooting is permanent. And here is the part the world forgets. The anemone does not apologize for receiving. It does not earn the current. It opens, and the ocean does the rest. Your work is the opening. The current is the Creator's business.

Hatonn closes the evening by returning to the carpet, and I want to leave you there. Some night this week, he seems to say, sit quietly and turn yourself over. Picture the worn side, all the scuffs and stains of the years, and then picture the other side. Vivid. Perfect. Untouched. That is not a metaphor for who you might become. That is who you are, right now, underneath the wear.

The evening's teaching comes down to this. You are double-sided. One side shows the wear of the world. The other side has never been touched, and never will be. When you meditate, you are turning yourself over. When you love, you are showing the unworn side to the world. And when you grieve, grieve the worn side if you must, but know that the person you miss is standing on the pristine colors, whole.

Turn over. The pattern is perfect. It always was.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Laughter of the Confederation
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the laughter of the Confederation.

It is a Wednesday in August, nineteen seventy-eight, and Hatonn is in a strange and wonderful mood. The evening's teaching is about desire, about good and evil, about the shape of the future. And threaded through all of it is something you do not expect from cosmic messengers. Humor. Delight. A confession that I want to read you in their own words, because it reframes everything you think you know about advanced beings.

We prefer laughter to power, he says. Sit with that. The entities who could cross the galaxy, who speak of densities and harvests and the architecture of the universe, are telling a small room in Kentucky that given the choice between laughter and power, they choose laughter. Power is a property of the illusion, he implies. Laughter is a property of the Creator.

The teaching on desire is the spine of the evening. Your desire shapes your future, Hatonn says. What you want, deeply and persistently, is the mold into which your experience pours itself. This is not positive thinking. This is mechanics. Desire is the steering wheel of the soul, and most people drive with their eyes closed, wanting vaguely, fearing specifically, and then wondering why the road keeps bending toward the fear.

So his counsel is two words that I want you to carry. Desire carefully. Not desire less. Not desire nothing, not kill the wanting. Desire carefully. Choose your wantings the way you would choose seeds for a garden you will have to live in. Because you will. The future is the harvest of the desires you are planting tonight. And notice what this implies. You are not a victim of the future. You are its gardener. The fears you rehearse are seeds too. The resentments you water are seeds too. Choose.

He gives them a practice for it, simple as breath. In your meditation, he says, look at what you want. Really look. Hold each desire up to the light and ask it one question. Does this move me toward the source, or away? The desires that move you toward, keep them, feed them, let them grow. The desires that move you away, do not fight them. Just stop watering them. Attention is water. Withdraw it gently, and the weeds of the soul wither on their own.

Then he takes on good and evil, and his definition cuts through centuries of theology like a clean knife. Good and evil, he says, are not two armies. They are two directions. Good is motion toward the source. Evil is motion away from the source. That is all. Every act, every thought, every desire either moves you closer to the Creator or further away. There is no third direction. There is only toward and away.

I love the mercy hidden in that definition. If evil is not a substance but a direction, then no one is evil the way a stone is hard. Anyone moving away can turn. Every moment contains the possibility of reversal. The compass never breaks. You can always choose toward.

And the unity teaching underneath it all. You are all one being, he reminds them, and the laughter and the desire and the direction are all properties of that one being discovering itself. When you desire carefully, you are not just gardening your own future. You are gardening the future of the whole. When you choose toward, the whole moves a fraction closer to the source.

Someone asks about the darkness in the world, the very real evil that seems to be winning, and Hatonn does not deny it. He only points at the compass. The ones who move away from the source will find, he says, that the distance itself becomes the teaching. Separation is its own punishment and its own cure. You do not need to defeat them. You need to keep choosing toward, desire carefully, and let the geometry of the universe do what geometry does.

I keep coming back to the laughter. A Confederation that prefers laughter to power is not afraid of the dark. It finds the dark faintly comic, the way an adult finds a child's monster-under-the-bed faintly comic. Not cruel. Just unafraid. And the invitation is to become unafraid in the same way. To laugh, to desire carefully, to keep walking toward the source, and to trust that the universe is, at bottom, a comedy with a happy ending.

Desire carefully. Walk toward. And laugh when you can.

Thank you for listening.

title: All Places, One Place
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: all places, one place.

It is a Monday in August, nineteen seventy-eight, the last session in this batch of the archive, and Hatonn seems to know it. The evening has the feeling of a summary, a gathering up of everything the two hundred sessions have been saying. His subject is place. Distance. The strange fact that every somewhere you have ever longed for is already here.

All distant places exist within you, he says. Every landscape you have dreamed of, every holy city, every mountain of the spirit, every star you have wished upon. They are not out there at the end of a journey. They are in here, at the end of attention. The journey was never across space. It was always into depth.

I want you to feel how radical that is. The seeker spends lifetimes planning pilgrimages, saving for journeys, imagining that the sacred is located somewhere else. And Hatonn says the geography is inverted. All places are one place, and the one place is the interior of your own consciousness. You do not need to go anywhere. You need to go in. The farthest country you will ever visit is the country behind your own eyes.

He is not dismissing travel, or beauty, or the longing for the distant. He is locating them. The longing for the far place is real, he says, but it is misaddressed. You are homesick for the interior. Every outer journey that ever changed a person did so because something in the outer landscape opened a room in the inner one. The mountain did not give you the vision. The mountain reminded you that you had it.

The teaching on the self follows, and it is the deepest water of the evening. The self you think you are, he says, the name, the history, the personality with its preferences and wounds, is a small room in a vast house. Unity is not the annihilation of the room. It is the discovery of the house. Dissolution of self does not mean you disappear. It means the walls become transparent, and you discover that your room was always open to every other room, and that the whole house is one dwelling.

And at the heart of the house, in the room behind every room, is love. Love, he says, is the heart of all education. Not a subject among subjects. The heart. Everything the soul learns, in every density, on every planet, through every joy and every wilderness, is curriculum in a single school, and the school's only lesson is love. The mathematics, the philosophy, the science of the Confederation, all of it is commentary on one text. Learn the text and the commentary takes care of itself.

Someone asks how to hold all of this while living an ordinary life, going to work, paying bills, dealing with difficult people. And Hatonn's answer is the whole archive in miniature. You do not need to leave the ordinary life. The ordinary life is the classroom. The difficult person is the lesson. The bill, the commute, the sink full of dishes, these are not interruptions of the spiritual path. They are the path, wearing work clothes.

All places are one place. The sacred mountain and the kitchen sink are the same address. The distant star and the difficult coworker are the same teacher. There is nowhere to go and nothing to escape, because there is only here, and here is infinite. And the one who knows this does not stop traveling. He travels the way the anemone travels, rooted and open, letting the current bring the world to him.

Two hundred sessions. And it comes down to this. Go in, not out. Let the walls go transparent. Study love, because it is the only subject. And know that every place you have ever wanted to reach was inside you all along, waiting for you to arrive.

You have already arrived. You just haven't looked around yet. And when you do, you will find that the room you are standing in contains every room, and the place you are contains every place, and the love you have been seeking was the floor beneath your feet the whole time.

Thank you for listening.

title: Every Moment a Miracle
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: every moment a miracle.

On September fourth, nineteen seventy-eight, in a Monday meditation, Hatonn and Laitos come through, and the evening turns on a single honest question from the group. Can you give me a sign, the questioner asks, so I know this is not just my own mind talking to itself? The answer Hatonn gives is not the one the questioner expected. It is better.

But first he lays down the foundation, the simple truth he calls the highest he knows. We are all one. The universe has been made up of one substance, he says, and that substance is love. You, sitting wherever you are sitting tonight, are one being with him, with each other, and with this whole beautiful planet. It is difficult to see, he admits, because you dwell in a dense illusion where energy seems to be mass, where emotions are masked so habitually that people speak falsely, and the falseness is believed as truth, and the separation goes on and on.

I love how plainly he names the political part of it. Those you choose to lead you, he says, do not lead. And by choosing them you have given up the feeling of responsibility for yourself, the confidence that you can stand a beautiful and perfect soul upon your own two feet and do the very best you can in clear conscience, whatever the outcome. The answers, he says, lie not in outward reforms but in the inner reform of each person, the kind that restores self respect and reliance and the ability to act on what you believe.

And then comes the paradox I keep returning to. Yes, we are all one. But each soul, he says, is a kingdom unto himself, a regal and imperial entity, unique and completely necessary to the creation. Without one of you, the creation would be incomplete. We cannot lose anyone. So the one truth and the many truths live together, and each of you stands at a unique place on the journey. When you make contact with your deepest purpose, he says, you will find that your deepest purpose is to seek the truth.

Which brings us back to the question about signs. How do you know any of this is real? Hatonn answers with what might be my favorite sentence in the whole session. We do not believe in faith, he says, and then he pauses for the pun, we have no faith in belief. What they offer, he says, is already known to you on a deep level. The signs and wonders are locked within yourself.

Listen to how he puts it. Do not let signs and wonders sway you, he says, for signs and wonders may be explained away, and faith may be broken by their absence. Seek the truth instead, and you will find that each moment is miraculous. The real sign, he says, is not a sighting or a healing or a bent spoon. The real sign is the power of one person to walk in another person's shoes. The power of love to reach and touch when those you call your enemies are attempting to build walls. If you can only love one another, my friends, he says, that would be the greatest miracle of all.

And the truth, he says, is subjective. You can never share it with another in the fullness of your inner understanding. You can only love. That is the whole of it. That is the miracle.

Near the end he shares their understanding of the beginning of all things, and it is worth hearing slowly. The Creator, he says, when there was a desire for self realization, took energy, which we now call love, and with this infinite energy created all that there is. Each of us was created to lend a realizing consciousness to the Creator. Whenever you realize that great force of love in your dealings with others, he says, you have given love to the Creator, for the Creator is in all that you see.

And here is the part that reframes every hard day. Each seeming difficulty, he says, is a quiz, a test, perhaps even the equivalent of a midterm. What you are is being brought to the catalyst of a situation in which you must discover the best way of showing love. Many of your people have been taught wrong information as basic as that two plus two is five, and they have absorbed it into their being. Your lesson, he says, is to find the harmony, to find that two plus two is four, and let that right understanding illuminate the situation and heal what can be healed. In healing yourself, in truth you heal the universe.

I want to close with the sentence Hatonn offers at the end of the night, because it frames everything about how to hear these voices. Listen to our words, he says, not as if we were wise, for we are not. Not as if we were perfect, for we are not. But as if we were your brothers and sisters. For this we are.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Larger Shell
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the larger shell.

On September eleventh, nineteen seventy-eight, in a Monday meditation, Hatonn offers an image so simple it carries the whole evening. A sea creature, he says, outgrows its shell and makes a larger one. And then a larger one again, in a beautiful and unending spiral, until one day it has no need of any shell at all, and the empty shells are left behind, having served their purpose.

That creature, of course, is you. Hatonn speaks of two stages in the development of your mental vehicle. In the first, the important thing is to know that in each situation there is freedom, that you are not iron bound by restrictions from the outside. And to build that awareness, you construct for yourself a larger mental shell, a larger home in which to grow. Each time a situation strikes you as limiting or difficult, he says, it is time for inner work, time to explore and discover the larger, more spacious mental atmosphere that your balance requires.

I love the gentleness of this teaching. He is not telling you to break the shell. He is telling you to outgrow it. And one day, he says, you will find you do not need the shell at all. In the vulnerable body of consciousness you may swim out into the waters of the universe and merge with all that there is. In that moment you will have discovered that there is no need for any vehicle whatsoever, for all things are one, and as your home is the universe, no protection is necessary.

He is honest that this second stage is, for most, a distant goal. But he wants you to know it exists, because knowing it changes how you live the first. Meanwhile, he says, enlarge your shell through meditation. Let contemplation open you within. For the world without only seems to press in upon you. In reality it is pressing upon itself, and you are free.

The question period that follows turns toward the body itself, toward the tiny coded blueprint that builds your physical vehicle. A questioner asks about the new science of that blueprint, and Hatonn's answer reframes the whole subject. The blueprint builds the vehicle, he says. The drives of hunger and reproduction and breath are blueprinted. But that which makes a being a being is not blueprint oriented. It lives in the eternal nature of the spirit, which inhabits the vehicle for the time it remains viable.

And here is a distinction I find clarifying. There are laws of cause and effect, he says, and then there is the genetic structure of the physical vehicle, and they are not the same thing. A soul does not build a body with an imbalance. A soul chooses a vehicle that already has it, because that vehicle suits the lessons the soul came to learn. The soul chooses the vehicle which best suits it. Listen to how quiet and unblaming that sentence is. No punishment. Only choice.

The same quiet runs through his answer to the evening's hardest question, about whether ending one's own life could ever be a kindness. Hatonn does not flinch and does not preach. Your life, he says, follows a natural rhythm and an ongoing purpose. To cut it short before its natural end is to stop that rhythm in an arbitrary manner, and more often than not the lessons the soul hoped to learn had not yet been learned. You are not given, he says, those things which you cannot bear. And so he asks only this: proceed with the rhythm of your existence, see the many lessons about you, and let the realization of love flow into you.

He closes the evening the way he always does, with a sentence that sounds like weather. Know that the love of the Father flows throughout the cosmos on the winds of all of the universe to you, through you, from you.

Thank you for listening.

title: Always Summer
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: always summer.

On October ninth, nineteen seventy-eight, in a Monday meditation, Latwii arrives with a specialty. Each of the voices, they explain, has its own bent, and theirs is meditation. What follows is one of the loveliest guided images in the archive, and I want to give it room to breathe.

In the busy hurry of your everyday life, Latwii asks, when do you have time to realize who you are? And if you do think about who you are, are you not judging yourself, asking yourself to be better, berating yourself for your failures? This is not what they bring, they say. They bring only the love of the Creator, which pours to you like the sun pours its warmth upon your planet.

And then the image. You humans, they say, have built walls between yourselves and love, so that you experience the winter, and you grow cold in your heart. But there is a place within you, they say, in which it is always summer. It is high upon a hill, and to this hill you must climb. Step by step, walk up an inner hill in silence, leaving behind that part of yourself that feels the tiredness and the toil of your everyday life. Cleanse yourself in the waters of the pond by the hill. Dress yourself in clean white garments and proceed upward.

Listen to what waits at the top. Sit in the meadow, they say, and listen to the birds sing, and smell the sweet smell of the flowers, and feel the warmth of the sun. This, my friends, is the Creator's love. It is infinite. It is omnipresent. It is closer to you than your own breathing and your own thoughts.

I keep coming back to the tenderness of their instruction: gently, they say, very gently remove your senses from the world around you. Not by force. Not by discipline that bruises. By gentleness. The place on the hill is already there. You are not building it. You are climbing to it.

Hatonn follows with a short story, and it belongs to the same evening's teaching the way a shadow belongs to a tree. A seed, he says, grew deep in the darkness of the soil, responding to its nature, and put forth one leaf, and then two, and then three, and then four, and then many, all in good time. At a certain moment its fruit was plucked and eaten, that which was useful, by the standard of the one who planted the seed.

And then he asks you to remember something, and this is the part I want you to carry out of tonight. You may see tension in your own life as you put forth your leaves, he says, for the seed knows not when the fruit may come. It knows only that the process must go on. Have faith in your mission, whatever it may be. Grow, he says, not judging your leaves because they are not fruits, but being in a state of complete joy that you are going forward, that you are producing your leaves, that you are alive.

There are many fruits, he says, that have been planted by the Creator, and they will all be true and found to be good in their own time. This time is not a time that you can tell. This goodness is not a goodness that you can tell. So the teaching of the evening folds into one motion: climb the hill to the place that is always summer, and then be the seed, putting forth leaves in the dark soil, trusting the fruit you cannot yet see.

Thank you for listening.

title: Declare Your Independence
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: declare your independence.

On October eighteenth, nineteen seventy-eight, in a Wednesday meditation, Hatonn asks the group for something larger than attention. He asks them to declare their independence from the world of man. And then he spends the evening explaining exactly what that means, and what it does not.

It does not mean running away. It does not mean physical reclusiveness or withdrawal from the activities of the world. It means, he says, committing yourself to understanding the lessons of the creation, those things that are true and all about you, those things included in seed and flower, in sunshine, in harvest, and in the infinite and totally balanced cycles of your natural world.

Listen to the contrast he draws, because it is the heart of the evening. There are two creations, he says: that of the Creator, and that of the sons of the Creator. Look at your planet, he says. It is more beautiful than most planets of your density in your entire galaxy. The wildlife, the trees, the things that swim and fly, each acts in service and love and balance, expressing that instinct which is love. And you, who were given freedom instead of instinct, have gone and created a world which does not, in any great extent, express the love that is the essence of the Creator. Misunderstanding piled upon misunderstanding, he says, and the walls that separate you seem incredibly permanent.

But they are not. That is the independence he is talking about. You can commit, in the middle of your ordinary life, to the lessons of seed and flower and sunshine. You can ask, of the two creations, which expresses love, and then ask how that love can be translated into the creation of man. There are no walls so high, he says, that love cannot express itself through. There are no doors that cannot be opened with love.

He takes up the saying of the master known as Jesus, I and my Father are one, and asks the question the way a friend would. Who is I? Is it a man known to you as Jesus? Or did he mean that all of us and the Father are one? There are no walls between us, Hatonn says. I need only open that inner door of consciousness and listen, and in the silence that still small voice may speak. What it speaks may not be words at all, only a sense of wholeness, of harmony, of balance, of that simple thing which we call love.

The questions that night turn to karma, and Hatonn gives one of the clearest explanations in the archive. Karma, he says, is greatly misunderstood. Primarily it touches your choices around relationships with others. But the day to day incidents of your life are not karma, he says. They are a kind of random pattern that gives you a path in each situation, each day. You have your choices to make, and they have not to do with karma but with love.

And when the difficult problems are indeed karmic, when they come from a relationship unbalanced in a previous time, he gives the whole remedy in one word. Forgive. To forgive completely is to remove karma from the situation. To love completely is to be free. If you find a situation especially difficult, he says, come out of your meditation with the question, how does this situation look now in the light of meditation? And then search it, objectively and carefully, for the lesson you are to learn.

I should mention, because it is part of the night, that the group also asked about the great earth changes, the earthquakes feared on the western coast, and Hatonn told them something startling: that groups meditating in love had already alleviated several series of earthquakes, so that smaller quakes happened in quick succession instead of one great destroying one. He does not ask them to pray for any one place. He asks only that each of them concentrate on being a loving person and send love to the planet as a whole.

And so the independence he asks for is not an escape from the world. It is the opposite. It is becoming a focus of love inside the world, so that the world of man can begin, day by day, to look a little more like the world of the Creator.

Thank you for listening.

title: As You Are, So Is the World
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: as you are, so is the world.

On January twenty-ninth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Monday meditation, Latwii stands in for Hatonn, who is on mission elsewhere, and delivers an evening that moves from the fate of the planet down to the quiet of a single meditator, and shows them to be the same thing.

Here is the sentence the whole night turns on. Work inwardly for peace in yourself, Latwii says, for as you are, so is the world. Each of you upon your planet is the world. In a way, a vote is taken at every instant, and the amount of peace within each heart is the peace of the earth. It has never been more important, they say, for you to be at peace within yourself, or to realize that you are responsible for mankind.

I want to stay with that for a moment, because it is both the heaviest and the most hopeful claim in the session. Not your votes, not your protests, not your arguments about who is right. The peace in your heart, added to the peace in every other heart, at this instant, is the peace of the planet. Your world is angry, they say, and in some places people have decided that God is on one side or another of their quarrels. God, they say, is on the side of peace, of forgiveness, and of brotherhood.

And then Latwii does something I did not expect. They take up the phrase love and light, the words that flow so easily from the channel's lips that she sometimes doubts she is really receiving, and they ask what the words actually mean. First there was consciousness, they say, which was the Creator, and this consciousness had a will, which manifested as the Word, and this Word is love. And as will imposed itself upon that which was around it, it formed that which was around it into a basic material called light.

Listen to this image, because it is beautiful. You may think of love as being heat, they say, random consciousness, everywhere without end and without beginning, without direction, but constantly in motion. When love takes form, it gains a direction, a rotation, and becomes light. Of love has been created light. And you, they say, are made of that one substance, in more and more sophisticated arrangements of energy. You are all light.

The meditation teaching that follows is practical and kind. Disturbances, of whatever kind, are meaningless, they say. The greatest ally you can have as a meditator is patience. You will fail each time, by your own judgment, to reach a perfect state of meditation. But you do not need to judge yourself. You need only attempt to seek the truth. It is in the attempt that the process takes place.

And then, in a passage I love, they invite you to picture yourself as you meditate as a nature spirit, one with the world, dressed as are the flowers or the trees in bark of leaves, laughing or dancing, resting in the motherhood of the planet which is Earth, reaching out for the fatherhood which is wisdom. You are in balance, they say. You are male and female. You are all that there is. You are all opposites. And in that knowing may come rest, and in that rest you may seek the truth.

The night's question on healing brings the teaching home. A questioner asks about the power to heal, and Latwii answers that healing is not created by any channel but by the Creator. The mold, they say, is perfect. The product of the mold can only become distorted by pressures that came to bear after it was taken from the mold. Sometimes an entity requests a limitation so that it may learn certain things. Sometimes healing is a matter of a very simple adjustment to thought. Each case is individual, and there is no case that is hopeless.

And then the sentence that lands like a bell. You yourself, my brother, are not D. You are light. You are love. And within you is a power so great that it contains all that there is. Find it and use it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Holy Joy
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: holy joy.

On February thirteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Tuesday meditation, Latwii answers a question about healing and ends up dismantling one of the heaviest ideas in spiritual life: the idea that learning a lesson has to take time.

The question is about a new science of healing, and Latwii is generous toward it. To speak of barking up the wrong tree is impossible, they say, when there are a forest of correct trees. A million ways exist to approach the problem of restoring the perfection of the original idea of an entity. But then they add the sentence that reframes everything. People upon your planet consider that it takes time to learn the lesson. It does not take time, they say. It takes a focusing of the will.

I keep turning that over. Not time. Focus. Will. And this, they say, must be done completely and freely before any new programming is attempted. The one thing that cannot be done is to reprogram before the lesson has been learned. It can be accomplished in no time, in a small amount of time, or in what you would call a lifetime. The difference is not the clock. It is the completeness of the will.

Latwii then speaks, with great tenderness, about the channel herself, and what they say changes how I hear every limitation I have ever complained about. This particular entity, they say, has been learning a lesson and offering lessons to others through what seems to be a physical distortion of the perfection of her nature. Her nature is so adventurous and enthusiastic, they say, that she programmed herself before this incarnation with a method whereby her activities would be limited, so that she could reach the goal of sharing with others what she knows, which she could not have concentrated upon had she been, as they put it, working full time. She has now become a being with very little of the lesson to learn. Therefore, they say, it is quite possible that a healing will take place.

Read that again slowly. The limitation was chosen. Not as punishment. As focus. A way to keep an adventurous, enthusiastic soul from scattering itself across a full and busy life, so that it would sit still long enough to write, and to be. I find that strangely comforting, and I offer it to you the same way they offered it: as a possibility, not a doctrine.

And then the evening turns, delightfully, to humor. One of the great graces of the one known as Timothy Leary, Latwii says, is a sense of humor, which we find absolutely essential for the progression of the soul. We find so often in your culture that seriousness is equated with holiness, and we say to you that this is, indeed, not so. There is, they say, a holy joy which should be connected with constant and unremitting discipline, to achieve the perfect balance between joy and the carrying of what you know as the cross.

Listen to how they put the balance. It is said in your holy works, Peace I bring to you, my peace I give to you, not as the world gives to you. It must be remembered, they say, that joy and the cross walk hand in hand. It is not an easy path, but it is a very joyful path, and approached with a sense of humor, each lesson can be reduced to no time instead of a small time, to a small time instead of a great time, to a great time instead of a lifetime, and so on. And thus, they say, you may consciously take charge of your life and goal.

So the teaching of the night is really one teaching with two faces. The lesson does not require time, only the full focusing of the will. And the will does its work best not in grim seriousness but in holy joy, in laughter at your own stumbling, in the peace that is given, not as the world gives. However long your own lesson is taking tonight, however many times you have circled it, Latwii's message is that the door was never locked by the clock. It opens the moment the will is whole, and joy, of all things, is the key that turns it fastest.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Rose at Dawn
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the rose at dawn.

On February eighteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Latwii opens with a statement of their whole philosophy in two sentences. The law of the Creator is one, they say. The understanding of that law is all wisdom and truth, and the best word for that law is love.

And then, with their characteristic humor, they add that from their point of view all of our questions are a little bit funny. Not mockingly. The way a parent finds it funny when a child asks, with total seriousness, whether the moon follows the car on purpose. We wish you to realize, they say, more than all else, that questions and answers are meaningless. Feelings and emotions are meaningless. All of the tools with which you are familiar are not helpful outside your locality. You have one useful attribute, and that is the quality of your love. Have you loved today?

The heart of the evening is a long exchange about the intellect, and it contains a parable I have never forgotten. A questioner has been reading deeply, chasing ideas about the mind and consciousness, and Latwii gently suggests that the intellect may be getting in the way. The key in all things, they say, is balance. Your intellect is a tool. But your intellect cannot synthesize information. It can only analyze. The activity of intuition must be sought within a different type of mental activity, below the conscious level.

And here is the parable. In one case, they say, a person reads that there is nothing so beautiful as a rose. He sees a picture of a rose, goes to the store, purchases such a blossom, puts it in his vase, and observes it, having been told that this is a beautiful blossom. This is programming from outside.

There is, however, another way of observing this same flower, and listen to how they describe it, because the description is the teaching. When one sees a rose at dawn on a spring day, with the dew still hanging from the tiny petals, with a bee still fluttering about it making honey, and the miracle and the wonder of this rose sink deep into your own understanding, and it is yours. It has come from inside.

The questioner pushes back, reasonably. Is the result not the same? Is it not understanding either way? And Latwii answers with the sentence I want you to keep. The difference, they say, is in the level of awareness to which that love has reached. On the one hand, it has touched that within you which will survive, that within you which is free from time and space. In the other, it has simply become something that you have experienced.

They are careful not to be down on all intellectual knowledge, and I appreciate the fairness of it. Without some intellectual knowledge, they say, the greatest of intuitions could not be shared with your fellow man. Therefore, always the balance. We are simply, they say, stacking the odds against ourselves by reading faster than we meditate.

The evening also gives one of the most practical exercises in the archive. A questioner longs for deeper connection with other people, one to one, and Latwii suggests this: gently place yourself face to face with another person and look at them for a period of time. Most of your beings cannot do this, they say, for it reveals too much of their true identity. However, there is a very loving link between those who can gaze upon each other for a period of time. Those of your planet, they add, have very poorly tuned receivers. They are not too bad at sending, but they are terrible at receiving. To encourage yourself in receiving, become very relaxed, very receptive, and very trusting. The gazing of eyes, they say, is a good exercise in receiving.

So the night's teaching folds together. Balance the intellect with the silence beneath it. Let the rose come from inside, not from the store. And when you want to know another person, do not analyze them. Look at them, quietly, for a while, and receive. Our words, Latwii says near the end, are nothing compared to your own efforts of meditation and understanding of the existence that is about you. You see, my brother, they add, we are not crazy about words.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Jewel in the Lotus
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the jewel in the lotus.

On March fourth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Latwii gives an evening about simplicity, and they begin with an image from the temple in the holy book. Imagine the money changers, they say, the noise of the trading and the bleating, the chirping of the sacrificial birds, the clinking of coins passing from hand to hand, the confused penitence of those who came seeking to find in themselves something they had lost. Something from which they were separated. Seeking to find love, and wholeness, in the knowledge that they were one with the Creator who loved them.

And we, they say, are not so different. As they look upon the peoples of this planet, they see us multiplying the details of our lives the same way. So many details between us and the one simple thing.

Then the image that gives tonight its name. Imagine, they say, the jewel inside the many petals of the lotus. How tightly are the petals closed about the jewel of love within you? How much do you have to peel away from your life before you come to the singular and single essence of truth that is all about you? Love is everywhere, they say. It sings in the wind. It sings in the trees. In the season now approaching, it will sing in the burgeoning greenery and blossoming beauty of your natural world.

And here is the practice they ask for, stated with a bluntness I love. Throw the details from your life at least once a day, they say. Remove the petals from the lotus, charming as they may be and as delightful as they may smell. Find the holy ground. Find the jewel, that which is love. Upon this ground you can stand without fear of falling, losing your footing, or being cast away from your place, for this is your birthright. Love is what you are. What you think you are, if you think you are not love, is an illusion, a mass of distorted detail that can be slowly weeded, or quickly weeded, from your life, as you would weed a garden, by the process of meditation.

I want to pause on that phrase, your birthright, because it changes the whole feeling of the spiritual path. You are not earning the jewel. You are not traveling toward it. You are removing what covers it. The jewel is already yours. The work is subtraction, not addition.

The evening also turns to a tender subject: our worry about other people, the ones we love who seem lost or stuck. Latwii asks us to remember that each person has a pattern for their life, freely chosen, and that in many cases the pattern has not been revealed to the person, either for lack of meditation or because it must stay hidden for a lesson to be learned. If you are concerned for another, they say, feel at one with the person, feel at one with love and light, and allow that unity to flow. Within the illusion you call physical life, you cannot tell what is good and what is bad, for often what seems to be a difficulty is in fact a prelude to a great learning and a great happiness. Therefore, they say, trust in the pattern of each unique being.

There is a lighter moment I want to include, because it shows who Latwii are. A questioner asks whether the little folk of legend, gnomes and such, are real, and Latwii answers with an analogy from the channel's own living room. Think of the television, they say. You hear one channel from the set in the next room, while other channels are being broadcast that this set is not picking up. With the turn of a dial it would pick up another channel, and you would see a different universe. The dimensions directly involved with your earthly plane, they say, are invisible to you in the same way, and they give the sphere you call your planet its life. Elves, gnomes, fairies, devas, spirits of all kinds are the elemental forms which govern the growth, the health, and the life of rocks, flowers, trees, grasses, and animal life. If you would improve your plant and animal and mineral life, they say, make contact in love with those things you know to be there but cannot see, sending them love and asking for their help.

And finally, the evening explains the name itself. Latwii confesses that it is a made up name, for they do not have names as we know names, only a vibration of light. In our language, they say, it means the double, or the second. It is simply the one who is standing in for Hatonn. We are your doubles, they say, and we send you double love and double helpings.

So tonight's teaching, from the doubles, is single. Once a day, peel the petals. Find the jewel. Stand on the holy ground that is your birthright, and let everyone else's pattern unfold in its own time, in love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Tree in Your Head
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the tree in your head.

On March eighteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Latwii looks at the most overworked organ in the spiritual life, the intellect, and gives it the funniest and most freeing image in the archive. It is as though, they say, you have great trees growing on top of your heads, with their roots very deep inside your brains.

And what do we do with these trees? We stand out in the rain, Latwii says, and let the sun and the wind pour over them and nourish their growth. We feed them. We water them. We are concerned about uprooting these great trees with their great and deep roots, and all the while we are the ones standing in the weather, helping them grow.

My friends, they ask, why do you worry? Why do you concern yourselves with those things over which you have no control? Why can you not pray and then let it go and act? Why can you not act and then let it go, be it error or correctness?

And then the practical teaching, which I want to give you exactly as they gave it, because it is so counterintuitive. The roots of that tree that grows within your brain, that tree which is called the intellect, cannot be uprooted by force, they say. The intellect can only be starved. Stay out of the rain, my friend. Avoid the sunshine. Do not think too much. It is as simple as that. Do not think about not thinking.

I love that last line, because it closes the trapdoor most of us fall through. The moment you try hard not to think, you are thinking about not thinking, and the tree gets another drink of rain. The instruction is not to fight the mind. It is to stop feeding it. Go into meditation, they say, with a free heart, not with a free mind. Let your mind do what it wishes. You are not concerned with your mind. Let it tie itself in knots. It does not concern you. It is a tool. It is not you. Shrug it off. Let it be unimportant.

They are not asking you to throw the tool away. You have a chemical body, they say. You must live in a chemical world. You must make decisions having to do with your chemical personality, and for that the intellect is very useful, like firewood for the decision making fires. Very well, then. Use it for that. For your spiritual thinking, stop it. That tree in your head, they say, is very useful if you need firewood, and you do need a certain amount of it.

But there is a deeper faculty in your heart, they say, and it is called the will. And they urge you, instead, to employ that. Will to know the original Thought of the Creator. Seek and ye shall find. How many times, they ask, have those who have spoken from the Confederation said those words? The advice is simple. It is not, think and ye shall find. It is, seek and ye shall find. Use your imagination. Use your faculties of hope and desire.

And as you seek, they say, let the journey be one of laughter as well as tears. Let yourself laugh. Let yourself enjoy that which is beautiful in each moment. Do not think too much. There is a love that created you, they say. In that love is all light and all joy. Joining it makes you as light as a butterfly. You have no gravity. You do not need to be serious. You do not need to heap blame or guilt for your past incorrectnesses upon yourself, nor upon others in any way, for others are only yourself, seen in a mirror so that you may see yourself better.

The evening's question time brings one more image I want to leave you with. A questioner is facing decisions and wants to know the right philosophy, and Latwii answers with a flower. A plant beginning to develop, they say, has no knowledge of its destiny, and yet it is unfolded perfectly day by day. The flower does not have the faculty of trust or patience. The flower simply knows that there is no time and that time is only an illusion. Thus, when it blossoms, it does so in a sweet surprise that is not in time but is at the proper moment. So you human beings are. You have a destiny. You have a time to blossom, a time to be picked. You can trust it with perfect confidence, knowing that all things, if you are in tune with yourself, will occur in the same harmony as the maturation of a flower.

So starve the tree, trust the flower, and let the journey be one of laughter as well as tears. That is the whole of tonight's teaching, and it is enough.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Road Goes On
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the road goes on.

On April first, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn returns to the group after an absence, and his first message is not about them. It is about himself. We of the Confederation need you, he says, just as you need us.

Listen to how he explains it, because it is one of the most human things any of these voices ever say. In our reality, he says, someone to love and cherish and help and inspire is as necessary to us as is food and drink to you. To us, those whom we have found to be serious students of the path are as delicious as your meat and drink is to you, for you are the means whereby we can enlarge our own horizons of understanding. As they watch human beings dwelling in the heavy illusion, fighting so valiantly to understand the intensive emotions of this vibration, they gain new depths of insight into the plan of the Father. We know that there is a plan, he says, but its beginning and its end are shrouded in mystery, even for us.

And then the image that gives tonight its name. We have not traveled to the end of the rainbow, he says. We have not found the pot of gold. We have only found that the road goes on and on, and that our companions became more and more loving, and the road more and more delightful.

I find that quietly staggering. These are beings far ahead on the path, and they are telling us there is no end of the road, only better companions and a more delightful road. So in your day to day efforts to find your road and follow it, he says, know in your heart that good will come of the effort. It is a private effort, not one which you can share, not one which others will understand.

The evening then turns to religion, and Hatonn says something I wish every argument about faith could hear. We do not use the personalities of masters who have incarnated upon your planet, he says, such as Jesus and Buddha and Lao Tse. Although we could, we feel more honest in telling you that there is a road paved with love, designed with love, difficult to follow but full of rewards. You can believe with all your heart in a master who has incarnated. It has no bearing on the road, for those things which one uses as walking sticks on that road are all acceptable. The road is the same.

And then, the sentence I keep underlining. When you hear religious and philosophical discussions, he says, know in your heart that each is correct, each is right. All disagreements are disagreements not about the road, not about love, not about the striving for truth, but merely about that stout walking stick which many use to give them confidence.

There is a gentler visitor mid evening, Telonn, who leads the group in a small exercise of imagination: a white globe of light in the center of the room, expanding until it engulfs each person, and then, in the spirit, floating up out of the dwelling place, above the clouds, looking down at the quiet house left behind. Feel the weight of gravity, Telonn says, and know that you will not always be so.

And Latwii closes the night with the harder teaching, about the earth itself. The sounds the group had heard, like distant thunder, came from energies within the earth, they say, and the reason is centuries old. All levels of your civilization, Latwii says, have been eaten by something we would call a cancer, and that is the cancer of separation: not knowing that all beings are one, and that what is done to another is done to oneself. These vibrations sink into the planet itself, and the most sensitive parts of the earth begin to move, attempting to relieve the tensions of the planetary consciousness.

But listen to the last image, because Latwii does not leave it in despair. Going from one density into another is like being born, they say, and your planet is being born at this time. The delivery, so far, has been difficult, but the baby is alive. There are those among you who wish to learn and wish to love, and we feel there is hope for you.

So the road goes on, the companions grow more loving, and the planet labors toward its birth. Our part, tonight as always, is the private effort: to find the road, to follow it, and to let the walking sticks be whatever they need to be for whoever holds them.

Thank you for listening.

title: Out of the Dead Ground
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: out of the dead ground.

On April fifteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, Easter Sunday, Hatonn greets the group on the day their culture calls holy, and he begins with a line of poetry the channel is carrying in her mind. April is the cruelest month, breeding lilacs out of the dead ground. He asks them to take the words personally. What, he asks, is the dead ground in your life?

Perhaps you know the answer already, he says. Perhaps there is all too much of it: the familiar, the simple, and the easy, those things concerned only with the transitory experience that began when you first drew breath in a chemical vehicle and ends when your last breath is expelled. In the illusion, this is called life, this breathing. But in reality, he says, the experience itself is without life. And yet, my friends, you are here, and it is a precious and unusual thing that you are.

Many are the souls, he says, who have wished at this time to draw breath upon your planet and experience what is occurring here now, for what is occurring is a change, the way a change in seasons may be called a change. You may say, why, spring is the same as winter, it is the same earth, the same trees. But the transformations are remarkable. Out of the dead ground there grow new things that are alive, and those that blossom and bloom. That which was skeletal and brown and bare became lovely, bursting with life and hope and promise. And so, he says, is your life at this tiny point which is the present.

And why is this a cruel process? Why is April the cruelest month? Why is change difficult? He turns to the story the holiday remembers. A master among men was taken to a tree and thereupon fixed until he was dead. Does that not seem cruel? You are in the midst of that which is cruel, he says. Cruelty is a part of change. Pain is the price of growth. When the one known as Jesus was lifted gently from that tree, he was dead, and yet it is this holiday you now celebrate on which he blossomed into that which was not transient but alive, conscious, and loving.

And then Hatonn says the thing that reframes the whole evening. Flowers are for a season, he says, and many of them do not regenerate themselves. But you are not flowers. You are seeds which are sown in the dead ground of a chemical body, that you may experience the thunder and the lightning, the rain, the snow, and the wind that only a chemical body can give you. For it is in those circumstances that your emotional reactions are intensified, invariably. And it is through this intensification, through this often painful process of emotional reaction and thought and contemplation, that you grow that within you which is alive, eternal, and loving.

I keep returning to that image. You chose the dead ground. You are a seed, and the whole point of being planted here is the weather: the thunder, the rain, the wind that a seed in a safer place would never feel. The pain is not a mistake in the plan. It is the plan, the price of the growth you came for.

There is a curious peace, he says, to be gained from knowing that you are capable of using those things which are given you, not just those things which are transitorily joyful, but those things which are of transitory pain. This peace passes understanding, for it means that in no circumstances are you without purpose, that those things which do not seem to have a purpose do have a purpose, and that purpose is to help you grow, not in this life only, but in the life that is real.

The channel spent her morning singing hymns, and Hatonn borrows her song and turns it back on the group. Alleluia, he is risen, she sang. Alleluia, you are risen, he answers. Your body is transitory. In meditation, allow that feeling of freedom, of love, of sweet companionship, of peace, to soak through your chemical body, to soothe those nerves frayed by the intense emotions of your experience at this level. Let hope come into your heart, for the Creator is forever full of hope.

Just as the one known as Jesus finished his stay to the bitter end and triumphed over cruelty, he says, take whatever cup is given to you and drink it unafraid. If it is yours, take it. But in meditation ask for the discrimination to know that which is yours and that which is not yours. When you feel that you know, you will be as one that has come forth in the spring, in your own way beautiful. Think of yourself as nothing less, for you are beautiful, each of you, as beautiful as the Creator, as lovely, and as loving.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Caretaker of the Garden
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the caretaker of the garden.

On April twenty-ninth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn tells a story about a gardener, and it is one of those stories that quietly rearranges how you treat yourself.

Once there was a gardener, he says, who year after year planted his seeds and learned much about his crops. He knew which seeds to plant against which, which crops to move so the land would not be depleted. He began to feel very powerful, for he had often been told that he had the best garden in all of his territory. And one day he was asked how his seeds grew, and he began to explain by taking a seed and separating it into its parts. As he took his knife and separated the seed and showed his students the functions of each tiny part of this tiny seed, he found that he had killed the seed, for much as he would try, he could not put it back together. And so he learned that he was not the originator of the garden, but only the caretaker.

And then Hatonn turns the story on the listener, the way he always does. Consider, he says, that you yourselves are seeds, planted in the garden of earth. You are whole and perfect. It is good to nurture yourself. It is good to understand yourself and to care for the garden you have created for yourself to grow in. But do not separate the parts of you too completely. Do not observe so closely that you peel away something necessary for the wholeness of your growth. Allow yourself to be, for in that way the instinct within you to become can have its way in its own time and at its own pace.

I love the precision of that warning, because I know exactly the temptation he is naming.
