Inspiration feels like the whole story when it arrives. The sudden clarity. The bright idea at dawn. The sense that the universe has handed you something precious and complete. But Hatonn, speaking on an August evening, gently disagrees. Inspiration, he says, is only the beginning of the work. What matters is what you do with it on the ordinary Tuesday that follows.

Listen to how they put it. The flash of insight is a seed, and a seed is not a harvest. Between the two lies everything unglamorous. The showing up. The tending. The refusal to abandon the bright thing when it gets difficult, which it will, because bright things always get difficult when they meet the real world.

This is where most seekers quietly fail, and Hatonn knows it. We collect inspirations the way some people collect stones from a beach. Beautiful, numerous, and entirely inert. The inspiration that changed nothing was not really received. It was only admired. Reception means manifestation. It means the inner flash becomes an outer form, through the slow discipline of hands and days.

I love the honesty of this teaching. It refuses to flatter us. It would be so much nicer to hear that enlightenment is a lightning strike, that one great insight will rearrange your life permanently. Instead we get the truth. Insight rearranges nothing until discipline carries it into form. The mystic and the carpenter turn out to need the same virtue.

And then Hatonn adds the part nobody wants to hear, which is probably why it matters most. Difficulty is not the enemy of the inspired life. Difficulty is its tempering. The disagreement that tests your conviction. The obstacle that forces you to understand your own idea more deeply than the flash ever did. These are not interruptions to the work. They are the work, finishing what inspiration started.

Think of a blade. The steel is the inspiration, full of potential. But no one cuts anything with untempered steel. It must be heated and hammered and cooled, heated and hammered again. The hammering feels like opposition. It is actually formation. Hatonn suggests our frustrations serve the same function, if we let them.

Compassion, in particular, gets tempered this way. It is easy to feel universal love in meditation, alone, undisturbed. It is another thing entirely to keep it when someone disagrees with you sharply, or when the project you poured yourself into collapses. The compassion that survives contact with difficulty is the only kind that counts, because it is the only kind that is real.

So the evening leaves us with a practice, not a platitude. Notice your inspirations. Write them down if you like. But then ask the harder question. What is the next small, concrete, unglamorous step that would bring this one into form? And will you take it when the glow has faded?

The universe, Hatonn implies, is not short on inspiration. It is lavish with it, broadcasting on every frequency. What is rare is the one who receives the signal and then does the patient work of building the receiver into something the world can actually use.

Be that one. Take the bright thing seriously enough to discipline it. Let the difficulties hammer it into shape. And watch what happens when inspiration stops being a visitor and becomes a craft.

Thank you for listening.

title: Free to Listen
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: free to listen.

Most of us listen the way we watch traffic. Partially. Impatiently. Already composing our reply while the other person is still mid sentence. Tonight the ones who call themselves Latwii suggest something quietly radical. That real listening is not a communication skill. It is a spiritual achievement. And it begins, strangely, with seeing.

The teaching is simple to state and a lifetime to practice. Every person who stands before you is the Creator, entire. Not a fragment. Not a flawed copy. The whole thing, wearing a particular face, carrying a particular wound, speaking in a particular voice. If you could truly see that, Latwii says, listening would stop being an effort. You would listen the way you would listen to something sacred. Because you would be.

I love that line of thought, that attention is a form of worship. We treat listening as the pause between our own performances. But what if the person talking to you, boring or difficult or rambling as they may be, is the one infinite mystery, trying to tell you something? You would not check the time. You would lean in.

Listen to how they put it. Becoming free to listen means becoming free of the noise inside that competes with every voice from outside. The rehearsing. The judging. The quiet cataloging of disagreements. Freedom here is not the freedom to speak your mind. It is the freedom from the tyranny of your own commentary, so that another's reality can actually reach you.

There is a homely image tucked into the evening that I keep returning to. A hand of cards. You are dealt what you are dealt. You can complain about the cards, and many do, at length, to anyone who will listen. Or you can play the hand with everything you have. Latwii uses this to talk about acceptance, but it applies to listening too.

Every conversation is a dealt hand. The other person arrives with their cards face up on the table, their history, their mood, their limitations. You did not choose the hand. But you are free, completely free, in how you play it. Listening well is one of the finest plays available. It costs nothing and it transforms everything.

And notice what happens when you truly listen to someone as the Creator. They often begin to speak differently. People rise, or sink, to the level of the attention they receive. The one who is heard as sacred begins to remember that they are. This is not a technique. It is a kind of quiet miracle, and it happens in kitchens and offices every day, unrecorded.

The evening does not ask you to agree with everyone. Seeing the Creator in a person is not the same as endorsing their opinions. It is deeper and more demanding. It asks you to hold two truths at once. This being is the infinite, and this being is also wrong about the thing they are saying. Both can be true. Listening freely means making room for both.

So here is a practice for the week. In your next conversation, try an experiment. Silently remind yourself, before the other person speaks, that you are about to hear from the Creator. Then listen as if it were true. Notice how your body changes. Notice how the urge to interrupt softens. Notice what you hear in the pauses that you would have missed.

You may find, as Latwii suggests, that the world has been trying to tell you something beautiful for a very long time. It was only waiting for you to become free enough to hear it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Stepping Outside Time
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: stepping outside time.

Time feels like the most solid thing in the world until you try to hold it. Then it behaves like water. Hatonn, on a late August evening, invites us to consider a strange possibility. That time is not the river we are floating down. It is more like a room we have chosen to sit in for a while. And we are free, even now, to notice the door.

Listen to how they put it. In meditation, in those rare moments of complete presence, the walls of the room grow thin. Past and future loosen their grip. You touch something that does not hurry, because it does not go anywhere. Hatonn calls this stepping outside of time, and he treats it not as an escape but as a homecoming.

This reframes everything about why we are here. If time is a room rather than a river, then the incarnation is not something that happened to you. It is something you chose. You looked at this particular era, with its particular confusions and its particular beauty, and you said yes to it. The way an athlete says yes to training. The way a student says yes to a difficult school.

I love that image, the incarnation as chosen training. It dignifies the struggle without denying it. The days that feel pointless are not pointless. They are repetitions. The griefs that feel random are not random. They are the heavy weights, and you picked them up on purpose, because some part of you knew exactly what they would build.

Hatonn is tender about how hard the training is. He does not pretend the room of time is comfortable. It is cramped. It is loud. Everyone in it is bumping into everyone else, learning the lessons of love at close quarters. But he reminds us that the cramped room is temporary, and the one who chose it is not.

There is a thread in the evening about beauty that belongs here too. We spend so much of our time-energy polishing the surface. The face, the body, the presentation. Hatonn suggests this is a case of mistaken identity. The beauty that matters, the only beauty that survives the stepping out of time, is the essence underneath. Love, not as a feeling but as the actual substance of what you are.

Think of it this way. When you step outside of time, even briefly, you stop seeing people as their surfaces and start sensing them as their essence. The annoying colleague. The difficult relative. Yourself in the mirror on a bad morning. Underneath the time-bound presentation, the same light. The training is learning to see it while still inside the room.

So the practice is not complicated, though it is not easy. Find a few minutes of stillness. Let the past and the future go quiet, the way you might let a noisy room settle. And notice what remains when time loosens. That remainder, Hatonn says, is the real you. The one who chose this. The one who is not afraid of it.

You are older than your biography and larger than your schedule. The room of time is real, and the training in it matters. But you are the one who walked in freely, and you are the one who will walk out, carrying everything you learned in your hands like gold.

Thank you for listening.

title: You Are Enough
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: you are enough.

There was once a young man, Hatonn tells us, who made a quiet vow. He had grown up hearing his parents say, over and over, that there was never enough. Not enough time. Not enough money. So the young man decided his whole life would be organized around a single goal. To have enough.

It sounds like a reasonable ambition. It might be the most common ambition in the world. But the story turns on a question the young man only learns to ask much later. Enough of what? And enough for whom? He chased the outer enough for years before discovering that the hunger was never really about money or time at all.

Listen to how they put it. Within your illusion, you will find what you consider to be shortages. Shortages of power, of money, of influence, of love. But every one of these shortages, Hatonn says, is a distortion of love. Not a fact about the universe, but a lens you are looking through. And a lens can be cleaned.

I love that reframing, because it is so practical. The lack of money, seen one way, distracts you from seeking. Seen another way, it produces a simplicity that frees you to love. The same circumstance. Two entirely different lives, depending on which way you turn it. The shortage was never the point. The turning was.

There is an old prayer woven into the evening. Give us today enough to eat. Not enough for the decade. Not enough to feel secure forever. Enough for today. Hatonn calls this an accurate view of the relative importance of having enough. The seeking for enough, pushed beyond what can be easily measured, goes awry and breeds frustration. Today is the unit that matters.

And then the line the whole evening seems to have been building toward. The inner work, the work upon the self, is not selfish. For it is only the whole self that can serve the Creator it sees in others.

Let that land. So many sincere people treat attention to their own inner life as a luxury, or worse, as self indulgence. They pour themselves out for others from an empty cup and call the exhaustion virtue. Hatonn disagrees completely. What you see is a reflection of what you are. If you have not found enough within yourself, you will see shortage everywhere you look.

The image he offers is an old one. A crowd on a hillside, thousands of hungry people, and one small lunch. A few loaves, a couple of fish. The one holding the lunch feels the inadequacy completely. But the inadequacy is the point. Love, flowing through from the infinite source, multiplies what it touches. That tiny bit you can bring through, that widow's mite of love, is enough. It was always enough.

So the young man's story ends the only way it could. He grows old. He never finds enough in the outer world, because enough was never there to be found. It was inside him the whole time, in the inner silence he kept postponing. You are enough, Hatonn says, and you have enough. Not as a pep talk. As a statement of fact about the structure of things.

Whatever went wrong today, whatever will go wrong tomorrow, be serene in this confidence. The small effort you can make, the tiny bit of love you can bring through, will multiply. You brought infinity with you into this life. Claim it. It is your birthright.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Heavy Crown
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the heavy crown.

We love the dramatic moment of choosing. The conversion. The resolution. The morning you decide, once and for all, to live differently. But Hatonn, on a September evening, is interested in what happens the morning after. What does the spiritual life look like when the drama fades and the long, unglamorous middle begins?

Listen to how they put it. After the great choice comes the heavy crown. Not a crown of gold and ceremony, but the weight of patient refinement. Day after day of small fidelity. The choice, it turns out, was the easy part. Wearing it is the work.

I love the honesty of this image. A crown is supposed to be glorious. But anyone who has tried to live by their deepest values knows the truth. The values are heavy. Forgiveness, when you would rather nurse the grudge. Honesty, when a small lie would be so much easier. Love, when the other person has not earned it and never will. The crown presses down. That is how you know it is real.

Hatonn does not offer a way to make the crown lighter. He offers a way to understand its weight. The heaviness is not a sign you chose wrong. It is the feeling of becoming. Gold is heavy too. The refinement is slow precisely because it is thorough. Nothing real is rushed.

There is a second movement in the evening, and it is the one that makes the weight bearable. The seeker, traveling far in search of the treasure, eventually discovers something the mystics have always reported. The treasure was the traveler. What you seek, at the end of every genuine road, turns out to be yourself. Or more precisely, the self you were underneath the seeking all along.

Think of the long search as a kind of sacred comedy. You pack your bags. You cross deserts. You climb mountains asking everyone you meet where the holy thing can be found. And one morning, exhausted, you sit down, and in the stillness you recognize the face you have been looking for. It is your own.

This does not make the journey pointless. Hatonn is clear about that. You could not have recognized the face without the miles. The seeking carved the eyes that can finally see. The heavy crown polished the brow it rests on. The destination was never a place. It was a capacity.

So if you are in the long middle, past the dramatic choice and far from any finish line, this evening is for you. The ordinariness of your days is not evidence that the spiritual life has stalled. It is the spiritual life, doing its quiet work. The crown is heavy because it is real gold. Keep wearing it.

And when the weight feels like too much, remember the secret the journey keeps. You are not traveling toward something other than yourself. Every step of patient refinement is a step toward recognizing who has been walking all along. The seeker and the sought were never two.

Rest in that tonight. The drama was the doorway. This, the faithful ordinary day, is the temple.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Inward Treasure
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the inward treasure.

You carry something that cannot be seen on any scan, weighed on any scale, or stolen by any thief. Hatonn calls it the inward treasure, and on an October evening he speaks of it the way a jeweler might speak of a rare stone. With reverence. And with a warning. Treasures attract attention, including your own, and not all attention is kind.

Listen to how they put it. The treasure is the deep self, the part of you that knows why you came here. It accumulates quietly, in moments of genuine love, in the stillness of meditation, in the dreams you half remember at dawn. And because it is precious, it needs protecting. Not with walls, but with discretion. With the wisdom to know what to share and what to shelter.

I love the practicality of this. Spiritual life is often presented as total openness, as if the enlightened person has no interior doors. Hatonn suggests otherwise. The seed needs the dark of the soil. The treasure needs the quiet of the vault. There is a time to speak of holy things and a time to hold them in silence, and knowing the difference is part of the path.

The evening moves into stranger waters, and they are worth entering. Thought pools, Hatonn calls them. Great reservoirs of shared thinking that we all swim in without knowing it. The moods of a crowd. The anxieties of an era. The sudden inspiration that seems to arrive from nowhere. We are not as separate in our minds as we imagine. We are fish in one another's water.

This explains so much. Why a room can feel heavy before anyone speaks. Why an idea whose time has come seems to occur to a dozen people at once. Why your own thoughts sometimes feel less like possessions and more like weather. The treasure within you is yours, but the waters around you are shared. Learning to tell the difference is a spiritual skill.

Dreams belong to this teaching too. Hatonn treats them not as puzzles to decode but as dispatches from the deep self, the treasure sending up signals. Pay attention, he says, not with the frantic analysis of the daytime mind but with the receptive curiosity of someone listening for a friend's voice in a crowd.

And then the turn that reorders everything. The message matters more than the messenger. We are endlessly distracted by personalities. The charisma of the teacher. The flaws of the teacher. The credentials, the scandals, the style. Hatonn sweeps all of it aside. If the words carry truth, receive the truth. If they do not, let them go. The vessel is never the point.

This is liberating in both directions. It frees you from hero worship, from needing your teachers to be perfect. And it frees you from the opposite trap, dismissing a true word because it came from an unimpressive mouth. The treasure does not care about packaging. Neither should you.

So guard the inward treasure. Tend it in silence. Learn the waters you swim in. Listen to your dreams the way you would listen to a wise friend. And judge every teaching, including this one, by the only measure that matters. Does it carry the ring of truth?

The treasure is already yours. It has been accumulating all your life, in every moment you chose love over fear. Protect it. Polish it. And when the time is right, spend it freely. That is what treasure is for.

Thank you for listening.

title: Lived Seeking
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: lived seeking.

There is a question that has launched a thousand arguments, and Hatonn approaches it sideways, the way he approaches most big things. Not with doctrine, but with a quiet redefinition. What if salvation is not something you believe? What if it is something you do?

Listen to how they put it. The Creator is not found in the correct opinion about the Creator. Opinions are cheap and plentiful. The Creator is found within, in the sanctuary of your own being, and then manifested, day by day, in the unglamorous details of a life. Seeking and serving. Those two verbs, repeated until they become a rhythm.

I love how this dissolves the anxiety so many people carry about believing the right things. The checklist faith. The fear that one wrong idea will disqualify you. Hatonn sweeps the checklist off the table. What matters is the direction of your life, not the precision of your theology. Are you seeking? Are you serving? Then you are already inside the thing you were afraid of missing.

The seeking comes first, and it is interior work. Go within, he says, in meditation, in silence, in the honest examination of your own heart. Find the Creator there, not as an idea but as a presence. This is not reserved for saints. It is the basic equipment of being human. The sanctuary is built in.

But the seeking that stops at the sanctuary door is incomplete. This is the part we tend to skip. Having found the love within, you are asked to carry it out into the world and spend it. On the difficult neighbor. On the tedious task. On the stranger who will never thank you. Service is seeking made visible. It is the inner discovery, translated into hands and feet.

Notice the order matters. Service without seeking becomes exhaustion, or worse, a performance of goodness that secretly resents its audience. Seeking without service becomes a beautiful private hobby. Together, they make a whole. The inward finding and the outward giving, breathing in and breathing out.

Hatonn is gentle with those who worry they are not doing enough. The service he describes is not heroic. It does not require a platform or an audience. It happens in kitchens and checkout lines. The smallest act of genuine kindness, done in the awareness of the Creator within, carries the full weight of the teaching.

So the evening leaves us with a question that is also an invitation. Not what do you believe, but how do you live? The beliefs will sort themselves out, Hatonn implies, in the wake of a life pointed toward love. Get the verbs right, and the nouns take care of themselves.

Seek, then. Go within and find what has been waiting there since before you were born. And then serve, carrying it outward into a world that is hungry for exactly what you found. This is the whole of it. This is salvation, not as a destination, but as a daily practice.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Pearl of Great Price
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the pearl of great price.

There is an old story about a merchant who spent his life trading in pearls. He knew their weight, their luster, their price in every market. And then one day he saw a pearl so perfect that everything changed. He went and sold all that he had, the story says, and bought it.

Hatonn takes up this parable on an October evening and turns it gently inward. The pearl is truth. Or the seeking of truth. Or the moment when you recognize, with absolute clarity, what your life is actually for. And the selling of all you have is not poverty. It is the glad exchange of everything lesser for the one thing that matters.

Listen to how they put it. Truth has a strange property. The closer you get to it, the larger it becomes. It recedes even as it reveals. Every answer opens onto a wider question. This is not a flaw in the seeking. It is the nature of what is sought. The infinite does not fit inside a conclusion.

I love that image, truth as a horizon. You walk toward it all your life and never arrive, and the walking is the point. The seeker who demands final answers will always be disappointed. The seeker who learns to love the widening will find that every step reveals more light, not less.

The merchant's joy is the key to the parable. He did not sell everything with a heavy heart. The story says he did it gladly. Hatonn lingers on this. The spiritual life, rightly understood, is not a long list of renunciations endured through gritted teeth. It is a series of discoveries, each one making the previous treasures look like toys.

You do not give up the lesser things because someone told you to. You give them up because you have seen the pearl, and next to it, they no longer shine. The letting go happens by itself, the way a child drops a dull stone when handed a gem.

And then the evening's quietest revolution. True wealth, Hatonn says, grows by being given. This reverses everything the world teaches about riches. In the outer economy, giving diminishes you. In the inner economy, giving multiplies you. Love spent is love increased. Wisdom shared is wisdom deepened. The pearl, once found, only grows more lustrous the more freely it is shown.

Think of the people you have known who live this way. They are not depleted by their generosity. They seem, impossibly, to have more to give the more they give. This is not a trick of personality. It is the mechanics of the inward treasure. What flows from the infinite source does not run dry.

So the question the evening leaves you with is the merchant's question. Have you seen the pearl? Not heard about it. Seen it. That moment of recognition when you know, beyond argument, what is most real. If you have, then you know what to do. Sell the lesser. Gladly. And watch the one true wealth grow every time you give it away.

The pearl is waiting. It has always been waiting. And it is worth everything you have, because it turns out to be everything you are.

Thank you for listening.

title: Beyond Change
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: beyond change.

Everything changes. The teaching begins there because there is nowhere else honest to begin. The body changes. The seasons change. The people you love change, and your love for them changes too. Most spiritualities try to comfort you about this. Hatonn, on an autumn evening, tries something bolder. He suggests you go beyond it.

Listen to how they put it. Beneath the world of change there is something that does not change. Not an idea about permanence, but a living stillness you can actually touch in meditation. The thoughts change. The feelings change. But the awareness in which they change, that remains. And that, he says, is closer to who you are than any of the changing things.

I love the plainness of this. It asks nothing of your beliefs. Sit still. Watch your mind do what it does, flickering from past to future like a restless bird. And notice the watcher. The watcher does not flicker. The watcher was there in childhood and is here now, unchanged by everything it has witnessed. Rest there a while.

There is a dizzying image tucked into the evening. The whole of creation, Hatonn says, can be found within a grain of sand. Not as poetry, but as perception. Look deeply enough into any small thing, past the surface of it, and you find the same patterns, the same intelligence, the same infinite depth that fills the galaxies. The part contains the whole.

This is why the mystics have always loved small things. A flower. A stone. A grain of sand in the palm. The infinite is not far away, hiding at the edge of the universe. It is concentrated everywhere, waiting for someone to look closely enough. Bigness was never the measure of significance.

And here is where the teaching becomes practical. If the whole is in the grain, then the stillness beyond change is not somewhere else either. It is here, underneath this very moment, underneath the noise and the hurry. Meditation is not a journey to a distant peace. It is the practice of noticing the peace that was already underneath the journey.

Hatonn is realistic about how hard this noticing is. The world of change is loud and insistent. It grabs the attention a thousand times a day with its urgencies. Going beyond change does not mean ignoring the world. It means learning to stand in the stillness while the world does what it does around you. The eye of the storm is not separate from the storm.

So the practice is simple and inexhaustible. Whatever is changing in your life right now, and something always is, let it change. Do not clutch it. Do not curse it. Instead, turn your attention to the part of you that watches the changing without itself changing. That part is not cold or detached. It is the warmest thing in you. It is love, before love took on a particular form.

The grain of sand holds the universe. The still moment holds eternity. And you, the watcher, hold both, without effort, simply by being what you have always been beneath the weather of your days.

Thank you for listening.

title: Yeast for Tomorrow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: yeast for tomorrow.

There is a kind of giving that looks like love and slowly becomes something else. You say yes when you mean no. You pour yourself out until there is nothing left to pour. And then, running on empty, you start to keep score. The generosity curdles into resentment. Tonight the ones who call themselves Latwii name this pattern with unusual directness, and offer a homely image to heal it.

The image is yeast. When you bake bread, you hold back a little of the dough, the living culture, to start the next batch. If you use it all, there is bread today and none tomorrow. Latwii suggests the spiritual life works the same way. Keep enough yeast for tomorrow.

Listen to how they put it. Service to others is the great work, and they never deny it. But service that costs you your own wholeness is not service. It is martyrdom wearing a costume. And martyrdom, however noble it looks, helps no one in the end. The burned out giver cannot give. The depleted servant cannot serve.

I love the honesty here, because it cuts against so much well meaning advice. We are told to give until it hurts, as if the hurting were the proof of the giving. But Latwii draws a cleaner line. Give until it helps. The moment your giving starts to corrode your own being, it has stopped being love and started being something else, however good it looks from the outside.

This is where self worth enters, not as selfishness but as stewardship. You are the instrument of your own service. A musician tunes the violin before the concert. A gardener waters the soil, not just the flowers. Tending to your own needs, your rest, your joy, your boundaries, is not a detour from the path of service. It is the maintenance the path requires.

The yeast image keeps giving. Yeast is alive. It needs feeding and warmth and time. Neglect it and it dies, and no amount of wishing will raise the bread. Your own aliveness works the same way. The part of you that loves to give needs to be fed, not starved in the name of virtue. A well kept giver is a renewable resource. A neglected one is a cautionary tale.

Latwii is careful to distinguish balance from stinginess. Keeping yeast for tomorrow is not an excuse to keep everything for yourself today. The bread is meant to be shared, generously, joyfully. The point is only that sharing works best as a rhythm, not a hemorrhage. Give, and replenish. Pour out, and refill. This is the sustainable way.

So notice your own pattern. If your giving leaves you bitter, the yeast is low. If your service feels like a performance of exhaustion, the culture is dying. These are not signs of failure. They are signals, the way hunger is a signal. Feed yourself. Rest. Reclaim the joy that made you want to give in the first place.

The world does not need your martyrdom. It needs your aliveness, steady and renewable, rising like good bread, day after day. Keep the yeast. Tomorrow's hungry are counting on it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love as Total Unity
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love as total unity.

On an Easter evening, the one who calls himself Hatonn offers what he describes as his simplest teaching. Not his deepest, not his most sophisticated. His simplest. And like all truly simple things, it turns out to contain everything else.

The teaching is this. Love is total unity. Not partial. Not selective. Not love for the lovable with exceptions for the difficult. Total. The recognition that there is one Creator, one creation, one life wearing ten thousand faces, and that to love is simply to see this clearly.

Listen to how they put it. Compassion is not a feeling you manufacture toward people you approve of. It is what remains when the illusion of separateness falls away. You look at the stranger and see, not a stranger, but yourself in different circumstances. You look at the enemy and see, with a shock, a brother. The unity was always there. Love is just its name when it is recognized.

I love the word total here, because it refuses every loophole. We are so skilled at partial love. Love for our own, indifference to the rest. Warmth for the agreeable, coldness for the inconvenient. Hatonn does not scold this. He simply points out that it is not yet love in the full sense. It is love with the training wheels still on.

Easter is a fitting night for this teaching. Whatever your relationship to the story, its shape is the shape of total unity. The willingness to hold all of it. The suffering and the joy. The betrayal and the forgiveness. Nothing excluded. The resurrection, in Hatonn's telling, is what happens whenever a heart stops dividing the world into the lovable and the unlovable and embraces the whole.

This is demanding, and the evening does not pretend otherwise. Total unity means the person who hurt you is included. The one whose views you find abhorrent is included. You yourself, on your worst day, are included. There is no one standing outside the circle, because there is no outside. That is what total means.

But notice the strange gentleness inside the demand. You are not asked to feel warmly toward everyone at all times. Feelings come and go like weather. You are asked to see truly. To recognize the one life looking out through every pair of eyes. The feeling, Hatonn implies, follows the seeing, the way warmth follows the sunrise. You do not have to force it.

The practice, then, is a practice of vision. In your ordinary day, with ordinary people, try to catch a glimpse of the unity underneath the differences. The cashier. The driver who cut you off. The friend who disappointed you. Each one, the one Creator, in costume. Each one, yourself, on a different road.

It will not happen all at once. Total unity is the simplest teaching and the longest curriculum. But every glimpse counts. Every moment when the separateness thins and you see what is actually there. That is Easter, happening quietly, in the middle of an ordinary evening.

One life. One love. No exceptions. That is the whole teaching, and it is enough for a lifetime.

Thank you for listening.

title: Reading Your Life Like a Dream
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: reading your life like a dream.

You already know how to do the most advanced spiritual practice there is. You do it every night. You enter a world where nothing is literal, where every figure is a messenger and every event is symbolic, and you navigate it with an ease you never question. Then you wake up, and you forget that the daytime world works exactly the same way.

Hatonn, on a spring evening, suggests we stop forgetting. Read your daily life the way you read a dream. The annoying colleague is not just an annoying colleague. The missed train is not just a missed train. Everything that happens is opaque on the surface and transparent underneath, if you learn to look through it instead of at it.

Listen to how they put it. Experience becomes transparent when you ask the dream question. Not what happened, but what does it mean? The dream never answers literally. Neither does life. The outer event is the costume. The inner meaning is the actor wearing it. Learn to recognize the actor, and the same old play starts to reveal new lines.

I love this because it dignifies the ordinary without making it precious. Your Tuesday is not trivial. It is dense with meaning, the way a dream is dense, if you bring the right kind of attention to it. The practice is not to escape daily life into spirituality. It is to discover that daily life was the spirituality all along, wearing work clothes.

There is a thread in the evening about pilgrims that belongs here. Fellow travelers on the road, each with their own destination in mind. Hatonn observes something quietly devastating. The pilgrims often learn more from accepting one another than from reaching the shrine. The stated goal gets all the attention. The companions do all the teaching.

Think of your own pilgrimages. The project, the journey, the plan you were so focused on. And then the people along the way, the ones who irritated you, surprised you, taught you without meaning to. In the dream reading of your life, they were never background characters. They were the curriculum.

This changes how you move through difficulty. The obstacle is not blocking the path. In the dream logic, the obstacle is the path, wearing a disguise. The person you cannot get along with is not an interruption to your spiritual life. They are your spiritual life, asking to be read more carefully.

So try it for a week. Treat your days as dreams. Each evening, review what happened and ask the dreamer's questions. Who appeared? What was the feeling underneath the event? What might my deeper self be trying to tell me through this particular symbolism? Write it down if you like. Dreams fade when they are not honored. Days do too.

You will start to notice patterns. The same figure returning in different costumes. The same lesson circling back, patiently, until it is learned. This is not superstition. It is attention, the most sacred kind. The universe has been speaking in symbols your whole life. It is only waiting for you to start listening in the language it uses.

Read the dream. Live the meaning. And be kind to your fellow pilgrims. In the end, they were the destination all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: Seeks, Finds, Is Found
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: seeks, finds, is found.

There are seasons when the spiritual life feels like being adrift. The practices that once glowed have gone dim. The sense of direction has dissolved. You are doing everything you were doing before, but the current has you, and you cannot tell anymore whether you are moving or only drifting.

Hatonn speaks to this exact season, and what he says is stranger and more comforting than any pep talk. The drifting is not the opposite of the path. Underneath the apparent aimlessness, a deeper movement continues. The One, he says, seeks, and finds, and is found. All three, all at once, even when you feel none of them.

Listen to how they put it. You are not only the seeker. You are also the sought. While you stumble around looking for the light, the light is looking for you, with far better eyes. The finding happens from both directions at once, like two travelers walking toward each other in fog. Neither can see the other yet. Both are on their way.

I love the grammar of this. Seeks, finds, is found. Active, active, passive. You do your part, which is the seeking, honest and persistent. The universe does its part, which is the finding. And then there is the third movement, the one you cannot perform at all. Being found. Being received. Being held by what you were chasing.

This reframes the adrift seasons completely. The feeling of being lost is real, but it is not the whole truth. Beneath it, the seeking continues in you even when you have stopped noticing it. The honest ache, the unwillingness to settle for less, the quiet turning toward the light you cannot see. That is the seeking, still alive, still working.

Hatonn asks for faith here, but not the brittle kind. Not faith as forced certainty, pasted over doubt. Faith as a loosening. A willingness to trust that the underlying unity is real even when the surface feels fragmented. The ocean does not cease to be one ocean because the waves are choppy.

There is a tenderness in the evening for those who feel they have failed at the spiritual life. The meditation that will not settle. The prayer that feels like talking to an empty room. Hatonn does not grade these efforts. He says the seeking itself is the connection. The empty room was never empty. The silence was never silent.

So if you are adrift, consider the possibility that you are being carried. Not abandoned, carried. The current that took your sense of direction may be taking you somewhere your direction could never have found. The One seeks through you, finds in you, and is found by you, in the very midst of the fog.

Keep seeking, then, even without the feeling of it. The fog is weather, not truth. And on the other side of it, walking toward you through the mist, is everything you have been looking for, looking for you.

Thank you for listening.

title: Every Day Is Harvest Day
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: every day is harvest day.

We tend to think of harvest as a season. The autumn reward for the spring planting. But Hatonn, on a May evening, quietly relocates it. Every day is harvest day, he says. Every single one. You are always gathering what was sown, sometimes by you, sometimes long before you, in the choices and the tending of ordinary hours.

Listen to how they put it. What you harvest is what was lovingly nurtured. Not perfectly nurtured. Lovingly. The distinction matters. Perfection is a harsh gardener. Love is a patient one. The seeds you tended with genuine care, even clumsily, even inconsistently, are the ones that ripen. The universe, it seems, grades on love, not on technique.

I love the daily-ness of this. It rescues the teaching from the distant future and plants it in this morning. The kindness you offered yesterday is today's harvest. The patience you practiced last week ripens now. And the seeds you plant today, in how you speak to the difficult person, in how you meet the tedious task, are already germinating toward some future morning.

There is a thread in the evening about prayer that deepens all of this. Prayer, Hatonn suggests, is a meeting place. On one side, your free will, choosing in this moment. On the other, the deeper intentions you brought with you into this life, the ones you set before you arrived. In prayer, the two shake hands. What you choose now aligns with what you intended then.

This gives prayer a weight beyond wishing. It is not a message sent outward in hope of a reply. It is a rendezvous. You show up with your present self, and your deeper self shows up with its older wisdom, and together you decide what this day will harvest. The meeting happens in stillness. The results show up everywhere.

The evening also touches, gently, on the seasons when nothing seems to ripen. The gray days when the heart is heavy and the garden looks barren. Hatonn does not rush past this. If you are in such a season, hear this kindly. The barren look is not the whole truth. Seeds grow underground long before they break the surface. And some seasons are for resting the soil, not for forcing the bloom.

A gentle note, then, for anyone walking through heaviness that will not lift. Be patient with the field. Tend it lightly. Ask for help, from friends, from counselors, from whatever support your life offers, the way you would ask for help with any real burden. The harvest teaching is not a demand to feel fruitful. It is an invitation to trust that the tending matters, even now, especially now.

For the tending always matters. Every act of love is a planting. Every moment of patience is water on dry ground. You may not see the sprouts yet. That does not mean the garden is empty. It means the growing is happening where eyes cannot go, in the dark, rich, patient earth of your becoming.

So look at today as harvest day. Gather what is ripe with gratitude. Tend what is growing with love. And plant, deliberately, the seeds you want to gather tomorrow. The field is yours. The seasons are kind. And the harvest, lovingly nurtured, never fails.

Thank you for listening.

title: Recovering Your Smile
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: recovering your smile.

There comes a point in every serious seeker's life when the seeking itself becomes the problem. The practices pile up. The standards rise. The spiritual life starts to look like a second job, complete with performance reviews. And somewhere along the way, quietly, the smile goes missing.

Hatonn notices. On a May evening, with characteristic lightness, he suggests that recovering your smile is not a distraction from the work. It is the work, or at least its truest measure. A transformation that costs you your joy, he implies, is not yet a transformation. It is a transaction.

Listen to how they put it. Joy is not a reward for getting everything right. It is an attitude you choose, especially amid the folly. Your own folly first of all. The earnest mistakes. The grand resolutions that collapsed by Thursday. The whole beautiful comedy of a human being trying to become something more. Smile at it. It is yours, and it is funny, and it is fine.

I love the permission in this. We are so hard on ourselves, we seekers. Every lapse becomes evidence. Every bad day becomes a verdict. But Hatonn sees the striving itself with affection. The universe, he suggests, is not grading your performance. It is delighting in your willingness. The smile is the sign that you have remembered this.

There is a deeper teaching folded inside the lightness. True transformation, Hatonn says, should not be hindered, and nothing hinders it like grimness. The clenched jaw. The furrowed brow of the perpetually self improving. Growth needs room to breathe. The seed does not strain toward the sun. It simply unfolds, in its own time, toward the light it loves.

Think of the difference in your own body. The tight, effortful reaching, versus the relaxed opening. One exhausts. The other renews. Joy is the body's way of telling you that you have stopped hindering yourself. The smile is not decorative. It is diagnostic.

This does not mean pretending everything is fine. Hatonn is not prescribing denial. The folly is real. The suffering is real. But alongside them, underneath them, there is a current of joy that does not depend on circumstances. Choosing it is not ignorance. It is defiance of the finest kind. The refusal to let the darkness have the last word about your day.

So the practice is almost embarrassingly simple. Notice when you have lost your smile. Not with self reproach, with amusement. There it goes again, the serious seeker, furrowing away. And then, deliberately, recover it. Soften the face. Remember the comedy. Let the joy back in, not because everything is perfect, but because you are alive, and trying, and loved in the trying.

The transformation you are seeking is already underway. It does not need your worry. It needs your willingness, and your lightness, and your smile. Give it those, and get out of its way.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love as Work
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love as work.

The ones who call themselves Laitos do not speak often in this archive, and when they do, they speak like engineers of the spirit. Tonight they take up the most mysterious word in the seeker's vocabulary. Transformation. Everyone wants it. Few understand what it actually is. Laitos offers a definition with the precision of a physics lesson.

True transformation, they say, has direction and speed. These are the components of motion, and transformation is motion. Not a mood. Not a revelation you have once and frame. A movement, ongoing, with somewhere to go and a pace to keep.

Listen to how they put it. Consider love as work, and work as movement, and movement as initiation, and initiation as transformation. Each term slides into the next like links in a chain. Love is not a feeling at the end of this sequence. It is the engine at the start. Everything moves because love moves first.

I love the unsentimental clarity of this. We tend to treat love as the reward for transformation, the prize waiting at the finish line. Laitos reverses it. Love is the fuel, the labor, the daily doing. The transformation is what happens to a life that keeps loving as a practice, the way a river is transformed by the water that keeps flowing.

And then the line that reorders the whole seeking enterprise. Your initiation will visit you. You do not call it. We spend so much energy trying to schedule our own awakenings, to force the breakthrough, to earn the revelation. Laitos suggests the deepest changes arrive uninvited, on their own timetable. Your work is not to summon them. Your work is to be moving when they come.

Direction matters here. Motion without direction is only agitation, and the spiritual life has plenty of that. The direction, they say, is always toward greater love. Not love as sentiment, but love as the original Thought, the one great pattern underneath everything. Every true transformation, in the end, is about this one thing. Remembering what you are made of.

There is a tender image in the evening, offered to someone in the circle going through a difficult passage. A cocoon. The most fragile, private, unobservable work in nature. From the outside, nothing seems to be happening. Inside, everything is being remade. Laitos does not rush the cocoon. No one can hurry it from outside without destroying what is forming within.

If you are in a cocoon season, hear this gently. The stillness is not stagnation. The darkness is not failure. Something in you is dissolving so that something truer can take shape. Do not let anyone, least of all yourself, tear the cocoon open early. The butterfly knows its own timing.

So the teaching comes down to something you can do tomorrow morning. Work at love. Not grandly. Concretely. The kind word. The patient response. The small, deliberate movement toward greater kindness. Keep the direction. Keep the pace. And trust that the initiation, the deep change you cannot manufacture, will visit a life that is already in motion.

Love as work. Work as movement. Movement as transformation. The chain holds. Pull on the first link, and the rest follows.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Floor Plan of a Life
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the floor plan of a life.

Hatonn begins with a picture. A castle in ruins. Gray stone. No smoke from the turrets. No banners in the hall. Battle has passed by, and centuries have passed too. And yet, he says, people are drawn to ruins. They walk the empty courts and read, in the fallen walls, the story of what was built there.

Then the turn. You are drawn to ruins because you sense, correctly, that you are building one. Your life is the castle. Not the stones of it, which will crumble, but the floor plan. The shape of what you made with the materials and the years you were given. You are a'building, Hatonn says, right now, whether you know it or not.

Listen to how they put it. When you have lived your life, you will not see each stone, each battle, each joy and sorrow in detail. What you will see is what you built. The layout. The whole design, visible at last. Some build small lives and some build great ones, cabins and castles, and the size is not the point. The point is whether you built with love.

I love the builder's honesty of this image. A life under construction is messy. Walls go up and come down. Sections get added, reshaped, torn out in the night. This is not failure. This is building. The only real question is the one Hatonn keeps returning to. Are you loving as you build? For love is what makes the floor plan something you can gaze on without regret.

There is a boulder in the evening too, and it belongs with the castle. The path ahead looks blocked. The obstacle looks massive, immovable. But Hatonn says the boulder is often not what it seems. Time and again, the thing that looked like it would take a lifetime to move shifts aside with a surprisingly light touch. Fear magnifies. Love right sizes.

And then the teaching that steadies everything. There is no time you must consider lost. Not the wasted years. Not the distracted months. Not the long nights when you could not sleep and had no one to talk to. In any moment, Hatonn says, you may turn fully toward your seeking, and that single moment will fill you for hours or for days.

This is because you never seek alone. I love this line, and I want you to hear it clearly. There is no second of time when one upon your planet seeks alone. Always, as you seek, you seek with a mighty company. Millions of seekers, visible and invisible, turning toward the light in the same instant you do. Your solitary midnight is a crowded place.

The evening closes with a smaller voice, the one called Nona, and a single sentence worth carrying. In the healing work, the worry, the fretting, is not the praying. Worry weakens what prayer strengthens. So when you catch yourself fretting over the castle, over the boulder, over the floor plan, lay the worry down. It was never part of the building.

You are a'building. Tear out a wall if you must. Add a section. Reshape what is not working. But build with love, turn toward the light in any moment, and trust the mighty company walking beside you. The floor plan is taking shape. And it is more beautiful than you know.

Thank you for listening.

title: You Are Not What You Do
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: you are not what you do.

Hatonn opens the evening with laughter. Literally. He rejoices, he says, while the group is laughing together before the meditation begins. Laughter is good medicine, and the peoples of this planet are far too serious. You work at everything too hard, he tells them, instead of living freely in the creative spirit of the universe.

He borrows a line from the teacher known as Jesus. My yoke is easy and my burden is light. I came to give you abundant life, a joyful life. I love that Hatonn reaches for joy first, before any teaching. As if to say, whatever follows will only make sense if you are smiling when you hear it.

Then the evening's strangest and most practical definition. What is magic? Not spells, not spectacle. Magic is tuning in to the light, the beauty, and the caring of the universe. That is all. The universe is rich toward those who trust its beauty, and you can tune to its harmony the way you tune a radio, or you can tune to the static. It is a matter of choice. A matter of willing.

Listen to how they put it. All other kinds of power are polyester, but truth is cotton. Money is power. Position is power. Knowledge is power. But these are synthetic fabrics. They wear out. They pill. They do not breathe. Truth is the natural fiber. It takes care, and it is costly, and it will not bend itself to flatter you. But it lasts, and it breathes, and it connects you beyond space and time to what was before the world began.

I love the homeliness of that analogy. No grandeur. Just fabric. And the point lands harder for it. How much of your life is spent pursuing polyester? The synthetic powers that glitter and fade. Hatonn does not condemn them. He simply notes their wash cycle. They rot with the bodies that sought them. Truth does not.

The evening keeps narrowing toward a single sentence. The race is not to the swift, nor victory to the wise, for all things are equal. The lesson is love. Against the hard wall of the illusion, where wisdom and folly prove equally useless, there is only this. In love, in the original Thought, all things are acceptable. All things teach love.

And then a new voice enters, brief and unforgettable. The one called Yadda, speaking plainly, almost bluntly. You are not anything like you think you are, Yadda says. You are not what you do. You are not nine o'clock, ten o'clock, eleven o'clock. Strip away the clothing, the name, the nationality, the neighborhood, all of it. Now who are you?

The question lands like a small explosion. We have built our identities out of schedules and roles and possessions, and Yadda sweeps the table clean. Not to take something from you, but to make room. To wait, as Yadda puts it, for you to add to yourself the Creator.

The closing image is mechanical and perfect. You are a spiritual engine, Yadda says. Made to do work. And every engine needs fuel. So the only question that matters. What is your fuel? If it is fear, the engine sputters. If it is love, it runs clean and strong, farther than you imagined.

You are not what you do. You are not your calendar. You are the one the calendar cannot contain, tuned to the light, fueled by love, laughing on the way. Remember that, and the yoke is easy indeed.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Disguise of Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the disguise of love.

There is a night in the archive when Hatonn comes with the simplest of messages, and warns you, almost apologetically, that it may sound like common sense. The greater portion of truth, he says, is what you call love. And love is hidden. Hidden within each portion of the creation, hidden within each entity, so that each might have the opportunity to find it.

Many do not know that they are love, he says, or that they seek love. Many do not know, in other words, that they seek themselves. But at some point the yearning becomes apparent, and the person becomes a seeker, a conscious pilgrim upon the great path. And then, Hatonn says, come the testings. The obstacles. The seeming difficulties upon the journey.

This is the part I want you to sit with. The difficulties appear threatening, he says, because they must seem real. The illusion has to hold, or the seeker would not participate, and without participating there is no strength gained. When it is clearly known that all is love, the testing is no longer necessary. The illusion is no longer necessary. Until then, the difficulty is the classroom.

So what carries the seeker through, when it seems there is not love anywhere — not within the self, not with the other, not anywhere in the life experience? Two things, Hatonn says, and he names them like old friends. Faith, and will.

Faith cannot be adequately defined, he admits. It is a kind of knowing — the roots of every being are one root, and that knowing takes the form of a trust that somehow, in some way, all is well and shall be well. And the will grows with experience, strengthened each time it is exercised, guided by the desire of the seeker, held upon the path of love by faith.

Listen to how he puts the promise. No seeker is given more than the seeker can bear. The testings are gradual. And you do not journey alone, though you are unique. There is a great company of seekers, seen and unseen, traveling with you, each encouraging each.

Later that same evening, Latwii takes up the same thread in plainer language. The difficulty, they say, is the disguise of love. A drought comes. The crops do not grow, and food is short. One person shares what little there is with all who ask, and in that sharing gives love. Another hoards, grows more separate, more distrustful. Same catalyst. Opposite responses. I love that line of theirs: it is the desire of each which determines the benefit which shall be derived.

So the teaching folds back to the beginning. You stand upon the foundation of love. You are that love. You seek that love. And all about you is some form of that love, made manifest and hidden within the illusion, so that you might have the opportunity of finding it.

If you are in the middle of a testing right now, this one is for you. What looks like the obstacle may be the very thing wearing the disguise. And the disguise, Hatonn says, comes off the moment you stop looking for the threat and start looking for the love underneath it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Trouble Bubble
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the trouble bubble.

Hatonn begins this evening with an image for anyone who has ever felt swallowed by their own mind. You know the feeling, he says — the ball of confusion. The more you struggle inside it, the more the confusion feeds itself. His suggestion is disarmingly simple. Sit down. Relax. Close your eyes. And see yourself rising to the top of the bubble, turning into a form of gaseous light, and escaping entirely.

From above, he says, you can see the confusion for what it is. It is not real. It is an illusion. And you may at any moment escape to your meditative state and find yourself in the palm of the Creator, where the confusion is no longer apparent.

I love the practicality of this. Not a theory about confusion — a way out of it. Look down upon the confusion rather than sitting in the middle of it, he says, and your thoughts begin to collect themselves. You begin to seek the simple truth. The one Thought cannot be confused. It is a simple Thought. Dwell in the love of that oneness.

And then he reframes the whole thing. Confusion, he says, is a tool. Like a saw, like a hammer. You use a saw to saw wood. You use your confusion to work upon yourself. You, in the midst of that confusion, are waiting to learn from it — waiting for the trouble to bubble up until you escape, look back, and learn from your experience.

What a fine tool confusion is, he says, and you can hear the smile in it. What a wonderful illusion you have. He knows you would prefer the security of simple rules. And there is one simple rule, he says. Love wholly and freely and without reserve.

But it takes a lifetime, he admits, for each entity to choose the manner by which love shall be shown, and to whom. So he gives a practice, not a perfection. Return to the one original Thought on a daily basis. It does not matter whether the meditation is five minutes or fifty. What matters is the discipline of turning, again and again, day by day, to the Creator.

He closes with a sound heard through the instrument's own ears — a lonely train going from somewhere to somewhere else, much like you, he says, on a lonely journey. And yet you are together, held on a straight and narrow track, for your vision is of love and your desire is for mercy.

Where is the Creator? he asks. Shall we say the Creator is you? You will not be satisfied. Shall we say the Creator is in the seeking? You will not be satisfied. Shall we tell you that your journey has no end, and that endless journey is the Creator? Perhaps, he says, we come closer to what you desire to hear.

Tonight, if the bubble has you, try it his way. Rise to the top. Turn to light. And look back down at the trouble from the palm of the Creator, where it was never real to begin with.

Thank you for listening.

title: Freedom Is a Risk
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: freedom is a risk.

Hatonn tells a story this evening about a young boy who searched for freedom. He felt the restrictions of his parents — the chores, the expectations — and he wanted none of it. So he left home and went out into the world to be free.

He was practical about it. He got money, so he could buy what made him happy. He found libations that made him feel happy, and chemicals that altered his consciousness, and pretty young girls for his pleasure. He bought the clothes he liked and lived the way he liked. And for a while, the boy was very happy, because he had found his freedom.

But there came a time when no libation made him truly happy, and no repetition of the drugs was enough, and no pretty girl could charm him completely. And the boy realized something terrible. He had bonded himself in slavery to his own desires. He had given himself all that he wanted, and he had lost his freedom.

Years passed. He put down roots, married, raised a family — and found himself once again surrounded by expectations, his and others'. And then, at last, the turn. He began to see beneath the surface of things. He found things to love. And it became very evident to him that he had found his freedom — not by escaping responsibility, but by choosing whom and what to love.

Listen to how Hatonn states the principle. You have one freedom, and that is that you may choose the manner of your being. The more your being has to do with love, the more your manifestation will be service. Each service you perform for others is a stride along the road of freedom.

And here is the part that stings a little. True freedom, he says, is a great risk. Before you gain a clear channel, you may lose much. You must put your foot upon ground you cannot see, because love has asked you to — and somehow, he says, the air begins to be solid, and you have ground beneath your feet that you could not see before.

What you seek when you seek happiness is an illusion, he says. And if you seek freedom from responsibility, you have created a dream within a dream, and you shall be a slave and no free man. But when the freedom you seek is the freedom to love and to serve, you stand on firm ground. Not safe ground — to love is not easy, to serve is most difficult — but firm.

Later, Latwii adds a strange and lovely footnote. The trees do clap their hands, they say, and the birds do sing for joy — at the very level of their being, where every portion of creation recognizes the One. And healing, they suggest, comes when a person can touch that level of rejoicing within themselves. The Creator heals when asked, and every remedy works only insofar as that contact is made.

So the evening leaves you with two images. A man stepping onto ground he cannot see, finding it solid. And a tree, lifting its fingers to the last rays of the sun, clapping its hands for joy. Both of them free. Both of them, in their own way, choosing love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Acorn and the Oak
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the acorn and the oak.

Hatonn wants to talk this evening about your relationship with the Creator, and he starts with the smallest possible things. Look at two bluebirds mating, he says. Is not the tiny entity that breaks through the egg a bluebird? Look at the acorn falling from the oak. In good time, does not the oak duplicate itself, so that yet another beautiful oak waves its leafy fingers through the winds?

The relationship, he says, is identity — an identity within which the uniqueness of each entity is preserved. And when you see one acorn, you have in a sense seen all acorns. Somehow you trust the identity to continue. And you know that the idea and the ideal existed before the first oak, the first bluebird, the first human. The source of those ideas is the Creator. And a portion of all things never comes into manifestation at all, but stays with the Creator — so that what the Creator has made is in the Creator, and the Creator is in what He has made.

Therefore, he says, you carry with you an identity with the Creator which is most usually not carried into manifestation. It is within you. The relationship is identity. You are the Creator, and the Creator is you.

It bristles with trouble, he admits, because it is so simple that mankind finds it almost impossible to accept. If this is true, why cannot your gestures manifest love? Why is this not the natural? Because, he says, the day distracts the eye and the mind. The fingers become busy with petty details. Moment upon moment is lost, and the life wears away without the person ever taking hold of the stream of time and making a conscious effort to manifest love.

So he recommends meditation, daily, and he is tender about how bad at it you may be. The intention to meditate, the setting aside of time, the attempt itself — all of it adds up to an increasing awareness of the sanctity you carry within you. It is not important to meditate well. It is important to desire to meditate well.

And a warning, which I love for its bluntness. That which you seek, you shall find. You will get what you want. Therefore, he says, be sure you are asking for what you truly want. Perhaps the greatest disappointment in many incarnations is the realization that one has gotten what one wished, and the harvest is an unhappy one.

Later, Latwii fields a question about angels, and gives an answer worth keeping. The Confederation, they say, may indeed be described as angelic — but the word angel is usually reserved for those of your own planetary influence who have graduated and chosen to remain, as guides and inner-plane teachers. The Confederation is made of many planetary influences, including your own.

So the evening gives you the same teaching twice, from two mouths. You are identical with the Creator. And you are watched over by those who were once exactly where you are, and chose to stay. Surrender yourself, Hatonn says, to the influence of love. Seek your identity. Begin to recognize who you really are.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Fatted Calf
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the fatted calf.

Hatonn comes this evening to speak about gratitude, and he reaches for a story the instrument knows well — the parable of the prodigal son. A wild young heir demands his fortune before his father's death, squanders it, and ends up eating the food he carries to the swine. He decides to go home and ask to be taken on as a slave. His father sees him from far off, rejoices, and orders a grand celebration. And the patient brother, who never left home, is furious. Why was there never such a party for him?

The father answers: you have always been here with me, and everything I have is yours. But your brother was lost, and now he is found. He was dead, and now he is alive.

Now listen to how Hatonn reads it, because it is not the reading you expect. The prodigal son was not grateful, he says — not when he left, arrogant, nor when he returned, unknowing what awaited him. The good son knew no gratitude either, jealous and wanting more than his share. The father alone was filled with gratitude — for a son who had betrayed him and squandered his inheritance. He could just as easily have been outraged. Instead, the idea of just portions was foreign to him. He gave all that he had, and then found more to give.

Spiritual gratitude is difficult, Hatonn says. It is one of the linchpins on which spiritual development rests. And here is the strange mechanics of it: gratitude calls to itself. It comes within the void of unknowing. The fatted calf is killed before the prodigal son reaches home — before the nature of this unexpected return is known.

So many experiences partake of this vulnerability. Something occurs, and by the nature of your illusion it tends to be more painful than pleasurable. And yet — be grateful for the challenge. Be grateful for the prodigal son offering you that challenge. Be grateful for the infinity of love which is your birthright.

Give thanks, he says, not for what you see, not for the kindliness of the Creator, not for the excellence of your circumstance. Give thanks because you are able to give thanks. Because you live and breathe and think. You define the nature of your being. No circumstance ever may, as long as this is understood.

Later, Latwii adds a companion teaching on transformation — that the seeker moves through boundaries that widen, that faith and will propel the journey, and that each new step is taken, as they put it, like the fool stepping into space. First the thought, then the step, and the step is taken because it is thought.

Tonight, try it the father's way. Find one thing — not a good thing, just a thing — and give thanks for it before you know how it turns out. Kill the fatted calf early. Let gratitude step into the void, and see what comes home to meet it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Stumbling Block
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the stumbling block.

Hatonn opens the evening with a story about a woman — hungry, he calls her. Hungry for everything life might teach, for every food life might give. She pursues one path and then another, physically, mentally, emotionally, spiritually. She marries, she has children, she knows pain inside every pleasure. And at the end of her life, she says, she was still hungry for experiences she felt instinctively were hers — and she did not know for what she hungered.

There is no separation between this woman and love, Hatonn says. Nor between anyone and that same love. And the teacher known as Jesus offered peace — but said clearly, this peace is not what the world thinks of as peace. When one of his followers asked what journey he was going on, he answered: each of us is the journey. The journey is not outside yourself.

Then Hatonn gives a practice. Walk up your own mountain in meditation. Picture yourself cleansing yourself at a clear, cool mountain stream. Then, in clean garments, visit the most high place of your being. Metaphysical peace does not deny the chaos of the illusion, he says. It reaffirms the perfection of the Creator — the Creator that is in you, and the you that is in the Creator.

The heart of the evening, though, comes when Latwii takes the questions, and someone asks about the stumbling block — that hurdle every seeker seems to hit, especially the urge to run around telling everyone about what you have found. Latwii's answer is one of my favorites in the archive.

The new seeker, they say, has a fire set within the heart, and the fire burns bright — but it can burn and singe as well as illumine. The seeker runs about with a torch, sparks flying, little fires smoldering here and there, quickly extinguished. It is most likely, they say gently, that the seeker shall find great difficulty in using this flame in a manner which is both loving and wise.

And the stumbling block itself? Every so-called stumbling block is most important for any seeker. It is not the purpose of your illusion to move smoothly. In the upsetting of the journey, all is shifted about, and there must be a reassessment of what has been gained and what is sought. Each stumbling block does not hinder the journey but truly speeds it — providing the opportunity for what is old and worn to be discarded, and for something new to be placed before the seeker's mind.

Then the image that stays with me. The spiritual treasures of this illusion, Latwii says, are very infrequently gained in a conscious manner. It is like a merchant who counts his gold at the end of the day — its purity, its weight. But when he reads his own book of life, he will find it was not the gold that mattered. It was the manner of the transactions. The love given. The love received.

You move in a darkness, they say, seeking small slivers of light. And it is within the heart of your being that such seeking is motivated and recorded in its true sense.

So if you have hit a stumbling block lately — if the path has jolted you — consider that it may be doing exactly what it is for. Discarding the worn-out. Making room. And the gold you think you are counting may not be the gold that counts.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Bars of the Cage
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the bars of the cage.

This evening brings a rarer voice. Oxal does not come often to this group, and they begin by telling you plainly who they are: those more involved in the questions of the mind than the heart. And then, with the dry honesty of the wise, they admit that their next lesson is the balance between compassion and wisdom — and they wish to speak to you of love from the standpoint of wisdom.

Perfect compassion, they say — which we call love, for want of a better word — is power. Power so disciplined, guided, and considered that all things work together in harmony. That which powers the universe is not understood. That which powers the universe is love. Wisdom is the vibration which love uses. It is the material the artist uses to create experience.

Then the image. A ship with its sails furled upon a great sea. It may seem you are victims of the wind and the waves. But within each of you, they say, is an innate guide, a rudder that steers you if you will let it. And what steers you is not a wisdom, but an association with love.

And then they say the hard thing, the thing this episode is named for. You are, they say, behind the bars of an illusion — the illusion that you were born and you will die and you will be no more. Within that illusion there are few good reasons for faith, for behaving ideally, for holding ideals. And yet the instinct of those who seek has put them in touch with the awareness that the true self — indeed, the majority of the self — is outside the prison already.

You put yourself in this situation, they say. And you have within you that which may remove you from the prison. Not death, though that will remove the bars. Your own ability to seek. So they urge you, at least once in your day, to say to yourself: the bars of my cage shall not hold me, for I shall sit beyond space and time, and I shall seek love, and I shall seek the truth, and I shall do it in silence.

In loving alone, they say, is there peace. If you love yourself completely, you are at peace. If you wish to serve others in love completely, you are at peace. Between these two points, in one degree or another, you shall not be at peace.

Climb the mountain slowly, they say. Slowly, and see each step clearly. What you are doing, what you are thinking, how you are seeking, how you are feeling — these are your tools. They can make you rejoice, even, perhaps, as you weep.

Later, Latwii answers questions about couples who seek together — about shared catalyst, shared lessons, and karma. And they offer a correction worth keeping: what looks like a karma-free bond is better described as balanced karma. To remove the karma, they say, would be to remove the experience — and the experience is the resource.

A word of care, since this evening touches on bodily aches and their meanings: Latwii is offering their own lens, their opinions, not medical counsel. Take what helps your seeking, and leave the rest — they would insist on it.

The bars are real to the eyes. But the majority of you, Oxal says, is already outside them. Sit beyond space and time, even for a moment, and seek love. The cage cannot hold what was never truly inside it.

Thank you for listening.

title: A Portion of Joy
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: a portion of joy.

Hatonn comes this evening to talk about reality — not your reality, but a kind of reality that is hard to discover inside the heavy chemical illusion you live in. It has been called, he says, the Kingdom of Heaven. And its most apparent condition, the thing you would notice first, is its harmony.

As he speaks, he says, millions of life forms are vibrating in harmony with you, adjusting their pitch and tone to meet yours. The very particles of air, furnished with light, scintillate in a dazzling display of harmony that ascends and ascends until all is white and light. This is occurring about you at this moment.

The Kingdom of Heaven is harmony, he says. It is fourth density, and many remember it the way you remember home. Beyond harmony is unity — the white light — the natural experience of fifth density, which many yearn to abide in always.

These experiences are within you to remember, not to gain, he says. And meditation is the key that opens the door — a reaching out and turning of the latch. Regardless of how well one meditates, one is still reaching. Often the first signs come distorted, in dreams or half-waking visions, personified by a teacher or a symbol that haunts you. Pursue them, he says. They are the road within yourself, guiding you past the blocks you set up against yourself.
