And then he says the thing about the mind that I keep coming back to. Your higher self, he says, intends for your illusion to block and block and block again every pathway — so that you may express love in the removal of blockage. The mind is a servant that is too often the master by default. So he asks you to ponder: what do you have that may seek, that you may trust more than your mind? What shall be the master of your mind?

And then the passage this episode is named for — the one I want you to carry. There is no justification for your existence, he says. Nor has there ever been. Nor will there ever be. You do not exist because you think, or because of what you have done, or because of who you know. You are a portion of joy which has no reason for being but itself. And there is mercy within you, like a pointer, saying: you need no justification. Come and follow joy.

You do not seek that which does not exist, he says, as he closes. That which you seek is within you, and is awaiting the reaching. You have hands. You have a will. Reach out, grasp, and open.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love With No Object
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love with no object.

Hatonn begins with the pulse. The heart of love beats, he says, and the entire creation beats with it — each star, each galaxy, pulsing its own slight variation on the universal signal. Much has been made of your astrology, he says, but the most vital portion of that art is the specific note of the music of the heartbeat which pulses from each of your stars.

These rhythms reach you — the beating of your heart, your breath, your cycles — like light shone through different colored lenses, each color affecting you slightly differently. And you, in your turn, affect the universe. When even two or three gather together to seek light and offer love, he says, they form a light as exciting and visible as one of your great cities. A group is not the sum of its parts. It is far greater.

Then the story. Once upon a time there was a king. Not a great king, not a cruel king — a mediocre king. About him were the queen with her feasts, the counselors with their advice, the tax collectors filling his coffers. And least of all in the kingdom, a beggar woman at the city gates — her back hunched, one eye looking east and the other west. All reviled her, including the king. And she blessed all who went by, those who gave money and those who did not.

This is a description, Hatonn says, of the different ways you look at love. It is assumed there is an object of love — in the story, the king. Some give the best of their hearts, some the best of their minds, some the gifts of their greed, some as little as they can. But the one who truly loves gives love with no object.

I want to read you that line again, because it is the whole evening. The one who truly loves gives love with no object.

Your minds will ask, he knows: how can I acquire this principle? I love a few special ones — they are the object of my love. But love is more simple than that. To love, to serve, involves moving with the heartbeat and being careless of the object. The heart does not always know how to serve. No gift is predictably correct. The heartbeat that pulses within each, for each, from each and to each, is one original Thought.

Later, Latwii is asked about the children born to those called wanderers, and about parents — whom Latwii calls, more truly, teachers. Entities choose their households before birth, they say, for the compass bearings they need. And the parents' part, in the end, is the same as everyone's: to love, and to let the prearranged lessons unfold.

Love that which is, Hatonn says, whether blessed or cursed by those images of yourself who pass you by. For the activity of loving is, in fact, the sharing of the Creator with the Creator.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Unseen Fruit
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the unseen fruit.

Latwii closes this evening with an image for everyone who has ever wept through the work of becoming. Know, they say, that your work in this illusion is work which produces a fruit from such pain, and from so many, many tears.

You exist within an illusion of great benefit, they say — a darkness, a forgetting, in which it is not easily apparent that you are the one infinite Creator. And that very darkness is what allows the fruit of love to be harvested. You gather the fruit of love, they say, with every movement of your mind, your life, and your experience.

It is also, they admit, the great deterrent to your enjoyment of the illusion. For it is difficult to feel inspired by a fruit which you cannot see, which you cannot taste. Yet such fruit is gathered in each moment of your experience — and enhanced, they say, by your continuing desire to give that which you have for that which you cannot see.

Earlier in the evening, they give the practice that goes with this. If your sensitivity is growing — if you are sensing more than you used to, in meditation or in daily life — then tune. Determine a means of tuning and challenging whatever you sense, so that you express only what is positive and beneficial. And use that same tuning in the daily life: set aside a time, preferably before the day begins, to set the course you shall attempt to follow — a course built upon service and seeking, illuminated by the light and love of the One.

A ritualizing of the tuning, they call it. It will not make the darkness go away. It will make you steadier inside it. And the fruit — the fruit you cannot see — goes on gathering, moment by moment, with every movement of the mind.

So tonight, before the day begins tomorrow, set the course. Tune the instrument. And trust that the tears are not wasted. They are, Latwii says, the very soil the fruit grows in.

Thank you for listening.

title: Four Small Letters
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: four small letters.

Hatonn begins this evening with a confession of sorts. We often have difficulty, he says, finding new and more exquisite ways of praising a message which is invariably simple and always the same. The message is the message of love. And no amount of words can ever express that which is so simple — so they must keep trying, in ever new words, to say the one word.

The meaning of the word often gets lost upon your planet, he says. Few stop to think about this word when it is heard or spoken. But the immensity in this single, simple word is truly overwhelming. The energy that goes into this word is more powerful than we are able to express.

To picture love as a very small and insignificant four-letter word, he says, is to deprive that word of its true and deeper meaning. Take not this word lightly. Take this word to heart, and within your own consciousness expand that simple word to its ever-reaching potential. Let not those four small letters get lost in a haze of many letters. Let them stand out and shine with the power that is truly within the thought behind the word.

Then he turns to something your culture gets backwards. He wants to speak, he says, of a characteristic often thought to be a hindrance — what you call weakness. Again and again, the compliments go to those seen as strong: strong-willed, strong in ambition, strong in the face of adversity. Far too little credit is given to weakness.

Weakness, he suggests, is frequently the appearance given by one who has such a firm grasp upon the situation that the entity is aware there is nothing that can be done — and therefore there is nothing to do. It may appear that such a person is weak. In actuality, the person is far stronger than the one who struggles and attempts to control others and forces beyond any reasonable control.

And then his example: water. For earth is heavy, fire is light, the air is whispering — and water, the weakest of all the elements, goes about its business as gentle rain. It soaks into the earth, runs to the ocean, rises again. It attempts no conquest. It is drawn to the living things that thirst, and to the low places it is called toward.

Do not mistake yielding for weakness, then. The rain does not argue with the mountain. It simply continues — and the mountain, in the end, is shaped by the rain. And do not mistake the small word for a small thing. Four letters, holding the immensity that made the universe.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Mute Question
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the mute question.

Hatonn opens with a line for the questioners. Poor indeed is the man who has never asked a question, he says, for riches do not lie in the answers but in the questions themselves.

He asks you to examine what questions you concerned yourself with today. Not your conclusions — he does not care about those. Only what was in the forefront of the mind. Are your questions petty and mundane, or have you asked for that which draws you outside the world you know? How rich you are, he says, if you have dressed yourself in seeking as if it were a festive garment, and gone forth with the rejoicing question: how can I perceive such loveliness as this day has offered me?

Your culture, he says, is interested in the bottom line — the final answer, the solution. Each of you has an inborn series of bottom lines, typical solutions, normal habits of mind. Without meditation, you bounce from situation to situation until you find one where your bottom line fits. There is a quicker way of learning, he says, and that is to focus upon the questions and not upon the answers.

You know the answers already, he tells you — what they say is so utterly simplistic and so repetitious that you can have no doubt. The bottom line is love. But what is the question? What will you ask? What avenues will you seek? How much of the truth do you want to know within this fragile cage of your physical body? What great heart do you wish to realize?

Meditation, then, is a form of reaching within the vast infinity of your own being with the mute question — the question that has no words. And because it has no words and is not articulated, it is the pure question, and you will receive the purest answer with it. For you listen in silence just as you ask in silence, and you shall be answered also in silence, but with a power that transcends expression.

You are what you seek, he says. Therefore the choice of what you seek is all-important. And here is the practice he leaves you: do not tell yourself what you are learning. Ask. What am I perceiving, what am I learning, where is love now, right now in this moment? You cannot tell yourself what you are learning — you must ask. And the answers may well be different than those you would create for yourself.

Later, Latwii is asked why the accounts of those who have contacted the one known as Jesus differ so much from one another. Their answer is gentle and exact. Each call is answered, they say — but the response is filtered through the beliefs, habits, and rituals of the one who calls. It is like a story whispered from ear to ear around a circle: by the end, it has some resemblance to the original, and some distortion. Do not be discouraged by distortion, they say. If there were no darkness and no distortion, there would be no experience.

And if you wish to serve one who seems to have stopped seeking — who sits upon a stone beside the trail — Latwii's counsel is this: make the offer. Offer your being, without dedication to any particular result. For who can say what path another should travel? One can only be, and offer being to another. This is love. There are no conditions, and no guarantees.

Tonight, then, do not reach for one more answer. Reach for the better question. Ask it without words. And listen, in the silence, for what answers back.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Two Carnivals
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the two carnivals.

Hatonn comes this evening with a parable about a fair — a grand and glorious carnival, a bazaar where merchants display their wares and thousands come to try their luck and rejoice in being part of a happy crowd. In a deep sense, he says, this is part of the motivation for those who incarnate upon your planet. From outside the physical vehicle, it looks easier than it is. The carnival flags can flutter dismally. The machinery that governs the rides may not always work.

Then he walks you out of the fair, onto a dark street. It is night. The fair is in a poor section of the city. Someone lies upon the sidewalk, lost in drink. And he asks you the question the whole evening turns on: shall you sit down and talk to the Creator now, or shall you pass him by?

For if you are open to hear the cries of those about you, he says, you will rapidly become aware that there is no day in which the poor, the hungry, the homeless, and the spiritually wasted are not crying out to you personally. You have a brightly lit carnival, and as you stroll through the gates you find a dark carnival. And what shall you do to be of service?

There was one among you, he says, who chose the darker circus. The teacher known as Jesus reached for disciples among poor folk — a prostitute, a tax collector, a persecutor. And yet he also rode the rides with the bright crowds, and spoke in the temples. All he did that was different, Hatonn says, was to point out that the heart is more important than the Law. Then he would walk forth into the streets and lift those from the gutter.

When the seats at the great feast remain empty, the teacher's instructions are simple: go out into the streets and gather all that you can find. Shall we condemn those who lie in the gutter because they have not legs upon which to stand? Shall we sneer at the hungry because we have not given them bread? When is a spirit not worthy to be fed?

And then the image I cannot get out of my head. The instrument, Hatonn tells us, once imagined this teacher coming back into the inner cities — sitting down in the gutter, taking a peanut butter sandwich, breaking it, and it would be food enough for all who came. Your daily bread is but a symbol, he says. Remember always that your peanut butter sandwiches, like fishes and loaves, are in infinite supply for those who wish never to hunger again. Break them and give them, for it is an infinite universe.

This is your chance, he says. You have undoubtedly bitten off more than you can chew — and of course you have. This is the essence of learning the lessons of love: to take more than you can chew, and then to pray your way, to meditate your way, until strength is given you, not from yourself, but through yourself.

If all things can become one to you, then you can become one with all things. And you may turn to all whom you meet and say: I shall meet you in paradise.

A word of care, because this session was spoken into real grief in that room — a death that came by a person's own hand. The voices are reflecting on loss, not prescribing anything about it. If you are carrying that kind of darkness yourself, please reach for a living hand: a trusted person, a counselor, someone who can sit down beside you on that dark street and stay.

Rejoice, Hatonn says, and love one another. Celebrate. Share what you have. And when you walk out into the cold, offer your jacket, your food, your substance, with gladness at heart. See the Creator — and so shall the Creator see you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Princess and the Road
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the princess and the road.

Hatonn tells a fairy tale this evening — and insists, for the purposes of the parable, that the heroine must be a princess. She is powerful and lonely beyond words. Courtier after courtier files by with gifts — livestock, pearls, kingdoms, new realms to govern. In none of these things is she interested. Feast day after feast day, she closes audience still powerful and still lonely.

Then an ill-garbed stranger comes to her court. He is not a courtier or a peasant. His home is the road. And in rough words he makes his plea. Milady, he says, I can give you nothing but my days, my nights, my love, and my road. I have nothing but my flesh and my heart, my mind and my honor, and I give these into your hands. Whether you accept them or not, you are and will always have been my love.

The princess comes slowly down from her high throne and takes his hand. You must help me too, she says, for I do not know that I have a road. I only know that I wish to find one. I do not know that I love. I only wish to find love.

They do not stop for retainers or chairs or any of the panoply of her circumstance. They begin to walk, and within the hour they are out of sight. And strangely enough, Hatonn says, the princess and the stranger were never seen again. As she became open to love, just so she became invisible to a great deal of that which mortal eyes may see.

And here is the teaching inside the tale. You feel clumsy and awkward in your flesh, Hatonn says — and so you are, compared to higher-density bodies. You feel numb, unable to see the larger picture. And yet yours is the splendor of giving the true generosity that only comes when you truly cannot see and cannot hear the divine, but only have faith that there is such a thing as divine love.

If someone gave you a perfect emerald, he says, and told you to swallow it and wear it within your body, you would think that man to be mad. And yet that is your consciousness — a perfect jewel, placed with care, with love, with wisdom, into flesh, that you may pour out your life beautifully if you wish, having nothing more to go on than the deep-felt feeling that this is your road.

The chances for courage, for serving, for allowing your flesh to become bread for others, are enormous, he says. How little you value yourselves compared to the reality as we see it. Never doubt your worth to those about you. And love, he adds — love is completing circuits. It is not necessarily giving.

What road is that, he asks, the road we have walked a bit ahead of you? Keep walking, my friends. You shall see. And it shall be a joyful thing.

Thank you for listening.

title: Only a Birthmark
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: only a birthmark.

This evening Hatonn does something unusual. The story is told through many instruments, the contact moving around the room from voice to voice — and the story it tells is about a little boy.

There was once a young boy not like the other boys — except that in every way that mattered, he was exactly like them. He laughed as other boys laugh. But he had been born with a terrible birth defect, which changed his appearance greatly. And so he was an outcast.

The boy knew that most of those about him could not see beyond his deformation. And he began to look about him at the world of trees and flowers and small animals — and he saw great beauty and variation of form, yet no shunning of one creature by another. He pondered long why people would treat him in a manner other than they treated each other.

One day he found his mother sobbing in her room, angry with the Creator for being cruel to her. How, Mommy, how? the little boy asked. He gave us your disease to bear before the world, she said. And the boy answered — listen to this answer — Oh, no, Mommy, that's not right. This is only a birthmark. But I think that many people have a disease in their hearts because they can't see me.

The mother looked into her son's eyes as she never had before, and saw love there, given as freely as rain falling from the sky. And she felt remorse for her bitter words — for the deformation she had felt such a burden was of no consequence beside the love her son could give.

I thought about it in the woods, the boy tells her. None of the leaves blames another leaf for being different. All the squirrels play together, even if one is browner than the others. It's only humans, Mommy, that see in a funny way. And they just can't see me.

And Hatonn turns the story on the listener, the way he always does. How many defects have you seen today? How many masks have you been unable to penetrate? How many bright and adoring eyes have you missed because of your judgment — because of the disease of your eyes, because of the lack of the loving and open heart?

Do you see yourself with love's kind vision? he asks. Are you aware that the Creator shines within you — a candle you cannot quench, and a light which you need not hide? To the pure, all things are pure, your holy works say. To the Creator, all things are the Creator.

Later, Latwii is asked about obstacles — those times when every step you try to take is thwarted, and you feel you are just hanging around. You cannot determine with certainty, they say, whether an obstacle is meant to test your desire or to stop your movement. But even resting can be the lesson. There must be faith, they say, that for this moment, resting provides the greater lesson.

So the evening gives you the boy's clear eyes for others, and Latwii's patience for yourself. See with love. And when the road is blocked, rest without shame — the resting may be the very lesson you came for.

Thank you for listening.

title: Throw Yourself Over the Cliff
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: throw yourself over the cliff.

This evening is a training session. The group has gathered for intensive meditation, and Latwii is working with new instruments — exercising them, conditioning them, teaching them, for the first time, how to lend their voices to something beyond themselves.

And the teaching they give these beginners is the same teaching the archive gives everyone, only plainer. It is difficult, they say, to know illusion from reality, falsity from truth. That which you receive, you shall receive subjectively. Each gives of himself, so that what comes through will feel like nothing more than one's own thoughts. This is part of the process of learning to channel.

So they ask the new instrument not to expect proof — only an urge, indistinguishable from any other urge to speak. Relax, they say. Empty the mind as far as possible. Challenge every urge by the white light, and all will be well. Above all, do not attempt to analyze. After the challenging is done, move as you feel. Speak as you are moved.

You do not know what the next word will be, they say. You do not know what the next thought will be when you channel. That is the way it works. And so they ask for something surprising alongside all that reverence: a sense of foolishness. A sense of throwing oneself over the cliff into thin air. A sense of being a clown.

I love that pairing — the utmost respect for the service, and the willingness to look foolish doing it. Those who speak most easily in ordinary life, Latwii notes, are often the hardest to train as channels, because the whole thing becomes too important to get wrong. The cure is to hold both: the honor, and the leap.

Since the first word is the most difficult, they begin the new channel with one word only. That word is I. Who is I, they ask, and can you tell a lie when you say I? Shall you channel I alone? Is there more than one I? That most beloved portion of the creation to whom we speak: I is all that there is.

And for those drawn toward the deeper trance states, they give safeguards, plainly. Tune first, as you would for any meditation. Surround your place of working with a wall of light. Undertake the attempt with great joy. And have another entity with you — someone in harmony with you — who can help you return, whether that means massaging stiff limbs or simply talking, to give you a point of focus on the way back.

The desire to do the work, they say, is the greatest portion of the work. The offering of the service is much like the performing of it: to have the desire, to be open to the opportunity, and then to move with the energy as it is presented to you.

Whatever your own cliff is — the thing you are afraid to begin because you might do it wrong — tonight's teaching is to leap anyway. Speak as you are moved. And trust that the first word, like the first I, already contains everything.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Fearless Child
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the fearless child.

Hatonn tells a short, strange parable this evening — about a young child who chose to travel among others of his nation. The child was young, Hatonn says, yet not afraid — for the child had yet to learn to fear his other selves. And fear, he says quietly, is an acquired trait.

So the child wandered fearlessly through forest and through city, perceiving no distinction between himself and the other occupants of his world. To the child's untrained mind, the blessings of the world were shared equally — and those of the second density, the animals and plants, seemed much less resistant to accepting the bounty that was their own. The child could extend love, and receive it, and travel peacefully through what you call wilderness.

Eventually the child sought the company of his own kind, and found instead bafflement. Those to whom the child extended love eyed him with suspicion, and returned only distrust. The child persisted — confident, from his way with wild creatures, that patience would win their trust in time. But the child had a patience of the soul that exceeded the patience of the physical vehicle. And eventually the child's body died.

One might call it a wasted incarnation, Hatonn says. No apparent communication established. No apparent acceptance received. But consider, he says — consider the blessings imparted upon a confused whole by the small part which had, however briefly, obtained inner balance. Is it not true that the plant, however unaware of the source of its light, will nonetheless thrive and grow in its presence?

And then the line this episode carries. Remember with pleasure and with love, he says, those who may have gone before seemingly unheard — for in truth the echoes of their efforts still resound throughout your spheres of existence.

Those who have ears may perceive the guides and pathfinders among you. But those who fail to hear are nonetheless served magnificently by those who break the trail, marking the signposts for those who would eventually choose to follow.

There is a lighter moment at the end of the evening. Asked for a story of their own, Latwii declines with a laugh — the parables, they say, are Hatonn's department, and they have done no homework. They will consider developing some backups.

So tonight is for the trailblazers — the ones who went first, were not understood, and kept walking anyway. You may never see what your walking made possible. Walk it anyway. The echoes, Hatonn says, are still resounding.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Use of Memory
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the use of memory.

A rarer voice opens this evening — Oxal, who tells you at once that they are more involved in the questions of the mind than the heart. And they have come to talk about your memory: how you use it, and how badly you usually do.

It is easy, they say, to gaze back into the misty and distorted realms of memory in order to chastise yourself — for what you did, or for what you did not do. And laid upon that, like a stone upon a rabbit, is a further distortion: judgment. The judgment of whatever deity you profess as yours.

Here is their first suggestion, and it is startling. You shall judge yourself, they say, just as you are now judging yourself. The deity implied in judgment — the higher authority — is and will be nothing more than light. Some thoughts set up a vibration that can withstand only a little light. Others allow a far greater portion of light to be enjoyed. That, they say, is judgment. It is completely and utterly objective. As simple as asking of a light bulb: can the current generate thirty watts, forty watts, a hundred? You are an instrument, and you are to some extent tuned.

But if memory is not for judging yourself by hindsight — and hindsight, they say, does not generate light — then what is it for? Have you considered, they ask, that it is the present to which your memory may best speak?

There are too many things in most entities' daily experience, they say. The mind is cluttered and works inefficiently. Each decision of the busy day can best be made in the light of all the experience held in your memory — but to use it, you must slow down the tempo of your living. You need not remove the tasks and commitments. You must remove the distractedness. Create your day, they say, rather than reacting to its events.

And for that, the old prescription: meditation, daily. When you meditate, you are seeking the truth, and that which you seek is like fire — powerful beyond your imagination. He who realizes light will heal. He who realizes love will bless. You can change your life, they say — you can do it in the twinkling of an eye — by changing the use of memory from hindsight to sightfulness of the present moment.

You are not a victim of your own behavior, they say. You are not nailed to the cross of your own previous thinking. The original Thought has the power to give you the peace of the present moment, the fullness of the present joy, and the discipline of one who creates.

Oh, to have the faith that you have, they say — for to you all that is essential is shrouded in mystery, and only through faith do you seek. It is not within our power, they admit. We refine. But you — you are mining. You are mining for your own precious heart.

Later, Latwii takes questions about spiritual community, and gives a line worth carrying into any group you belong to. The ideals begin a group, they say — and the feet of clay continue it. When clay feet can be continually transformed by the ideals, reborn moment to moment, then you shall see the continuation of such a group.

Tonight, then: stop using memory as a courtroom. Use it as a lamp for the present moment. The past cannot be re-lit. But it can light the step you are taking right now.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Book With a Mirror
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the book with a mirror.

Hatonn retells an old story this evening — one the instrument does not know, he says, though it is written among your older works. It is about a young man determined to learn the truth.

He had studied the natural world and the world of books, and nowhere could he find the metaphysical base for existence that accounted for all his experience. So he sold all that he had — and he was a wealthy man — bought a great ocean-going ship, hired a crew, and set out to find the one teacher with the one body of teaching that would contain all he needed to know about who he was and where he was going.

He sailed the seven seas. He climbed mountains on many continents. And one lined face after another told him the same story: that although he had a ship and they did not, they were on a journey together — and they had not found what he was seeking either.

At last he climbed a holy mountain, bathed in a mountain lake so placid it looked like glass, and found his clothing replaced by a simple white garment. He followed a trail upward — someone had made that trail, someone had gone before him — until he reached a mesa, and a castle of stone, and a man so ancient he seemed held up by his robes, holding a large leather book.

Sire, the young man said, kneeling, I have come to find the one teaching that will inform me on every matter. The old man laughed. You are not the first who has come looking for such a book, he said, and you shall not be the last. I have it. Here it is. Take it away with you if you wish.

The young man's heart was in his throat. He fumbled the fastenings open — and looked in. It was a mirror, intricately set, bound within the leather. For a few seconds he gazed dumbly at his own image. Then he grew angry and threw the book back. You told me you had all that I wanted to know, and then you give me a mirror.

The old man was still laughing. Young man, he said, I have never known a single seeker who did not throw that one total and complete authority back in my face.

It is not always easy to accept your own nature, Hatonn says. And yet perfection lies within the very eyes that meet yours each time you gaze in the mirror. The final authority is yourself. You may find things which illumine and heal and enliven you — but you will not find the unalloyed truth except in the wordless depth of your inner silence.

Later, Latwii is asked about the price of all this seeking — the young man sold everything, after all. And they answer with the parable of the pearl of great price. What you pay, they say, is a sliding scale: you surrender all of it, whatever it is. The widow's mite and the millions are the same amount — everything. The price is putting nothing before the seeking.

And money itself? There is nothing wrong with money, or power, or position, they say — they are tools, like a carpenter's saw. It is the love of them that stops the seeking. A spiritual seeker may well have money, so long as there is no emotional load upon it, and it is held simply as a means.

So the evening ends where the young man began — at the mirror. Settle down in front of it, Hatonn says. Gaze within the self, and you behold the universe. The book you have been sailing the seas to find has been bound inside your own chest all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Hairline Shadow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the hairline shadow.

It is a few nights before Christmas, and Hatonn comes to speak about light. From the beginning, he says, there has been darkness. From the beginning, there has been light. Side by side were these two created. Darkness does not comprehend light — so it is written in your holy works. Neither does light comprehend darkness.

You live, he says, upon the hairline shadow which lies between light and darkness. Your illusion is that of twilight. It is especially noticeable when you spend your time with the outer darkness — but even on the brightest summer day, with the butterflies dancing, you are still in shadow. This is your density: the density which chooses, between the effort to comprehend the light and the effort to comprehend the darkness.

In each situation there is darkness and there is light, he says. Your choice is your own. In the darkest and most difficult of situations, there is light. You yourself are a brightly burning fire — created, and creating, consciousness. You may create darkness. You may create light. Each thought and action will reflect your choice.

And then the promise, which I want you to hear slowly. The love and the light of the infinite Creator, he says, is quite literally at your beck and call. It is your calling that draws the light unto you, that bridges the void which you call darkness. It is the intensity and the faithfulness of your calling that sustains that bridge.

In your world you are taught to fear many things, he says. But your fears are groundless. The one whose birth you celebrate once said: I am with you always. Your birthright is the right of choice — and your road homeward is simply to choose to follow the light home.

At the very end of the evening, a brief voice sounds — Amira, chiming like a bell rung one tone higher each time. O precious the moment, all glorious the hour, when first you are born, they sing. All that is old may now be put away. The manger of your light is ready for the babe. Now you are new.

My children, my children, this is always true, Amira says. Do not forget, but turn and rejoice.

So on the hairline shadow, in the twilight, the teaching is simple. Call, and the light bridges the void. Choose, and the road leads home. You are new — not once, at Christmas, but always. Now. Again.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Center of the Storm
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the center of the storm.

It is the last evening of December, nineteen eighty-four, and the voices that come through call themselves Hatonn and Latwii. The circle has gathered for an intensive meditation, and Hatonn begins not with a teaching but with a story. I love how they do this. The story is about a storm, and a couple, and what survives when everything is taken away.

The clouds had been gathering for a day, Hatonn says, and the electric tension of the storm was in the air. A man and a woman stood on an exposed outcropping of land and asked themselves the oldest question of all. Shall we stay where we are, or shall we go somewhere safe? They chose a middle path, retiring a short distance inland, hoping to feel the thrill of the storm without the danger of it.

But the storm had other plans. The waves thrashed the beaches, the winds flattened everything that reared itself from the earth, and all that the couple owned was destroyed. Much else was destroyed too. And Hatonn says something I want you to sit with. The storm laughed, for it was a wind that carried the cruel and merciless order to extinguish, to cleanse, and to remove.

In the aftermath, as the couple planned to rebuild, they discovered something. As they considered what was truly valued, each by each, it was brought home to them that the love which bound them together was the most cherished thing in their lives. They had lost everything they could touch, and found the one thing they could not.

And then Hatonn turns the story. For another storm grew, this time within. With money now easier to come by, every choice about how to spend it became an argument. Two people, Hatonn says, only two children of the one Father, and there were numerous irreconcilable differences of opinion. And the storm laughed again. The woman thought, what did I ever see in him? The man thought, what can we possibly have in common? And they looked upon each other, Hatonn says, and did not behold love.

I will not soften this the way a fairy tale would, and neither does Hatonn. Instead he asks the question that this whole evening turns on. What was the greater loss, the loss of every possession, or the loss of one human relationship?

Things are never what they seem, he says, and then adds the driest line in the archive. This is an old and worn out statement, he says. The reason it is so worn is that it is, insofar as we know, the absolute truth. Your third-density experience is made of whole cloth an illusion. No part of it is real. Only that which comes from beyond it and manifests through it has a more lasting reality.

Then comes the turn toward hope, and it is magnificent. The one original Thought of the Creator, Hatonn says, is expressed perfectly in your being. Not in an idealistic sense, but in the sense of here and now. Bitterness, wrangling, disputes and disharmony are all part of the rough and ready perfection which the Creator praises in you. Each of you is perfect, yet each seeks the harmony it seems not to have.

To you, he says, falls the drama of wresting the one original Thought from each storm. Yours is the privilege of becoming. And then the question I want to leave ringing. Does the storm toss you away, or shall you find the center of that storm?

You cannot stop the laughter of the storm, Hatonn says. Its cruel and mocking tongues will follow all who seek the truth, and indeed those who are deep asleep. But your nature, your birthright, your power is in that which cannot be denied, that which is from everlasting to everlasting. Choose, my friends, he says. Choose with joy, and learn to laugh ever more deeply, resting in arms polished smooth by trust.

And one more thread, from Latwii, who spent the evening answering the circle's questions. Asked what a relationship is, they said this. A relationship is the interaction of portions of the one Creator toward a purpose, that purpose being that each should aid the other in realizing that the one Creator dwells in both. And the ideal toward which any couple might strive is not a perfect partnership, but a perfect attitude. Unconditional acceptance and forgiveness of all.

So tonight, if there is a storm laughing somewhere in your life, consider the possibility that it is asking you a question. What is the greater loss? And having answered it, find the center, choose with joy, and laugh a little more deeply than you did yesterday.

Thank you for listening.

title: Petals for the Creator
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: petals for the Creator.

January sixth, nineteen eighty-five, a Sunday meditation, and the evening opens with Oxal, a voice we do not hear often. What Oxal says that night is one of the strangest and most tender ideas in the whole archive. It begins with a question turned inside out.

Within your minds, Oxal says, there is always the question, is there a Creator? It might surprise you to experience the reversal of that question. Is there anything which is created? Yes, there is that which is created. And then the deeper question. Why should the Creator of all that there is create that which is thrown apart from the Creator, divided by illusion upon illusion, separated by dreams and fantasies and phantasmagoria of all kinds?

Listen to the answer, because it changes everything. The reason for your being, Oxal says, is very simple. You are experiencing, as we are experiencing, as if you were separate from the Creator. Picture a vast bleak winter landscape, the skeletons of trees against the sky, dead leaves scurrying in a bitter wind. That is the creation without the created. All is potential. Nothing experiences.

The Creator could have simply created beauty according to a pattern of Its own choosing, Oxal says. This the Creator did not do. It is our understanding that our Creator is hungry for that which It cannot Itself will, and that is the fruit that you bear in your experiences. Each day you bloom a little. You send out petals of anger, forgiveness, love, kindness, jealousy, hunger and thirst for that which is physical and that which is metaphysical. And all these things are to the Creator as flowers, delicate and beautiful, too insubstantial to pluck, but to be watched with great joy.

I love that line. Too insubstantial to pluck, but to be watched with great joy. You feel joy and the Creator feels joy. You feel hope and the Creator hopes again. All things that you feel are gifts, your gifts to the one infinite Creator.

And here is the part that undoes me. Do you feel that you have made many errors today, Oxal asks, that you have somehow gone astray, that your energies were scattered or low? Then do not judge, not in this moment. For that too is a gift which the Creator treasures. All the colors of emotion and feeling, all the distortions of the one original Thought which can be developed by an independent consciousness, are as blooming flowers against the bleak winter landscape of the uncreated.

Gaze into the face of the deep, Oxal says, gaze at that which you might call darkness, and you shall see nothing. And then see yourselves, vivid, beautiful and lovely, as the vibrant colors of your personal feelings, your highest hopes and your deepest sorrows, all brighten the deep.

Love cannot speak to itself, react to itself, or even feel, Oxal says. That is reserved for those like you, and like me, who are as yet partially unaware that we are the Creator. Therefore we feel and we sense. We do, we think, we act. And those gifts are priceless.

The rest of the evening belongs to Latwii and the circle's questions. One seeker asks how to prepare for pending decisions, and Latwii's answer is worth carrying. Do what can be done, they say, and then give over your will to the greater will of the one Creator. Realize that you cannot make what you call a mistake. Each path before you offers the opportunity to learn and to serve. Sow your seeds as a conscientious gardener, and then give the other forces time to work with what you have sown. Watch for the first sprouts. Water them with your attention, and follow them to the table that has been prepared for you.

There is also a tender moment I want to handle gently. One of the circle speaks of grieving, of feeling suddenly vulnerable in meditation and in sleep, and asks for a tool beyond medicine. Latwii suggests what she has already begun, some form of tuning and protection, and affirms the inspirational readings she turns to before meditation and sleep. Such passages, they say, focus the inner being upon the light which exists in every experience. If you are walking through grief yourself, please hear this as the companionship it was meant to be, and keep close the human supports that hold you, whether they are friends, counselors, or healers.

So tonight, whatever you felt today, the bright petals and the bruised ones alike, consider that none of it was wasted. It was all blooming. And somewhere, it was watched with great joy.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Humble Tavern
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the humble tavern.

January thirteenth, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn tells a story about a tavern by the side of an old muddied road, and by the end of it you will never think about an ordinary gathering the same way again.

It was not a wealthy tavern, Hatonn says, but the tavern of those who work hard and long for the little pittance that enables all for whom they are responsible to live. Farmers, herdsmen, those who ran the toll road. Through the years they fell into such a habit of coming that the place became something other than a tavern. It became a haven.

Many came not just for the drink and the food, Hatonn says, but for a certain kind of comradeship which those who labor long and hard enjoy after the day's laboring is finished. They came with a childlike anticipation, for this time of gathering was as a reward for the labors of the day. And a certain vibration grew about the tavern as a result of those who came often and found relief within its humble walls.

Then Hatonn draws the people, one by one, and I want you to see them. One steady customer had a wife legendary for her scolding and nagging, but at the tavern the man was never scolded nor nagged. He became someone other than the person who worked so hard in the fields only to be scolded upon his return. One man had no knack for keeping his money, gambling away what would be food for his wife and children, but at the tavern his friends bought him rounds, and he was no longer without money. Another was ugly in countenance, and yet to his friends he looked hearty, healthy and fine.

Their only answer to lives they could not fix, Hatonn says, was to go to the tavern. And there, within the flowing of energies, each saw the other without the appearance that each had manufactured to cope with the hardships outside. Within the tavern, each saw the other's essence, the love that was each and flowed between each.

And here is the turn, the reason this story was told to a meditation circle and is being told to you. As those who labored long came to the tavern, Hatonn says, just so do you come to such a group as this. When two or three are gathered, that which is asked will be given. The whole is always greater than the sum of its parts, and each of you being a portion of the group are healers of yourselves and of each other.

The polarization is very much greater in a group, Hatonn says, which causes the light to develop a color, a bloom, even a song, a melody that enhances the wisdom for which each seeks. Each of you is purely magical. In a group such as this that magic is seen, each by the other, so that each may be healer for each, each may care for each, each may love each. And so a spiral of energy begins, glowing golden and white.

Never be self-conscious or analyze too much the magic of such groups, Hatonn says. It is only important that you know that you are at this very moment each a healing force to each other. And as you sit in the darkness, there is a radiation which is a source of light for those whom you will never know, never see, of whom you will never be aware, but who are being healed in some way by the change in vibration. You are larger than you think. You are better than you think.

Look at yourself through the eyes of your friends, Hatonn says, and discover your purity, your beauty, your delightfulness. In your meditations, rejoin this group. The energy will still be there. The feeling, the support, and the love will still be there.

The evening's questions wander far afield, to a group of beings called Yadda and whether Latwii numbers in the millions. Latwii answers, with their dry humor, that they number approaching twenty-three million entities, all of the fifth density, all one in seeking. But the heart of the night stays with the tavern. And with Nona, who closes the evening with a healing melody sung through the instrument, no words at all, only sound.

So tonight, think of the rooms where you are most yourself. The kitchen table, the circle of chairs, the late-night call. Whatever mask you wore to get through the day, you might try leaving it at the door. Someone in there already sees the essence, and loves it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Fool Steps Out
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the fool steps out.

January twenty-second, nineteen eighty-five, an intensive meditation, and the voice is Laitos, working with a new instrument who is learning to channel for the first time. What follows is really a masterclass in beginning anything that frightens you.

There is a saying among your peoples, Laitos says. Nothing ventured, nothing gained. This is extraordinarily true of metaphysical work of all kinds. The one who takes no risk is the one who will not advance. The more carefully one guards one's gifts, the less that gift will come to mean and the less good that gift will come to offer.

It is as though there were inflation in spiritual gifts, Laitos says, so that it is necessary always to attempt more and more regardless of what has gone before. One which has little must attempt enough that that little may become a bit more. One which has already had much must attempt a great deal. Seeking does not end. The road does not end. The journey goes on and on, as far as we know, forever.

Then Laitos gives the image I will never forget. One who channels, they say, is a fool stepping off the cliff into thin air. It is necessary for the preservation of free will that the contact not be unmistakable but be subtle. Once the first step is taken, subjective proof may begin to come forth. At first, though, it is usually the case that a great deal of faith is involved in speaking the first few words.

And the technique itself is beautifully plain. When a thought comes into the mind, speak it. It is like catching a long-thrown baseball, Laitos says. You catch the baseball and you pitch it again as accurately as possible. Only when you have pitched it and your glove is empty can you catch another.

The new instrument worries that he cannot tell their thoughts from his own. Laitos is honest about this. Your thoughts and ours feel the same, they say, because in truth, when you speak at all, you are channeling from some portion of your being thoughts of a nebulous nature which you translate into words. You do not know the next complete sentence you will speak. Neither do we.

So the instruction is simple and terrifying. Stop analyzing, and simply speak those words which you hear. And when the instrument finally manages it, when the words come through trembling and half-doubted, Laitos rejoices. The desire to perform this service, they say, is as a great light within the metaphysical realms. Though it cannot be seen with any of your senses, we can assure you that it does shine quite, quite brightly.

Whatever your cliff is tonight, whatever first word you have been afraid to speak, consider stepping. The air may hold you. It usually does.

Thank you for listening.

title: One to Be One With
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: one to be one with.

January twenty-seventh, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn tells a story about a horse, and it is secretly a story about loneliness, and about what finally answers it.

Once there was a horse, Hatonn begins. A young horse with a wild mane and a flying tail that roamed free across a plain where no people lived. Untrammeled and bridleless, the horse went its way. It would sip water and eat its grass and roll in the sweet timothy fields. Trees nodded serenely. The sun shone in summer and in winter. However, the horse, though free, and though unknowing, was unwittingly very lonely.

The horse wandered seeking it knew not what, Hatonn says, for although alone, it had an inner feeling and an inner knowing that it was not alone. It roamed high mountain pastures and lush green valleys, satisfied by the food of the grasses and the waters of the streams, and yet within this creature existed a yearning for a greater kind of experience.

Then one day the horse came upon a new being, a man, a young pioneer. The man wished to capture the horse, for that was truly a prize. He laid a trap and roped it. The horse was furious. It reared and kicked. Its high whinnies echoed to the heavens. It wanted nothing more than to be released and to be alone once again.

But the young man persevered. He grew to love the horse. He named the horse Daedalus, and told the horse that his name was Luke. Slowly the horse stopped thinking, when called Daedalus, I am not Daedalus, and began answering to the name. The man asked work of him, but in return the horse was always given good food for which he did not have to hunt. And then something the horse had never felt before began to grow.

The horse began to feel affection for Luke, Hatonn says, and looked forward to the opportunity to serve in his work, and to the times they would ride in the mountains and the forest, and most of all to the moments when Luke would talk with him, for he understood in his way that these moments were special between them.

It was not long before the horse had discovered the true secret answer to its loneliness and to its seeking, Hatonn says, for the horse was no longer alone. The horse was one in love and service with another entity, each giving of itself to the other, each caring, each being the nature that each was intended to be. And for the first time, looking at the trees and the mountains and the beautiful water, the horse felt truly at one with them.

And then Hatonn says the sentence this whole story was carrying. My friends, it is impossible to be friends with all that there is unless there is another one to be one with. Many sages have sought their own counsel. Their wisdom has been great. Their polarity has suffered.

When people's paths include others, Hatonn says, it may often seem that all is scattered and amiss, awry and out of tune. However, in this way does the Creator know Itself, and in no other. Consciousness is, but consciousness only becomes with the other to mirror, watch, and speak.

The evening also belongs to Laitos and a nervous new instrument learning to channel, trembling through her first attempts. Laitos is tender with her. You are but the telephone, they say, picturing a very old telephone, wires a little tattered, connection somewhat weak, but the operator is on duty.

So tonight, if you are roaming your own wide plain, free and unwittingly lonely, consider the horse. The answer was not more freedom. It was one other, to be one with.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love in Turbulent Times
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love in turbulent times.

The same day, January twenty-seventh, nineteen eighty-five, but the evening session. Hatonn speaks briefly about being channels for love, and then Latwii takes the circle's questions, and the questions that night are the hardest kind. Broken relationships. A church tearing itself apart. People starving on another continent. Why war never ends.

One seeker asks about a relationship that ended painfully, and whether the mistakes of the soul can be repaired. Listen to how Latwii puts it. We do not see mistakes, they say. We see two portions of the one Creator that have been in relationship with each other and have through that relationship sought to know the one Creator. When difficulties occur, it is not so much a mistake that has occurred, but tests of a more intensive nature which for the moment exceeded the limits of those within the relationship, so that love was more difficult to discover.

As you begin what you have called the healing, Latwii says, you begin to find that love which always was there, which needed more attention in order to be discovered. The intention to heal and find that love is of primary importance. To attempt that which is difficult is more important than to accomplish that which is easy.

Then a question about a church in conflict, two sides struggling, each truly loving the church they are fighting over. Latwii's counsel is simple and demanding. See each of them as the one Creator, each and every one. Open yourself to that love that you might be a vessel through which it moves. Remove your own will, that the greater will of the one Creator might move through you.

And then Carla tells her own story, and it is heartbreaking in its smallness. The church she grew up in fought over an organ. Some wanted a new one, some did not. About twenty-five people left over that organ, the whole choir. Within the year they got the new organ anyway, but the breakage remained. We all tried to act as peacemakers, she says, and we failed. Can you speak to the apparent failure of our good intentions?

Latwii's answer is one I want you to keep. As one has attempted to love and to give of the self without thought for the self but only with thought for others, they say, then one has expressed the heart of love. And if love has been expressed, how can there be failure in truth?

Within your illusion you shall not see the world respond as you think it should, Latwii says, for it exists as an illusion that when love is born it might be tested. The times that are tranquil and full of peace are indeed restful, yet they do not test love. Love is strengthened in those times of turbulence.

The hardest questions come last. What of the multitudes starving in Africa, where is the love of the Creator in that? What in human nature makes war upon war? I want to be honest with you about how Latwii answers. They speak of lives stretching far beyond this one, of lessons chosen before birth, of the nearness of harvest intensifying all catalyst. These are their opinions, offered humbly, and they will not land the same way for every listener. What is unmistakable is the practical turn they insist on. To those who are starving, they say, it is quite fit that food be given, that medicine be given, that the physical needs be tended to. These entities provide the rest of the planet with the opportunity to be of service. Various portions of the one Creator offering opportunities to other portions of the one Creator to know Itself through love.

And on war, this. What enables human beings to make war is the perception of separateness, self from other self, self from Creator. That lack of perception is both the lesson of this density and the opportunity. If you choose service to others, you must perceive the unity by intention, like a knight seeking the holy grail who never allows his glance to waver from the miraculous image.

There is no sin, Latwii says, only conditions in which the entity is provided with opportunities to make choices. And the enhanced awareness that suffering can bring to those who witness it is real, but those situations were not staged for an audience. The focal point, they say, is for those who are on the scene.

I will not pretend this evening resolves the hardest questions. It does not. But it leaves us with a practice for the turbulence we can touch. Love, and continue to love, through all seeming failures. Let that love be the shining star which lights your way, however difficult the journey, however winding the road.

Thank you for listening.

title: Use the Eraser
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: use the eraser.

February tenth, nineteen eighty-five. Three voices share the evening, Hatonn, Oxal, and Latwii, and each one is circling the same wound from a different side. How do you serve others without breaking yourself? How do you face the past that meditation keeps dragging into the light?

Hatonn begins with service, and with a warning I think every eager helper needs to hear. When each individual embarks upon the spiritual journey, he says, there is a time when the seeds of seeking are tender and young and need to be guarded carefully and in private. But then comes what he calls spiritual adolescence. The seeker has become excited by the power and mystery of the path and is on fire with the desire to share the awakening with others.

And here is the folly, Hatonn says. Within the well-intentioned there is such a desire to be of service that it is easy to find oneself deciding what is needed for another. The excitement is relayed, and there is often puzzlement and sad feeling when the attempt to serve is not accepted but rebuffed.

Service to others is one of the great paradoxes, Hatonn says, for one is of service to another to the extent that one ceases to attempt to give to another. Begin instead by attempting to see the creation through the eyes of the one who is to be aided. The end of service is to see the Creator in another, for by seeing the Creator you reflect that which may be the mirror in which that person can discover himself. The gift that you can give is the vision of the Creator.

Notice, Hatonn says, that in all of this he has said nothing about doing, only about your manner of being. If the technique is not learned, no matter how great your enthusiasm, how beautiful your message, how inspiring your words, that which you give another is part of your own energy and it will not last past your leaving. When you give another self himself in a new vision, the consequences are far more lasting, and there is no infringement of free will.

And before you can serve others, Hatonn says, be of service to yourself. Stop judging yourself. There is within you a greater self that you may call upon, in order that your mind and your emotions may serve you instead of your being a slave to them. Spend yourself freely in order to be, not in order to convince.

Then Oxal takes up the other half of the wound. Meditation is central to spiritual evolution, they say, and yet it is inevitably painful, for it is a tool whereby realizations occur. One learns about oneself, then turns to the self and begins picking at past experiences which have been less than perfectly resolved. Bitter fruit crops up among the fruits of meditation.

This is an excellent sign, Oxal says, and I want you to hear the gentleness in that. Rejoice when a past misalliance comes to mind as unfinished business. It is now time to finish the business. The appropriate action when faced with your own past is to take the past from your shoulders, to refuse to carry it further, but rather to put it down and gaze at it until all is well, until there is no emotional pull or push to the experience.

My friends, Oxal says, you are carrying around a collection of unsolved but simple arithmetic problems. When one adds two plus two and writes down five, one has made an error. Later one may erase the error because of new and life-giving knowledge. That is all that your past is. The answers usually have to do with forgiveness of the self, and a willingness to use the eraser.

You do not have to live your past, Oxal says. You are responsible for the new life of the present moment. If you have not made amends to another, by all means do so. Usually, however, it is the self that is the great scapegoat. Remove this identity from yourself. Be patient. Loving your mistakes, loving your perfection, and being willing to be accountable for that which you are now, not in the past and not in the future.

To be light of heart, joyful and free is the sign of the child, Oxal says, and it is that small one within you that is the best learner. The universe gives back that which it feels. So use your eraser. Pluck the bitter fruit and cast it aside, so that new fruit may be born in its time.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Travel Is the Objective
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the travel is the objective.

February seventeenth, nineteen eighty-five, a Sunday meditation. Hatonn tells a small story about a small creature, and it lands like a parable about every journey you have ever resented.

It concerns, Hatonn says, a small elfin creature. It had found itself alone and in doubt as it left its home, searching for what it was not sure it was searching. For it had come to the age when the urge to leave the security and warmth of the family is felt. Though it loved its family, it proceeded into a world unknown.

Like many of us faced with departure, Hatonn says, the creature first sought the security of a destination. For in your world, does not one who dives from the springboard immediately seek the reassurance of an arrival in the pool, rather than the interim where one is suspended in midair?

The creature chose a distant point of which it had some secondhand knowledge and set out, unaware, like many of us, Hatonn says, that the travel was the objective rather than the arrival. The trip was long. The distractions, the dangers, the need to seek food, the uncomfortable climate, often drove the destination entirely from the creature's mind. At night, in loneliness and discomfort, it would envision ways the travel could be accomplished without stress, imagining itself alighting from the vehicle with hair unmussed, clothing unwrinkled, and growth complete.

Many of us are like that creature, Hatonn says. We have all set our feet upon a path, a road that leads through immense valleys of distraction, of hardship, of disquiet, and we sit and wonder what led us to this choice. We envision paths of learning devoid of hardship, which allow us machine-like to simply record the knowledge we seek.

Hatonn will not tell you the hardships determine the value of the education. That, he says, must be decided within the heart of each, and those answers, with complete honesty, may differ. What he offers is this. Each of us made certain choices, often from reasons dimly understood or not understood, but choices which lead each of us to a path of perfection which impeccably suits but one individual.

Accept with serenity, Hatonn says, the knowledge that the choices you have made lead you upon a path of your own making, a path leading to your own perfection, a path which within your soul you know is the only path you may follow.

So if you are suspended in midair tonight, somewhere between the springboard and the pool, consider that the interim is not the delay. It is the destination, wearing a disguise.

Thank you for listening.

title: Your Own Backyard
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: your own backyard.

February twenty-third, nineteen eighty-five, a Saturday meditation. Hatonn tells a parable about an old man with a walking stick, and it is one of the most human stories in the archive.

Once upon a time, Hatonn begins, there was an old man making his way through the cobblestones of the village in which he had lived, and his father before him, and his father before him. He had married, and his wife had died, and in dying had lost their only unborn child. More than years bent the old man's back as he picked his way along.

He felt very lonely and desolate, Hatonn says. He wandered through the town and saw many familiar faces, for it was a small village and he knew each person, their children by name. He had always found comfort in this village, but today he felt alone. He felt he had lost his only life in the loss of his great love.

And so the old man did what grieving people have always done. With a few possessions and his trusted walking stick, he set out over a mountain pass and wandered as far as his legs would carry him. Though he knew not his final destination, there was a small measure of comfort in the journeying itself.

He traveled for days until he was so far from his village that no one had ever heard of him. And at first he was lonelier than ever, and wished he had not forsaken his home. Here, he felt, no one would love him. Here no one would pick him up should he fall, tend him if he grew ill, wipe away his tears. And though love whispered in the trees and murmured along the grasses, his ear did not hear, nor did his eyes see.

Until the day his heart failed him on a dusty trail outside another small and unknown village, and he went to his knees. He lay there feeling alone in the universe, until some children passing came upon him. One knelt to wipe the hair from his brow while another ran home for help. And the old man received tremendous love and comfort in the light, cool touch of a little child's caring hand.

He awoke in a bed in a room full of strangers, Hatonn says, and yet the eyes of these people were the same eyes he had loved in the town behind. Women served him broth, a man built a fire, children laughed in the other room. Although he knew not their names, he recognized the sameness of people and the caring in this new village.

There he befriended a young man who dreamed of leaving his small town for somewhere larger and more exciting, certain happiness waited elsewhere. But through the old traveler's eyes, the young man began to see his own village with new awareness. He heard the laughter of the children through new ears. He realized the happiness he was seeking could be found in the small village where he lived. He need not venture on a long journey, Hatonn says, for he took that long journey through his sharing in the awarenesses gained through his friend.

This story applies everywhere, Hatonn says. Though you may travel from city to city, from mountains to sea, searching as the old traveler did for the answers to your loneliness, you may wish before venturing out to listen to the children outside your window, to see the eyes of your neighbors and feel the hearts of your friends. The answers, my brothers and sisters, may be in your own back yard.

And whenever your heart fails because of overwhelming circumstances, Hatonn says, never fear. Be of light heart amidst the complexities of the dark world. There is no moment which does not contain all that is needed, all that is good, all that is beautiful, and all that is true.

Thank you for listening.

title: Build Your Wall True
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: build your wall true.

February twenty-fourth, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn tells a story about a man building a wall, and then turns the wall into a mirror.

Once there was a man who wished to build a fence of bricks, Hatonn begins. He was a proud man and he wished his wall to be perfect. It was with exquisite care that he laid the plumb line and found the perfect horizontal level. The sun shone down upon him until he was very warm, yet he welcomed the sun. Indeed, he welcomed the chance to do the work necessary to begin to build his wall.

He welcomed the labors, Hatonn says, for he welcomed the opportunity to place his efforts in attunement with the pace of the universe he sensed in operation around him. For just as the plumb line was true and the level a perfect one, so also did the universe about him operate with perfection. And as his efforts were directed truly toward the completion of this perfect wall, so his contentment grew, and his sense of fulfillment in this manifestation of the force he could feel about himself.

When it was done, another entity questioned the value of a wall, an object often used to shut other selves out. His contentment remained undisturbed. His reply was that the perfection lay within the object he had created, and that it would remain perfect regardless of the efforts another might make to corrupt that perfection through misuse.

A wall is but a wall, Hatonn says. An act of creation is simply an act of creation, which may be used as a tool toward selflessness or selfishness, and it is not always easy to perceive the intention in the mind of its creator. Be cautious, my friends, that you might avoid misunderstanding the efforts of another through your perceptions of similar efforts on the part of those who have gone before. For it is within the heart of the builder, not the hands, that the potential value may grow.

Then Hatonn turns the parable inward, and this is where it gets sharp. Relationships with others might be likened to walls, he says, but even more, the wall speaks about yourselves. An attempt to come into right relationship with another is an attempt to cross walls. And the first wall which must be true is the structure of your own being.

Perhaps your basic character is excellent, Hatonn says, the lines true and straight, yet they have become dilapidated, bricks missing, mortar failing. When contemplating the experiences which arise within a relationship, it is well to begin with an objective gaze inwardly directed at the structure of the self. If the base is not perfectly horizontal, if it is not quite plumb, then all will seem out of tune, out of order, shaky and fraught with difficulty.

So use meditation and contemplation, Hatonn says, to build yourself, as inspiration gives you one piece of knowledge and then another, as you move along the pathway of discovery. And remember that the walls you build within yourself are energy fields. They are moveable. The stance you take, the wall behind which you choose to hide within a relationship, must be observed and balanced in such a way that the wall becomes permeable, so that two walls may meet.

The evening's questions range widely, from competition to the nature of the heart. On competition, Latwii offers a clean lens. It is a tool, they say, like any tool, which may be used to radiate one's gifts outward for the enjoyment of many, or to gather recognition inward for the self. On the heart, they speak in the language of energy centers, of the green ray of unconditional love, and of blockages finding symbolic expression in the body. I want to hold this part the way it was offered, as opinion and metaphor, not medicine. If your body is speaking to you through pain or illness, please keep your doctor in the conversation alongside any meditation.

The practice, then, is simple to say and lifelong to do. Before you judge the other builder's wall, check your own plumb line. And where your wall has grown rigid, let it become permeable, so that love can pass through.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Catcher's Mitt
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the catcher's mitt.

February twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-five, an intensive meditation devoted to one thing, learning to channel. Laitos speaks at length about what vocal channeling actually is, and the explanation is so plain it feels like someone finally telling you the trick.

The process of channeling is in some ways simple enough that it confuses those who are attempting to learn the techniques, Laitos says. But the simplicity, once understood, is almost stunning. If one has the catcher's mitt and the baseball is thrown, the catcher will catch that ball. However, he will immediately have to throw it again, hopefully with careful direction, in order that his glove is empty once again as the next ball hits the glove.

This is the way of channeling, Laitos says. We work within the levels of the mind which throw off to your conscious mind the concepts which you then clothe consciously with a vocabulary. And here is the part that surprises people. We by no means wish to be one hundred percent responsible for the content of the message. We wish roughly twenty-five to thirty percent of the message to be shaped by the instrument, who calls upon his vocabulary, his imagination, and his special gifts as a person.

I love the reason they give. In this way, Laitos says, our simple message gains a multitude of conveyances. The person who cannot grasp the poetic will yet have the opportunity to grasp the practical and down-to-earth, and the person who cannot grasp either of those still has the chance to hear it from a scientific or technical mind. This is why vocal channeling is a partnership.

Unlike a trance channel, the vocal channel is alert, Laitos says, and though relaxed, quite awake and able to discriminate. This is our chosen method of speaking to those who would wish to hear.

And the first barrier every new instrument must breach is wonderfully small. It will feel as if you have thought the phrase yourself, Laitos says. This is the first barrier which must be breached. It will be months before you are convinced that we indeed are not simply a portion of your inner mind. We ask that the new instrument relax, remove any preconceptions, and wait for the concept to come into the mind.

There is a warning tucked in, too, and it is worth hearing. There are those who would wish to eliminate yet one more light giver, Laitos says, by mimicking the vibratory patterns of those who wish only to serve. So tune carefully, remain surrounded in white light, and challenge each and every entity, each and every time.

Whether or not you ever channel a word, the image holds. Catch the thought. Speak it faithfully, in your own voice. Empty the glove. Be ready for the next one.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Song from the Road
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the song from the road.

March third, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn tells a story about a boy who hears a song coming from the road, and follows it past the point of no return. It is one of the most beautiful parables in the archive, and it was told on an evening when the circle needed beauty.

It was a hot, hot summer day in Mexico, Hatonn begins. The land was arid, water was priceless, and a young boy sat by the roadside and asked his mother where the road goes. How should I know, she answered. The road leads from here to another place or places, she told him, and the choices are yours. Whether to travel at all, in which direction, and whether to be satisfied where you have stopped or to continue further.

But the boy could hear something no one else heard. There was no song in the whole town, Hatonn says, no lullaby at night, no anthem in the morning. But even above the loud throng of insects he could hear a song coming from the road. He gazed into the shimmering distance and could see no one and nothing that would account for it. When he put his hands over his ears, the song became louder. And one day he knew that he must go.

He packed a small bundle, and his mother looked at him imploringly, and asked if this was truly his heart's desire. He replied that there was nothing else that held any interest for him, and though he did not know what he would find or precisely why he must go, yet he must go.

The road rose to meet him, Hatonn says. His bundle seemed lightened. The rhythm of his paces soothed his aching, and the song pulled him onward. He dreamed of the road even as he slept. And then, by mid-afternoon one day, the murmuring before him became the voice of eons of tides breaking against a shoreline, and for the first time the boy beheld an enormous quantity of water, so great he had never dreamed it could exist.

He waded into the breakers with a shout of joy, Hatonn says, and then the crushing discovery. He could not swallow this water. The road ended at the ocean. He was no longer in the land he understood.
