The instrument of seeking, your consciousness, exists only in the present moment. Every spiritual practice ever devised, he says, is a device for returning the attention to now. That is all any of them do.

And he connects this to the nature of the Creator in a way that quietly changes everything. The Creator, he says, does not wait at the end of time. The Creator is not a reward for a life well postponed. The Creator is the substance of the present moment, fully present in it, whether you notice or not. Eternity is not a long time. It is no time. It is this time, seen clearly.

There is also a gentleness here about the past that I want to hold onto. The mistakes, the wasted years, the seeker looking back in regret, he says, are looking at something that no longer exists. The past is a story the surface mind tells. The only thing that is real is the now, and in the now, everything is still possible. Regret, he says, is the mind's way of postponing in the other direction.

So the teaching tonight is almost insultingly simple, which is why it is so hard. Stop waiting. The eternal is not coming. It is here. The now is not the preparation for the spiritual life. It is the spiritual life. Step into it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Learning to Ride
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: learning to ride.

The voices called L/Leema offer an image tonight that anyone who has ever wobbled down a sidewalk will recognize. Learning to ride a bicycle. And they mean it as a complete description of the spiritual path.

Listen to how they build it. No one learns to ride by studying balance, they say. You cannot think your way onto two wheels. You get on, you wobble, you fall, you get on again. The learning is in the body, in the doing, in the repeated willingness to look foolish. And the falling, they say, is not failure. It is the tuition. Every fall teaches the body something no lecture could.

I love what they do with the moment of actual riding. There comes a point, they say, when the wobbling stops, not because you have mastered it, but because you have stopped trying to master it. You relax. You trust the motion. And the bicycle, which was your enemy, becomes an extension of yourself. The seeker, they say, knows this moment. It is the moment the practice stops being effort and starts being flight.

And then the image deepens. The bicycle, they say, only stays upright while it is moving. Stop pedaling and it falls over. This, they say, is the whole secret of the spiritual life. You cannot balance statically. You cannot achieve a state of enlightenment and then park it. The balance exists only in motion, in the ongoing pedaling of daily practice, daily kindness, daily seeking. Stop moving and you tip.

There is a tenderness here about falling that I want to linger on. You will fall, they say. Everyone falls. The path is full of potholes, loose gravel, sudden stops. But the fall is not the end of the ride. It is a feature of it. What matters is not whether you fall. It is whether you get back on. And every time you get back on, they say, you ride a little steadier.

So tonight, if you have fallen, and who has not, the teaching is simple. The bicycle is still there. The road is still there. Get back on. Wobble. Pedal. Trust the motion. The balance you are looking for cannot be found standing still.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Open Verdict
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the open verdict.

The voices called L/Leema speak tonight about judgment, and they begin with a distinction most of us never make. There is, they say, a great difference between discernment and prejudice. Discernment looks, listens, and then decides. Prejudice decides first, and then arranges the looking to match.

Listen to how they describe the mechanics of prejudice. The mind, they say, is a categorizing engine. It meets something new, and before the new thing has had a chance to speak, the mind has filed it. Good, bad, safe, dangerous, like me, not like me. And once filed, the mind stops seeing. It sees the category, not the thing. The person, the idea, the experience arrives, and we greet our own label instead.

I love the image they use for what this costs. Prejudice, they say, is a closed verdict. The trial is over before the evidence is heard. And the one who pays the price is not the judged. It is the judge. For every closed verdict shrinks the world a little. Every category unexamined is a door locked from the inside. The prejudiced mind, they say, lives in a smaller universe than the one that is actually there.

Discernment, by contrast, is an open verdict. It looks carefully. It weighs. It notices. But it never stops noticing. It allows the thing to be more than the first impression, and more than the second. It is, they say, the difference between a mind that uses categories as tools and a mind that is used by them.

And they are honest about how deep the habit runs. Prejudice, they say, is not always loud. Sometimes it is quiet, respectable, dressed up as wisdom or experience. I have seen this before, the mind says, and stops looking. But nothing, they say, has ever happened before in exactly this way, to exactly this person, in exactly this moment. The universe does not repeat itself. Only our categories do.

So the practice tonight is a small one, and a radical one. When you catch yourself filing something before you have seen it, pause. Reopen the verdict. Look again, as if for the first time, because in a sense it is the first time. The world is larger than your labels for it. Let it be.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Loving Gaze
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the loving gaze.

Hatonn closes this movement of the archive with a teaching so simple it can sound like nothing, until you try to live it. In every experience, he says, there is love to be found. Not added afterward. Not imagined. Found, like something hidden in the scene, waiting for the eye that knows how to look.

Listen to how he describes the practice. Whatever comes before you, a joy, a difficulty, a dull afternoon, a painful conversation, ask of it a single question. Where is the love in this? Not whether love is there. Where. The question assumes the answer. And the assuming, he says, is what trains the eye.

I love the realism with which he admits how hard this is. Some experiences, he says, seem to contain no love at all. They seem to be made of pure friction, pure loss, pure irritation. The seeker looks, and looks, and finds nothing. And Hatonn does not scold this. He says the love is often deeply buried, under layers of pain and confusion, and finding it may take time. The practice is not to find it instantly. The practice is to keep looking.

And he connects this to the inner weather in a way that feels deeply kind. The voice with which you speak to yourself, he says, is part of the practice. The seeker who berates themselves for failing to find the love has missed the point twice over. Be gentle, he says. The harsh inner voice is not discernment. It is just another layer to look through. Speak to yourself as you would to a friend who is learning something difficult. Because you are.

There is also a quiet promise here. The gaze, he says, changes the gazer. The more you practice finding love in experience, the more love you find, not because experience changes, but because you do. The eye that has learned to look for love starts seeing it everywhere, in places it never thought to look. The world does not become easier. It becomes more transparent.

So tonight's teaching is a practice, not a proposition. Wherever you are, whatever is happening, ask the question. Where is the love in this? Ask it of the good hours and the bad ones. Ask it gently, and keep asking. The loving gaze, turned on the world long enough, turns the world luminous.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Spiritual Present Tense
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the spiritual present tense.

There is a story from the Zen tradition that the ones called L/Leema loved to tell, and they tell it tonight in answer to a question every one of us has asked in one form or another. What do you do with stress?

Once upon a time, they say, there was an old man who sat in his room and prayed. When he was hungry, he went into the market and begged with his bowl, then went back to his room and prayed. A young woman, with child, blamed the child on him, and left the baby with the hermit. He got up, they say, and nursed it, and fed it, and worked hard as a laborer for two years. The child prospered. Then one day the woman saw the child in the marketplace, the child pleased her sight, and she claimed it back. The old man gave her the child, and returned to his prayers.

That is the whole story. No outrage. No defense. Each day given to its own hunger. I love how L/Leema frame what the story is really about. Stress, they say, is due to an emotional tension regarding the outcome of events. Some who have nothing to worry about can worry themselves into an early decline. Others who by all rights should be beside themselves exhibit a marvelous lack of tension from within. The difference is not circumstance. It is where you live in time.

Listen to how they put it. The spiritual tense is the present tense. The unspiritual tense is tension. They do not ask you to forget your history or give up your hopes for the future. They ask for something smaller and harder: a detachment, born in meditation, from the crying needs — little and large — that fill your days and nights. If you were inspired yesterday, the world will have moved in upon that inspiration by today. That is what the world is for, they say. It is intended to encroach upon your peace of mind in order to test it.

And so they offer an image. In the garden of your life, make yourself a comfortable seat — and this seat is within your mind. In the quiet of this inner garden, plant what you want: the glory of flowers, the singing of birds, the lifting of the breeze. It is to this garden that you return for your solitude. You can have it, they say, if you are in prison, or in chains — or, as is more likely, bound by your desire for outcomes, living a life less full than the principled life you intended.

Then comes the line I want to sit with. You will fail, they say — not once, but frequently — to avoid stress. The habit among your peoples is great. Do not feel cast down when you fail, for each moment is here. Each moment is a moment in which you have not failed. Clinging to what troubles you about yourself or others makes you forget the electric present moment. This moment is infinite.

Meditation, they say, is how you come to know the thought patterns — complex but predictable — that will stress the mind and the body. Much unnecessary illness comes from this same stress. And here is the comfort they offer: it is not mistaken, only unnecessary. When you are uncomfortable, you begin to pay attention. And once you begin to pay attention to your thought patterns, it becomes easier and easier to stop hanging, as they put it, like a terrier onto the hem of your worry.

In the present moment, they say, there is naught about which to worry. Not because the world is safe. Because the present moment is the only place where you actually are. Thank you for listening.

title: Midnight and Noon
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: midnight and noon.

Tonight the ones called L/Leema take up a subject most spiritual teachers would rather skip. Despair. They divide it into three: the despair of the mind, the despair of the body, and the despair of the spirit. And what they do with each one is not what you would expect.

The despair of the mind, they say, is an empty thing, full of no virtue except that of self-destruction. The mind despairs of its very limitations — and in truth, they say, there are no limitations, only challenges, lessons, and glory. Yes, they say glory, for the stronger the despair, the more glorious the battle that may be waged to outlast the helplessness and the doom. And yet — and this is the honest part — mental despair is almost always unproductive. It is useless. But it is also common, a constant undertone in every life, available to everyone at some point. Between its pole and the pole of pure joy, they say, you may read your true position in the learning of love. That is the phrase that gives this episode its title: the dynamic of despair, they say, is midnight as opposed to noon.

The despair of the body is a reflection of the despair of the mind. When mental despair is not moved into a productive mode of thinking and acting, it settles into the body. Thence comes disease, they say, and ultimately death. Form follows function. It is a sober teaching, and they do not soften it.

But then they turn the whole thing over, and this is why I wanted to read you this session. Spiritual despair, they say, is an absolute necessity. Not a zero — a moving dynamic. It is the recognition that you know nothing, that you have lost control of everything, that you are faced with complete darkness of soul. And it is precisely that darkness which forces consciousness to turn, transform, and begin anew — not leaving the old behind, but accreting more wisdom, more compassion, more unity. A unity you can only receive, they say, when you have become desperate enough to release the expectation of any knowledge whatsoever.

And here is the practice. You cannot analyze despair and rise transformed. You cannot act it out through illness and rise transformed. But you can transmute mental despair into what this tradition calls the dark night of the soul — as alchemists change lead to gold, they say, so mental despair may be changed into the dark night, burnished and shining. That spiritual despair then transforms itself into great revolutions, and positive, forward changes within the spirit.

It is rare, they say, that anyone enters or graduates from any initiation without the impetus, the pain, and the challenge of spiritual despair. Therefore — listen to how they put it — if your soul is in agony, rejoice, for it is from this point that all good comes.

A gentle word, if you will allow me one. These voices speak of despair as a teacher, and there is truth in that. But if despair is sitting with you tonight in a way that feels heavier than teaching, you do not have to transmute it alone. Speak to someone you trust, or to a counselor. The dark night is real. So is the morning. Thank you for listening.

title: The Doll and the Cat
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the doll and the cat.

Tonight begins with the ones called Yadda, who drop in at the top of the session to ask a question that sounds simple and lands like a stone in still water. What is prosperity? There is a rumor, they say, that prosperity is unhappy or anti-spiritual. That is a misperception. There is another rumor that prosperity is all you need for the life experience. That is a misconception too. Look at the riches of your world, they say — they come in different forms, but they are equal in one thing, and that is energy. Release the fear of prosperity, release the hunger for it, and rest in the knowledge that prosperity is infinite. And then, with the mischief that is their signature, they add: be careful what you seek — for you shall receive it.

Then Hatonn takes the floor, and tells a story. Once upon a time there was a little girl who had a beautiful doll, with blue eyes that opened and closed and yellow hair that felt like silk. The child spent many happy hours dressing it, speaking to it, making up stories with it, until the doll became her companion. One day the mother realized that the child spoke to the doll and listened to it with equal sense of reality for both. And the mother became concerned. Was this normal? Would it harm her daughter's development? She did not know what to do.

I love what happens next, because Hatonn tells it so plainly. The worried mother says aloud, to no one in particular, whatever shall I do — and her cat answers, meow. She thanks the cat. She keeps talking to the cat. She walks out into the yard, the trees whisper, the leaves rattle, and slowly, in the giving up of the daily rush of thoughts, an answer comes.

And here is Hatonn's reading of the whole thing. This is a story, they say, about a child talking to a doll because the mother talked to the cat. It is also a story about each of you, and the little things that etch your indelible character upon the consciousness of others. The child learned how to converse with the unseen from watching the mother do it without thinking.

My friends, you do not know what you do, Hatonn says, and yet that which you do is perfect. But you are seekers, asking to become more responsible on deeper levels — to know where the roots of your consciousness are, and in what soil they grow. You are responsible for watering the roots of the tree of your consciousness, that it may blossom and share its beauty with those about you.

So be graceful in your ways, they say. Let your smile be sweet and your words soft. For all wish to be peaceful and humble and kindly affectioned one to another — and it is beyond human telling to do these things consistently. It is not, however, beyond that which we call grace, which Hatonn chooses to call contact with the source of your being: that one great original Thought of love. Love is what you seek, they say. Love is what you will find. For all things are love. Thank you for listening.

title: The Wellspring Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the wellspring within.

Tonight Hatonn begins with an image and never really leaves it. Picture, he says, a mountain stream gushing forth from a living spring — ever fresh, ever beautiful, moving and singing along its bed, refreshing all that lives in it. Such, he says, is the living wellspring of your spirits.

Then he asks the question the image is really asking. Where do you go to find such a wellspring? Into the city, among the crowds and the cries of those who barter and sell? It would take a special person to find sanctuary and nourishment there. Into the country, to watch the trees change with the seasons? A lovelier haunt — and yet, he says, the wellspring of spiritual life is not easily found from without, even under beautiful circumstances. Into the ocean, away from all land, into the simplicity of waves and sky? But here is the difficulty with picturing a better and better environment: into such an environment you bring yourself. The self that is you is always with you, and into each place you project your opinions and biases, your pains and pleasures. That which is outer cannot bring to birth that within you which is to come in your search for the truth.

I love the example he reaches for next. The small cat playing about their feet during the session, he says, is a living example. To the cat, the room is warm, the food bowl and the water bowl are full, and all seems perfect. The cat plays and is happy. But where shall it go that its spirit may progress? If you are seeking to survive, he says, find the correct environment. If you are seeking to grow, know that the only environment that matters is within you. You are the wellspring of your evolution in spirit. You are the fountainhead of your birth into that new portion of yourself which you wish to be lifted up in love.

And then the turn that makes this more than encouragement. You do not carry this within you as if you were a basket and it the precious cargo. No, he says — you are far more like the pipe through which is funneled the clear, precious water of the fountainhead. Things do not come from you as much as through you. There is no situation in which you are not channeling, being used as an instrument by yourself, by others, or by circumstances themselves. The great choice, then, is the choice to allow through you that which you desire to be spent through you.

Listen to how he puts the practice. If you would be a channel for love, open yourself inside to that spring of living water in which your soul may bathe and become clean and shining pure — and from which, and through which, a great light may shine in a dark world. The pure channel, he says, is an impersonality: clear and exquisitely pure. Personalities have often been confused with pure channels. They are not the same thing.

You are the wellspring, and you are the pipe. The water is not yours to own. It is yours to let through. Thank you for listening.

title: The One Architect
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the one architect.

The question put to L/Leema tonight is about houses — where to build them, how to place them, what shapes are best. And the answer they give begins by almost dismissing the question, and then goes somewhere much deeper.

The placement of spiritual dwellings matters little, they say, except in specialized instances. Then the deeper answer: there is one architect. This architect has been called the Creator, and from the Creator flow many ideas, many shapes, many possibilities concerning houses. Some shapes may be more easily attuned for certain work than others. But all shapes in general have equal potential — for it is not the builder of the house but the architect to whom praise may be given, and that architect works not through board and clay and stone, but in the heart and spirit of those who build.

And here is the stern caveat they send out with it. It is the love for the architect that invests the house with excellence of vibration. With this love, any shaped and placed dwelling shall be magical. Without this same love, the most carefully designed and placed house shall be dead in a spiritual sense. When quarrelsome and divisive entities build a house, they say, that house shall be a house of shame. When the humblest dwelling is put up with loving hands and adoring hearts, that dwelling shall be full of love.

Then the turn inward, which is where L/Leema always seem to be heading. You already dwell within a house, they say — and that house is your physical vehicle. Have you caused it to dwell in holy places by the purity of your thoughts and the love within your heart? Or have you made your body dead by pursuing endless divisiveness? So it shall be, on the metaphysical plane, for any structure built by human hands. Build in love, in unity, and in praise of the architect who is no man, but the very Creator.

Later in the session, someone asks about the stages between light meditation and deep trance, and L/Leema offer one of the loveliest images in this whole stretch of the archive. Picture the mind as a tree, they say. In the conscious mind you live out on the limbs and branches, where the winds of conversation blow and gust. As you quiet the mind, you move down the branches to the trunk — the deeper levels of meditation. Quieten further, focus on fewer and fewer points, and you move down the trunk into the roots — into the subconscious, where experience not consciously known becomes available to your attention. That movement, they say, is the movement from conscious meditation to the trance-like state.

And whether you remember what happens down in the roots is a function of practice. Many enter the roots every night in dreams and remember nothing, for no conscious effort has been made to retain it. The practice of remembering — in trance or in dreams — is gained by repetition. The tree is always there. The question is only how far down you are willing to climb. Thank you for listening.

title: Freedom From Fear
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: freedom from fear.

There is probably not one among humankind, Hatonn says tonight, who does not question the reason for all the difficulties of the incarnational experience. So tonight he addresses it — in yet another way, he admits, for the archive returns to this the way the tide returns.

Each of you has what seems to be a self, he says — two hands, two feet, a face with mobile features. This seems to be the self. And yet wisdom will tell you it is not the self, for where in your arms or legs or face can you locate yourself? You are in this incarnational experience, he says, as one who views a movie. To consider that you are a portion of the movie is accurate — for every motivation you carve into positivity and joy raises the amount of light you can receive. But the body you inhabit is evanescent in the extreme. You as a spirit are older than some stars, and will outlive some stars. That part of you which is infinite shall never have its foot dashed against a stone. It would be impossible, for your nature is like that of the Creator. You have chosen to dress yourself in flesh so that you may experience a large number of seeming difficulties.

This brings him back, he says, to compassion — to love and wisdom. If the beginning of love is the acceptance of the self, the beginning of wisdom is freedom from fear. For what can happen to you? Should you be killed? Each body shall die. Should you be hungry or cold? These things occur. What is your reaction to them? Difficulties, he says, are what they seem in the illusion, and it is your challenge within the illusion to deal with each difficulty with as much love as possible. So you learn the lessons of love. So you see, in part, through an illusion. So finally you have no need of it.

I love the honesty of what comes next. Hatonn says he can feel the fear in the room — fear of upcoming surgery, fear of pain, of dying, of losing a beloved relationship, of growing older. He does not wave these away. He asks you to reach for the measure of wisdom in you, and as fears and doubts overcome you, to find the part that says: the beginning of wisdom is freedom from fear. Give praise, he says, to the Creator of your difficulties, and thereby move your center of attention onto higher ground. Each fear, each difficulty, each doubt is a challenge — a force against which you have the opportunity to push, in order to carve ever deeper the attitudes of thanksgiving, joy, and love.

A gentle word before I close. These are brave teachings about fear and pain, and they were spoken to people facing real surgeries and real losses. If you are walking through illness or fear tonight, take this as an invitation, not a prescription — an invitation to lay the fear down for a little while, and to remember that beneath the experiencer who suffers, there is a seeker who cannot be harmed. Thank you for listening.

title: Love in the Insult
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love in the insult.

The question tonight is one of the most human ever put to these voices. What opportunities are presented when you are in a disharmonious relationship with another? What do you do with hurt feelings, with insults, with the person who wrongs you?

L/Leema begin where they always begin: with the appearances. It seems to be a vast universe of separate suns and separate people and separate thoughts. All of these appearances are appearances of separation. In truth, there is one creation, one consciousness. So when it seems there is a lack of communication between two entities, when there are hurt feelings and insults — look, they say, to the love in the insult and the love in the hurt feelings. Both of these pains belong to the emotional self, and are a distortion of love.

They dwell first on the one who is hurt. The hurt one is experiencing a distortion of love in this: it is not being appreciated for the gifts it gives. And yet — listen to how they put it — is the gift any less because it is not appreciated? Is the giving less pleasurable because compliments are not given? One with a heart full enough of love can give without need for compliment or thanks or payment of any kind, emotional or otherwise. Why should the creation need to thank itself?

I love the image they give for this. Imagine each gift you give as the arrow sent from the bow. It will find its target more and more purely as the giver gives with less and less expectation of any reward — giving for the upwelling joy of the gift given. Take the challenge up with joy when it comes, they say, and offer the same constant love to those who wrong you and those who praise you. Cast a cold eye on the difference between the two. All things are one, and the love in all things must needs be found.

And then they turn to the one who insults, and their compassion widens instead of narrowing. One cannot insult oneself except by insulting another, they say — the illusion calls up in those who insult a need to pick out in others what they find lacking in themselves. So in any insult, look to its reflection upon the giver of revilement, and have compassion on a soul that is hurting itself unknowingly, falling into a vortex from which it is sometimes difficult to emerge unscathed. Feel compassion and blessing, they say, and an upwelling of joy in aiding such a difficult entity — for this entity is in great need of stable, sturdy, calm and constant joy that radiates and can never be extinguished.

They know this is difficult. If there were no challenges, they ask, why would you enter into incarnation? The heart of the lesson is not to win the argument. It is to find the love in the insult, and the love in the hurt, and to keep giving the arrow its flight. Thank you for listening.

title: Find Where Love Lives
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: find where love lives.

Hatonn opens tonight with a picture of the Earth at night — the dark side of the planet, darkness within darkness. And then, one small flare of light. You know what that is, he says. That is one entity whose will has been turned to offering the one love and the one light of the original Thought. What a glorious light in such darkness when one entity alone orients itself to the One.

When groups of entities meet together, he says, the light blazes far brighter than by mere addition — for each gives each strength and clarity, each giving unto each the gift of light. That is why your light groups are crucial, always have been, always shall be. And those who have watched from their side, he says, have seen more and more lights glowing in the darkness, their radiance growing brighter, networks forming — traceries like lace encircling the darkened spiritual planes of your world.

But he will not let the group become the point. Each entity goes forth from the group still holding, as in a holograph, all the light of consciousness. Value yourselves, he says — not for anything you have done or will do, but because of your innate nature. It is your birthright to be the Creator, and your challenge to find that same Creator in all that you meet, whatever the outward circumstances, whatever the challenges of personality.

Then the part I want you to hear slowly. Pretend you are a small child on a path, kicking pebbles, the sun of childhood's fall warm and golden. As experience bruises you, that sun seems to sicken — and yet, he says, this is in no way necessary. One may retain that golden childhood. One merely needs to surrender the bruises, the anger, the hurt and pain that have grown up around various circumstances. These experiences are like old, heavy clothing. They have done their service. It is time to shed these garments and put on fresh linen and go forth into the golden sunlight once again.

And the lesson of the pearl. The oyster does not turn its back upon the gritty sand of experience. When sand irritates the inside of the shell, a pearl begins to form. The irritation may continue, but the pearl grows more beautiful, more lustrous, more full of light. Look to the gritty sand of your experiences, he says — for within that experience is love, and the fruit of that experience is crystallization and radiance, if you but choose it.

Near the end of the night, Latwii are asked how to become more perceptive of the needs of those around us, and their answer is the title of this episode. Penetrate the surface, they say. In your meditation, look to the heart of the interaction. Find where love lives. Find where love has sought to be known, and has for the moment gone unrecognized. That which they share with you is love seen in many disguises. Do not let disguise fool you. It is there to teach, and there is one lesson. That is love. Thank you for listening.

title: The Tapestry of Return
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the tapestry of return.

Tonight Hatonn speaks to a concern every serious seeker meets sooner or later. There are so many philosophies about how best to travel the path, and no matter how many sources you consult, there are always more — even divergent ones. So what, the seeker asks, is truly of value at this moment in the process?

His answer is not another philosophy. It is a friend. When you discover a teaching that feels like kin to you, he says, there has been a recognition upon some level of your being for that which you seek in that which has come before your attention. That harmonious feeling — that intuitive inspiration welling up from the deeper portions of your being — becomes the great ally of the seeker. For the mind can construct many magnificent structures of thought, and if you are left only with intellectual evaluation, it is easy to become confused when one philosophy sounds as good as another. And indeed, he says, this may well be true — each philosophy is a construction of a portion of the one Creator. But to discern not with the intellect but with that feeling from within, that spontaneous recognition of what is most helpful now — that is to rely upon a more trustworthy friend.

I love the metaphysics underneath it. At its heart, he says, seeking the truth is a process whereby you call for a greater portion of yourself, from yourself. Each portion of the creation is contained within each individualized expression of it. So when you seek, you seek more of what you are, from your own self. Analyze with the conscious mind, yes — but then give over the analyzing at some point, so that the greater portion of your being may move through the channel your desire has created and make itself known.

Later, Latwii are asked about something many of us have felt: people who go away and return, go away and return, like comets in their trajectories — some influences beneficial, some destructive. Picture a tapestry, they say, of many colors moving in and out, each with the other, in a rhythmic yet irregular pattern. Before the incarnation, each of you made general and specific agreements with many other seekers. During the life, there is the attempt to fulfill those agreements, to provide the lessons and services deemed necessary. So the pattern of a life finds its movement in and out of other selves who join in the rhythm of the learning and the serving.

And a small addendum, which I think is the wisest line of the night. What appears to the naked eye, they say, may not agree in essence with the appearance. What seems most helpful and harmonious may not yield the harvest of lessons that a situation which seems traumatic and frustrating might yield. For it is within the bounds of the difficulty that spiritual strength is put to the test. Thank you for listening.

title: Gentleness With Yourself
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: gentleness with yourself.

The group question tonight is a single word. Guilt. And L/Leema answer it by talking, beautifully, about identity.

Each of us is unique, they say — not a uniqueness that is attempted or worked at, but one harmonious chord of being, unique in the whole creation, infinite in its beauty, and irreplaceable. And so you sit in circle, each chord blending with each chord, as the whole group becomes one identity seeking the One which is not unique but limitless.

Then they turn to the pressures — the shoulds and musts laid on by society, family, church, and by the voices inside that sound just like them. You who are unique cannot pluck this or that pressure from yourself, they say, for you have chosen the pressures, the musts, the shoulds, and all the confusion that follows, in order to further develop your uniqueness. How could you develop without stimulus, even if the stimulus is painful? Look at the world, they say, with a kind eye, a gentle eye, a forgiving eye.

And here is the practice they recommend — one way among many, they are careful to say. Gentleness with yourself. If you can see yourself as that unique being, not threatened with extinction by any force from without or within, then perhaps you can offer yourself the gift of gentleness, patience, and kindness — by the self, to the self. Take a pressure that is causing you anguish. Turn it about in your mind. Test it. Let the uniqueness that is you impinge upon that illusion. Then, with kindness, thanking the source of the pressure, allow the self to sound its chord.

I love how unsentimental they are about the heaviness. The heaviness of the illusion is not an error, they say. There is a design. Whenever the tangle of experience becomes heavy, take your fingers from the knot and rest. Rest within the infinite invisible world which is the creation. Rest, knowing you do not have to be you by expressing or changing or doing anything. You cannot be puzzled and be active and find change helpful, they say. You can be puzzled and be silent — and find that change, development, and love bubble forth in good time, with messages you would never have developed without the seeming pressures.

Later, Latwii take up the group's other thread — sacrifice, and its old companion, guilt. What seemed to be a sacrifice made out of guilt, they say, may, as the layers of the illusion are peeled back, become a gift of love to a beloved portion of your own being. When one has worked long enough upon the concepts of sacrifice and limitation, and discovered through many experiences that what is necessary is always provided, then what was seen as sacrifice gives way to another opportunity to give freely of the infinite love available at each moment. The sacrifice becomes the honor, they say — for there is no thing as important to one as loving another. Thank you for listening.

title: Cells of One Body
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: cells of one body.

Hatonn begins tonight by answering a question nobody asked aloud — both people in the small circle were wondering whether two was enough for a good contact. One times one is two, he says — the multiplication of strength has begun, but only begins to become noticeable with the third present. And he borrows the old line: whenever two or three are gathered together in the name of the One, the strength is there. I have always loved that these vast intelligences pause to reassure two tired people in a room.

Then the teaching. Where, he asks, does it flee — this consciousness of the one original Thought that we bring from sleep and touch in our best moments? Where is it buried, so that lives are lived with the sensation of separateness and the lack of plenty? One great source of the feeling of apartness, he says, is the institution of trading money for the things the body needs to survive. There is that about money which is finite, in the heaviest illusory sense of the word. The spending of money — the bills, the budgets, the planning — is one of very many ways that lead to separation.

And yet. Look at those in your own city who are hungry this day, who have no adequate clothing for the chill. This is likely to grow, he says, as times become more confused. One does not have to look far to find ways to share. And here is the liberation: there is a great freeing in the sharing of what in the illusion seems to be what you need. It liberates an entity plunged into the illusion from the illusion — precisely insofar as the entity gives great gifts with the desire to serve the one great Self that knows no separation.

Listen to how he widens it beyond money. When is a smile stopped upon the face because an entity is plunged too far into separation to share joy? When is the young shut off from experience but when the giver feels it too expensive to spend time in merely speaking? All those about you, he says, are cells of your body — living portions of your reality. To open your heart, when done consciously, is a polarizing action, whether by the giving of money, of time, of attention, of sympathy.

Later, Latwii speak to someone passing through a strange, drifting transformation — a seeming void where the will has gone quiet. They compare it to the first movement as the mythical phoenix rises from the ashes: the being which is to be is as yet without definition. There is a void which shall draw into it the essence of the new being — an essence you yourself shall determine. Now, as the Creator, they say, it is up to you to desire. What shall you desire? Who shall you be? And the paradox they leave her with: surrender the will to the desire to serve the One, and by doing so daily, strengthen the very faculty surrendered. One receives the gift, gives it away, and receives it yet again. Thank you for listening.

title: The Eternal Beginner
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the eternal beginner.

It is the first of December, and outside the circle the harsh winds of winter are beginning. Hatonn begins there, with the weather — and then with the weather inside. There are severe patterns of internal weather too, he says, for the illusion is as dense within the mind as without, unless steps are taken. So tonight, simple principles.

There is that which is unchangeable. This is not within your presence — this is what you seek. Upon your Earth, all that you see is changeable, and all that you see within yourself may seem all too changeable and undependable. If what you seek is the unchangeable, then there must be tools to find that kingdom within the illusion. These tools, he says, are the will to know, and the faith to believe that grace will offer you what there is to know.

Then a teaching for anyone whose will has ever broken down — which is to say, everyone. When the force of will breaks down, the illusion is complete, and many things may be distorted. Worry, fear, and apprehension have a nature which subtracts positivity from the entity that harbors them. This is not for those who sleep, he says — they learn at their own pace from the catalyst itself. He speaks to those who have seized the path and named it their own. When one is overcome by the illusion, it can feel like violence to the inner self to impose affirmations and meditations upon it. So he suggests something humane: declare a period of examination. Allow the self to be, for a little while, without influence from within or without. A day, he suggests — no more. Then, when all that is observable has been observed, recall what invigorated you and sent you on the journey in the first place. It is easy to begin a journey, he says. It is difficult to retain the energy of it until one has made a complete and irreversible choice. The fidelity of will is most important.

And then the line I carried away from this session. When the air grows dark and the winter of the soul sets in, know that all seekers are ever beginners — and the simplest rules apply. Seek, and seek, and seek yet again. Do not feel you have let yourself down when you have fallen away, wrapped in overwhelming experience. Without judgment and without impatience, turn again to seeking. Cry your tears when tears are to be shed. But in the morning, turn again and begin again. Know yourself as the eternal beginner.

A gentle word, if I may. This session was spoken to people acquainted with real suffering, and it speaks of dark winters of the soul. If you are in such a winter now — and especially if you are having thoughts of harming yourself — please reach out: to someone you trust, to a counselor, to a crisis line in your country. You do not have to turn toward the seeking alone. The night ends. Thank you for listening.

title: You Never Left Home
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: you never left home.

It is early December, and Hatonn begins outside the door: the trees stand dignified in their winter clothes of bark and root, the roadside pale in the short day's dim light, the moon working its special magic. All of nature, he says, has gone home for its season of gestation and inner growth. And what of you? Each of you seeks a home. Let us go on a journey, he says, to find that most precious of all things.

So they take you traveling. First to the smallest atom, to stand within that nexus of energy and see the path of creative power, of articulated light. This is your home, he says — this is part of your home. Then away from the planet, out into the blackness, gazing back at the beautiful Earth: you are a citizen of all that there is. Then further — flung into reaches of space and time beyond any telescope, beyond any human experience. You may fall onto a planet of fire, and yet that is home. You may come upon a planet of ice, cold as absolute zero — and that is your home, your hospitable and welcoming home.

Then slowly back: the solar system, the planet, the streets of your cities. Look into the faces of your people. Look into the eyes of the man who is poor, and you see the light of home. Gaze into the eyes of a couple in love — you are still home. Exchange glances with one who lives a dark life — you are still home, for you are a citizen of the creation, part and parcel of everything that is. What must be stripped from the concept of home, he says, is all concept of physicality. Home is invisible to the physical eye. Your metaphysical home is a thing of mystery and omnipresence. You cannot leave home. There is no home to find.

I love the bluntness of what follows. Many, he says, would have no idea what he is talking about — and to those people he says: enjoy your sleep. Wake up when you wish to wake up. Let no word of ours interfere with the pleasure of your dreaming. For seeking one's spiritual home means the discipline of transformation — a transformation in thinking which eliminates limitations and makes all things in creation one great being, full of love and creative energy, whose great heart is beating and will continue to beat infinitely.

Until you look for that in you which is eternal, he says, you have not begun seeking your true home, nor earned your citizenship in the creation. And the quickest way to empower the desire to seek is meditation — for if your consciousness of yourself is that of a citizen of the creation, a co-creator with the One, how can you be so far removed by emotion from your home? The illusion may seem to take many homes away from you. In reality you have never left home. You have merely veiled part of it from yourself, so that you might come to an illusion and refine some lessons in how to love one another. Freely and gladly, he says. With a clear conscience and a pure heart. Thank you for listening.

title: Service Is Unseen
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: service is unseen.

Tonight Latwii tell a story — a long one, a patient one — and it is about judgment. Not the judgment of others. The judgment of yourself, and of what counts as a life of service.

Once there was a boy with a wise father, eager to be of service and to show through his life the love and light of the Creator. He questioned his father about every choice before him. Shall I be a soldier, to protect my country and stand for its ideals? That is a way to serve, said the father — and would say no more. Shall I be an athlete, winning hearts by my skill? That would certainly be a way to be of service. Shall I sing, and serve the many who hear my songs? The answer was the same. Exasperated at last, the son cried: shall I become a hobo, begging my living from strangers? That would be a way to be of service, said the unruffled father. Very well, said the son — I shall choose a life of crime! That, came the answer, is a way to be of service.

The young man never got his answer. He married, had children, worked hard to support his family, grew middle-aged still puzzling over his father's riddle. And then, as his body began to show the turning of the years, he felt he was beginning to understand — and went to his aged father. Father, he said, it has been the goal of my life to be of service, and yet of all the things I thought of, I did none. Instead I did what I did not comprehend or anticipate. And I believe I begin to understand.

Very good, my son, said the father. Tell me, so that I may bask in the reflection of my wisdom. Well, faltered the son — I think I have found that service is something I cannot see. Very good. What else? I believe I have begun to see that I do not see very well. Very good. What else? The son mustered his courage. Father, I believe that I am of service — and that I cannot help being of service.

Sit down, my son, said the delighted father — for now we can talk together. And he pointed to the springtime flowers. Which of those flowers is not beautiful? They are all beautiful, said the son. He pointed to several that had withered early. Do you find these beautiful? No, said the son — they are dead, they should be removed. It is time for you to consider, said his father, whether you are alive or dead. For if you are alive, you are as beautiful and fragrant as any human that dwells upon the planet. You may run a country well, you may inspire by song, you may heal, or you may feed your family. Or indeed you may do nothing. But if you are alive within yourself — if you question rather than accepting blindly — then you are precisely as beautiful as all who share your condition.

And here is Latwii's point, stated plainly. That which is action on the physical plane is illusory. That which is intended within the heart is of the spirit, and is eternal. When you leave this incarnation, you shall judge yourself — not by the effects you produced, but by your state of mind and heart. That is why there is no judgment possible among peoples. The most apparently criminal of entities can choose, under the press of experience, to turn toward the light — and be far more zealous for the good than those who never lived the darker life. There is no situation which is not also an opportunity. Thank you for listening.

title: The Timelessness of Giving
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the timelessness of giving.

It is three days before Christmas, and the circle is small, and one of its instruments is unwell — so Hatonn comes through another voice, briefly, unwilling to tire anyone. What they say in that short visit is worth the whole season.

This time on your planet, Hatonn says, is one of both celebration and inspiration. The collective subconscious of your peoples focuses upon the timelessness of giving and sharing. The giving of the one you call Christ in the past is remembered. The giving of the present is celebrated in your customs. The giving of the future is contemplated. All of it resounds harmonically — and attunes your planet to a greater receptiveness than normal to those influences which characterize service to others.

It is therefore not only a time of celebration upon your planet, Hatonn says, but among those who attempt to serve your planet as well. And then comes the line I want to hold up to the light. In giving, my friends, there is always a receiving — for such is the nature of your universe.

They turn it on themselves, with a humility that disarms me every time. We of Hatonn have attempted to share what little we had to offer, in hope our efforts might bear fruit for your group and your planet. That was our attempt to be of service to you. And yet, they say, an unexpected bounty has been reaped by those of us involved in this service — through the love and light which you yourselves have given in return to us. For this, they say, we are sincerely grateful. For the lessons you have extended to us, we are also quite grateful.

I love that — the teachers confessing they were taught. The givers confessing they received. It is the whole law of the season in miniature: no one only gives, no one only receives, and the attempt to serve is never a one-way street. Whoever you are giving to this week, and whatever you are receiving — some of it wanted, some of it not — may you feel the harmonic they describe, the past and present and future of giving all resounding at once. Thank you for listening.

title: Time Is on Your Side
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: time is on your side.

Four days after Christmas, a voice new to this stretch of the archive takes the floor. The ones called Oxal — and they have come to talk about time. About why it seems to speed up as you get older, and what, if anything, you can do about it.

Time and space, they say, have a reciprocal relationship — and are allegories of love and light. Another word for time, they suggest, is experience. And here is the crux: it only seems untrue that some moments contain more experience than others. When there is no distortion in space, each finite moment becomes a unified, cosmic moment — a thing with the properties of timelessness. It is during timeless moments, they say, that experience is seated within the seeker.

Catalyst — everything that happens to you — is given moment by moment. Look at young souls, they say, and see what can be made of the catalyst of the moment. Children, less used to wasting moments, instinctually approach each piece of catalyst as that which will become experience. But as the child grows, the fullness of catalyst begins to feel more like a burden than a pleasure. Overwhelmed, we cease processing it into experience. The space required to use one unit of time becomes distorted — time buckles and bends and shrinks, because the space with which time is paired has not room enough for the transformation.

And they mean space in a metaphysical sense, too: the spaciousness of your point of view. The room you allow for turning what comes at you into seated experience. No wonder time seems to move faster and faster, they say. Unprocessed catalyst carries over into the next unit of time, and the next, until opening yourself to the present moment takes real courage.

But listen to the other side of it. When the seeker chooses consciously to use catalyst — when you are ready to be conscious of the moment, the present moment being one with itself, full of time and equally full of space — then you have the opportunity to experience a timeless moment in which all time is one. Within this moment, they say, an infinite amount of work may be done in consciousness. The activity of meditation is a great help in reconciling catalyst with the self.

Before the night ends, Yadda slip in with their own sermon, and it is pure mischief. You are all lawyers, you people, they say. Why are you so in love with laws? Do you think that if you obey all the laws of the land, or of the church, you will be good, or capable of advancing into knowledge of the truth? There is no truth in that which is finite, they say, for every law is made to be broken. There is something called faith which defeats all laws. Your path is your law, they say — personal, intimate, found only as a product of the faith that there is a truth beyond all that you see and hear. Close the cookbook, shut up the mind, and wait in faith.

And then, with something like a wink, Oxal note the first line of a popular song running through the instrument's mind: time is on your side. This is very true, they say. May you use your time — and find timelessness. Thank you for listening.

title: Permission to Rest
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: permission to rest.

The new year has just turned, and Hatonn meets the circle with unusual tenderness. He speaks tonight for the seeker who is tired — not the beginner full of fire, but the one whose feet are dusty and whose staff has grown heavy.

As the seeker gazes down at the dusty road, he says, at the dust upon his feet and sandals, he may well doubt the road and the promise of the journey. The staff meant to aid becomes heavy. The few belongings become a burden. And so the seeker sometimes steps off the dusty path into a beautiful valley — a meadow, well-watered, forested, full of small animals and sweet flowers. It is good, Hatonn says, for the seeker to rest there. To go upon the journey is to become terribly vulnerable — to risk all for no obvious reward. When the burden becomes too heavy, it is good for the seeker to choose his own pasture and measure his own time of recovery.

It is acceptable and laudable, he says — I want you to hear how deliberate those words are — for a seeker overborne by experience not only to rest beneath the tree but to fell great trees, dry the wood, and build a cabin for shelter. There is no shame in resting until the burden again becomes as nothing, and seeking fills the soul and mind and the will. It is not recommended, he says, that the seeker goad himself as if he were an ox or a mule. The spiritual path is narrow, and the difficulty of walking it is various for each entity. It is not a path to be walked when the will is not strong.

But there is a danger in the resting, and he names it honestly: the temptation to feel that the cabin and the meadow are the end of the path. In an infinite journey, he says, there are pauses between learning experiences — but never the full stop where you lie back and say, now I understand, now redemption is complete. There is always the next learning. So rest as long as is necessary, he says — but do not allow your spirit surcease from silence.

And here is the sentence I will carry from this session. Beyond words and concepts there is the one original Thought which is love — which cannot be defined, but which can be praised and shared, not by words, but by the quality of silence between two seekers. For companionship lies between the words, the sentences, the talking and the doing. Spiritual companionship lies in the resting that one silence may give to another. You are always alone, he says, and never alone. Always alone, in that your path and your perception are unique. Never alone, in that entities both incarnate and discarnate share the intensity of your seeking, and are closer to you than many of your thoughts. For silence is more intimate than any word.

Later in the evening Yadda arrive, as they do, with mischief and a pointed question: why families? Families are difficult, they admit — a pain in the neck, in their words. But with family you cannot say, you are not family, go away. You have to take care of each other. And that, they say, is the lesson: duty and honor. Service, not because it is always fun, but because service is freedom. If you choose not to serve, you have stopped your progress.

So build your cabin when you need it. Judge yourself not if you must pause by the way, or even build a hut against the winter of your flagging faith. Live through those times, blaming not yourself and not the path. Rest — and let the silence do its work. Thank you for listening.

title: The Star of Hope
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the star of hope.

Tonight a new voice enters the archive. The instrument hears something like "Ku-ohl" — and the contact resolves into the name Q'uo: a Confederation source speaking, they say, from the density this instrument calls wisdom. They are candid about being new at this, and about being fallible. What they offer is a teaching on service — and it begins in darkness.

Service to others, they say, is not an end product of meditation itself. Then they ask you to see yourself as earth and water — the vehicle and its elements, and the metaphysical waters of the deeper mind. When the seeker first sets foot on the path, the seeker invites the great seed of consciousness — and metaphysically speaking, you are in darkness. It is within this darkness that you seek knowledge of love, of light, and of unity.

I love how unhurried this image is. Much of understanding, they say, comes from seeking within the darkness of inner vision — this is seeking unmanifested. The only light visible to the seeker is like the light of the night sky: the stars, the reflected light of the moon. Metaphysically speaking, they say, that star is called hope — or faith. It is not a light which ameliorates the darkness. It is a signal. A sign that light there is, and light abundant.

Then the bridge — and the paradox. There is a bridge between the darkness of hope, faith, and will, and the noonday sun of manifested service. That bridge, they say, is the surrender of the very will the seeker has been marshaling. For in the attempt to be of service lies the implicit seed of failure to be of service. The harder the seeker attempts to be of service, the less chance of being led by inspiration to right service — service that leads toward harmony and the feeling of kinship with the one served. The full light of day dawns, they say, as the seeker sincerely and completely yields itself to grace.

Listen to how carefully they frame the yielding. They are not suggesting a force outside the seeker to whom you must yield control. The Creator is far closer than that — indeed, they say, the daylight is within the heart of the darkness. The difficulty is that words cause paradox, and the deeper the understanding, the more plentiful the paradoxes. So: begin seeking in darkness, and when you come from your sanctified ground wishing to give glory back to the Creator — who appears to you in the guise of other entities — yield your conscious will, utterly and completely, to a higher knowledge, a higher wisdom, a higher compassion.

One who has yielded, they say, and moves in rhythm with the deep winds about the innermost self, becomes touched with radiance — a radiance completely positive, the analog of your sun body. And in that radiance lies manifested service. So worry not about how to serve, they say. Be disciplined as the earth and water within you become more articulated, and the star of hope becomes ever more central in your inner sky. And when the moment comes to move from meditation to action — yield yourself, again and again, to that great fiery strength which is the property of higher will. Thank you for listening.

title: The Water of Life
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the water of life.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story — told through two instruments trading passages back and forth — about a young man who leaves home to find what is missing. It is one of the longest parables in this stretch of the archive, and one of the most quietly devastating.

There was once a young man who, while young in years and strong of body, determined to make a journey out into the world and seek his fortune. The small community of his raising moved at a slow, steady pace — secure, grounding, but not sufficient for his yearning spirit. So he left, with few possessions and no map, for his concept of freedom suggested no reliance on any plan. He signed onto a great ship bound for places with exotic names. Ports flashed by. Then, restless again, he went ashore in a far land — mountains circled with clouds, valleys rich and lush, nut-brown people who welcomed him not as a stranger, for in that land there was no concept of that word.

He sat at the feet of those he considered wise. He walked through valleys thick with fog, the sun refracted in a million tiny sparks. And slowly a puzzlement grew in him — for had he not seen trees and fog and light in his own birthplace? These experiences were not new, and yet their effect upon him was new. For the first time, he began to ponder the meaning of the cycles that produced such simple miracles. The people of this land moved to a rhythm not unlike the one he had left — and yet here, for the first time, he noticed the center of things.

Why, he wondered, had he traveled so far to see things that, on close examination, seemed so like his home — yet only here began to see beyond the surface? At the next village he stopped a young woman and demanded, in so many words: what is it that you know? She laughed, and put down what she was carrying, and went to the well, and pumped him a cupful of water. What do you see, she said. Water, he said. Mere water. Only water, in a cup.

And here is her answer — the heart of the whole long story. To one, she said, the water in this cup may be mere water, good for quenching the thirst of the moment. To another, the water may be the symbol of that which is greater than any moment, and which gives birth to each moment. For within the water of life do we all not move and have our being? If that is so, the young man protested, why have I come so far to do this simple thing, which could have been done anywhere — which never required leaving home at all?

Listen to her reply, for it is the moral Hatonn spent an entire evening building toward. You seek not that which is other than yourself, or far distant from yourself, she said, but that which is within yourself. The world about you will help you by showing you that which beats at the heart of all creation. When you learn to look beyond seasons and cycles and sameness, you will find your quest lies not in things or places or people — no matter how distant, exotic, or interesting — but within your heart of hearts. And this goes by many names, she said, but I will share with you mine: it is love, beating with a rhythm known to any heart.

The young man returned to the land of his youth — and found the feeling of newness had come with him. His eyes looked upon a new world, no longer bounded by the surface of things. Breathe in the new, Hatonn says in closing. Breathe out the old. See, taste, touch, hear — and love that which is holy. And know that you are in love with the universe, and all that lies within it. Thank you for listening.

title: The Power of Forgiveness
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the power of forgiveness.

Tonight's story is told through two instruments, with pauses and restarts and one instrument honestly admitting he has lost the thread — and Hatonn praising him for the integrity of saying so. The story that finally comes through is about a young woman who had everything, and could not understand why.

She was quite sure of herself and her abilities. She conversed easily with peers and elders, solved new problems, managed her affairs — success, in the terms of her day, at her feet. Her mind moved quickly from social acceptance and career success to a more abstract discomfort: why had her life unfolded with such ease, when so many around her struggled for a fraction of what she reaped? It is not acceptable to me, she said to herself, that there should be such disparity between my good fortune and others' ill luck. Who am I to have been born under such a fortunate star?

She had no teacher — those who tried to teach her could not move as quickly as she, so she became the teacher and the teacher the pupil. And then she was granted the wish she did not know she had. Another young woman, of a different creed and color, joined the company where she worked — her equal in competence, her superior, perhaps, in the one quality the first woman lacked. To this new friend she carried her ponderings about the unfairness of life, her great good fortune, her power, and others' lack of it.

Her friend gazed at her, smiling very slightly. Girl, she said, you are working so hard to pat yourself upon the back within the illusion that you have forgotten what power really is. What do you mean, asked the young woman. Do you think power is money? Position? Great intelligence? That is the way the world measures power, she said — and that is why the world is so unfair.

Then the lesson, staged as a small confession. Last week, said her friend, I cut in front of another car driving to work. I did not stop to see if there was damage to the other car. What do you think of that? The young woman shrugged — that sort of thing happens all the time. Then do you forgive me, said her friend. If you need to be forgiven, yes, I forgive you. Aha, said her friend. Now you are exercising power. Do you forgive those who kill and are put in prison? Would you set them free today? No, said the young woman — the streets would not be safe. Ah, said her friend. You have not forgiven. And so they are bound in chains by your power — for if you do not forgive, then there shall be no forgiveness.

I do not buy that, said the young woman. What can my opinion be worth? And her friend's answer is the thesis of the night. The hardness of your heart or its softness, its compassion — these are all in all. There is no power for justice greater than the opinion you hold within the silence of your own mind. As you open your heart, so you exhibit power for that which is beautiful and good. As you harden your heart, so your denial becomes law, binding those whom you would bind. Yours is the ultimate power — yours and mine and all peoples.

Dwelling upon your great good fortune will get you nowhere, literally, her friend tells her — for when you accept the illusion and see life as a game to win or lose, you become imprisoned by that which is not. And Hatonn's closing widens it to all of us: reconsider, if you need to, your good fortune. Use whatever seeming advantages you have to list what is of the illusion — and then find, for yourself, what is not. As your heart warms and becomes soft and radiant, as you forgive, as you give up yourself — so shall your seeking produce great fruit. And remember, they say: you too must be the object of your forgiveness.

Thank you for listening.

title: A City of Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: a city of light.

This is an evening about togetherness. The ones who call themselves Monka are asked, what makes a spiritual community actually work? And they begin somewhere you might not expect. Not with rules, but with freedom.

Freedom is the hallmark of successful community, they say. Freedom to be yourself. Freedom to experiment, to make mistakes, to be at risk, and to grow. I love that line about risk, because so many groups that claim to seek the truth ask you to surrender the very strangeness that makes you worth knowing. Monka asks for the opposite. Hold the deeper currents that brought you together, they say, and at the same time be militantly aware of the individual tides in each person. Let each be each.

And then they turn the question inside out. Community begins with one entity, they say. You yourself are the first community. Think of it. You are a digest, an amalgamation of many and sometimes conflicting experiences, ideas, opinions, and goals. You have to harmonize the self with the self before you can harmonize one self with another. And it is easiest to see, in your own case, how quickly the light dims when you lean on analysis alone, without contact with that infinite source of intelligence which is love, available from within, in the silence of the heart.

From there, they move to joy, and they are honest about its limits. Happiness is real, companionship is real, but they are transient. To expect a community to supply you with happiness is unrealistic. Not because happiness is scorned. It is to be savored. But to cling to one happiness is to lose another. They give an image I cannot shake. Laughing too long at one jest, you may fail to hear the next cause for laughter.

So what holds a community together, if not shared happiness? Two things, shared regularly. The food and drink which are symbolic of so many other necessary foods, for the soul, for the mind, for the heart. And the coming together in meditation, in thankfulness, in praise. Monka says that great ideas without perseverance, a sense of humor, and the light touch will dim. If each person brings a light, those lights together form a great light. A city of light, in the metaphysical sense.

There is also a warning in here, gently given. When you give of yourself in community, give freely and in joy, but without diminishing yourself, and without diminishing those over whom you may have undue influence. Influence is the shadow side of community. The antidote they suggest is exaggerated respect for each person's freedom in spiritual seeking.

I want to note one more thing Monka says about why community matters beyond the people in the room. The coming together of entities to form spiritual community is an event, they say. And the event causes a message. That message is heard by those whom you do not know and can never know, and it allows transformation among others. So before joining together, let the overriding goals be grasped in a unified manner, and let some form of ritual for the remembrance of that goal sit at the very heart of the community. Not taken for granted. Remembered, surrendered to, again and again.

Monka closes with a benediction that sounds like a wish for all of us. May you be one. May you be one, my children. And may you love each other, serve each other, and cause your events to serve as a message that will aid others who are seeking their own ways.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Beacon Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the beacon within.

Tonight's session opens with the ones who call themselves Q'uo, and they want to talk about love. But at first it will not sound like love at all, because they begin with phenomena. Astrology. Tarot. Prophecy. Channeling itself.

They are not here to discredit any of it. There is validity in these arts, they say. But they want to look at what happens between the one who gives information and the one who receives it. A talent for phenomena, they say, is not a sign of spiritual advancement. It is more like being a world-class pianist. It means you have spent more than one incarnation developing that characteristic. Phenomena, they say, and I love the bluntness of this line, is another way of saying things.

And here is the turn. It would be a poor argument indeed to debate the possibility that spiritual advancement is aided by things. The spiritual stance cannot depend upon any thing. Dependence upon anything outside the self denies the self the greatest opportunity for learning there is, and that is the untutored and unbiased circumstance. Your instantaneous reaction, your action in the face of circumstance, that is where the opportunity lies.

Listen to how they put it when they turn to the seeker directly. Neither walking for peace for many months, nor giving all that you have to the poor, nor any great sacrifice, will necessarily make you progress spiritually. Turn from the outside manifestations. Turn from your own opinion of yourself, your own judgment of the fruits of your labors, and from any prophecy about your probable future. And instead join the great darkness of the sea of mystery.

This is the passage the whole evening is built around. You cannot see or hear or feel or taste or smell anything in this darkness. The path is narrow because it is only the span of footsteps. There is no luggage. There is no rest, and there is no turning back. Why do you think the spiritual path is so narrow? If it needed to be wider, it would be.

And yet. Within the darkness that is complete lies your heart, beating without sound, gleaning that light as you intensify and intensify your seeking, to the point at which your inner beating heart is manifested as the star of hope, the beacon of faith. At that point, Q'uo says, you can see the star. That is all you can see. It does not shed light upon your path. But it is yours, kindled within your heart and within no other. Walk on in majesty. Walk on in humility. Walk on in trust.

Then the closing of the discourse, which is almost a plea. What a treasure your hearts are when they love. I beg you to love. It does not matter that you do not love perfectly, or that you do not love all the time. What matters is that you see your inner state of love as the cornerstone of your existence, your seeking, your destiny. For this universe is one thing and one thing only. It is love.

Later in the evening, Latwii takes questions, and one answer belongs here too. Asked how to know when a change has been thought about enough and should be left alone, they say this. Early on the path, guidance comes like a two-by-four between the eyes. But as the seeker matures, the signs grow subtler, so that the faculty of free will might be enhanced. You may be better advised to look within your own being for that still, small voice, which when consulted gives the answers most appropriate for you at that time.

So the evening holds together after all. Put down the things. Walk the narrow path in darkness. And trust the star you kindled yourself.

Thank you for listening.

title: Seeds in Barren Soil
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: seeds in barren soil.

Hatonn begins this evening with doubt. Not the dramatic kind. The ordinary kind that visits you on a Tuesday. And he suggests something you may not have considered. That doubt may be the child of abundance.

Look at what your peoples have, he says. Shelters from the elements. Clothing. Food. Relationships. Means of communication. Work and leisure to focus your attention. Paths by which a seeker may find the Creator. Yes, you have all these things in great abundance. And yet, he says, it is this very abundance of things, of ideas, of groups, of possibilities and opportunities, that provides the basis for much confusion and doubt. With such great variety, how do you decide, in each particular instance, what is the most appropriate choice?

And then he takes you into the daily round. You have been there. The misunderstanding with a fellow being. The intention was pure, the gift was given freely, and yet the result was disharmony. The harsh word. The cold silence. The heart wounded, the mind confused. And you walk away wondering, where was the missed step?

Listen to what Hatonn does with this. He asks you to adopt a different attitude toward the disharmonious relationship, the angry word, the shriveled silence. What you have, he says, is not so much the missed opportunity as a renewed opportunity for that which seems lost. When you have known the smoothly functioning relationship, the joy of sharing time and words, you are living on the fruit of a harvest completed. And now you may move into a new experience. Another opportunity to plant a seed of love.

This is the image I want you to carry. Take what has been completed and move into the barren field. Plant the seed of love there. Nurture it with will and faith, with perseverance, with the kind gesture, the loving word, the respectful attitude. Watch it take root. It may be a great portion of time before the seed sends a shoot into the light of your daily experience, and an even greater portion before it bears fruit. Yet is this not what each of you has come to do?

I love how practical he makes it. If you look upon the purpose of your incarnation not as experiencing love but as discovering and nurturing love where it has not been, then the daily round becomes far more acceptable. Where you find yourself in your daily round is where you have planted yourself, so that you might tend the field in the most loving fashion that you may. It is not so much your ability to change those about you that matters, he says, as your ability to look upon those about you in a new way. To give acceptance and love as freely as you are given the air you breathe.

And there is a promise at the end, plainly spoken. The one Creator is simplicity itself. There is no place beyond your reach where love may be hidden that you may not find it. Persevere, he says.
